News.title: My evil dad raped me in blind rage – then I was sick & horror reality dawned… mum’s reaction made it so much worse
News.content:
Next

AGED just 13, Allison was curled up by the fireplace when her father came home in a blind rage and raped her.

A few weeks later, she was talking with friends at the playground when she passed out and woke up covered in her own vomit. She soon realised she was pregnant.





Brave Allison Siddall, now 60, says she was forced to undergo an abortion without even understanding what it was.

As she sobbed to her mum and confided in her about the horror ordeal, she kicked Allison out in disbelief.

The mum-of-five is now speaking out and waiving her right to anonymity after her evil biological dad Clive Siddall, 81, was locked up – more than 40 years after he committed his sick crimes.

He was only caught after she sought medical help for drinking problems and confided in her doctor about the trauma of her rape.

In July, Clive was jailed for 12 years after being found guilty of one count of rape, one count of indecent assault on a girl under the age of 16, and four counts of indecent assault on a girl under the age of 14.

Speaking after the sentencing, Allison said: “It is still haunting me now. I am grateful that he is locked away, I really am.





“I just want to know why he would do this to me. He is an evil man.”

Allison says she was aged 13 when her mum packed her a bag and told her that she would be going to live with her father.

He came to pick her up and she moved in with him, his wife, and his two children, in Walton-on-Thames, Surrey.

She says life was normal for the first few months, with Siddall barely home – until one day when Allison was left at the house alone.

Allison was asleep in the living room when the brute attacked her, pinning her down and using his hand to stop her screaming.

She said: “He came home in a mood, and he took it out on me. He did the unthinkable, and he ruined my life completely. Even to this day, I still remember it like it was yesterday.”

“I was covered in bruises and there was lots of blood. It was a good few hours before I actually moved.”

Allison continued with normal life afterwards and went to school the next morning, not truly understanding what had happened.

But later, when she passed out on the playground, Siddall took her to see a doctor and she was informed that she was pregnant.

She added: “The doctor said I was pregnant and I didn’t understand how it had happened. I couldn’t comprehend it at all.



“I ran out of the doctor’s room crying my eyes out. Clive dragged me back in shouting that I needed an abortion. I didn’t even know what that was.”

After the abortion, she was taken back to her mum’s house where she cried and told her what happened – but claims her mum didn’t believe her.

Allison says her mum kicked her out as they disapproved of the abortion and didn’t believe what had caused the pregnancy.

She said: “No one spoke to me. No one asked me anything. It took me a few days to get the courage up to say something.

“I just wanted someone to talk to, someone to understand, someone to let me know what was going on and what had happened.

“My mum went absolutely ballistic. She thought I was a bad person. I tried to explain to her that it was Clive but she wouldn’t believe me.”

Allison went on to have five children.

She is still severely traumatised and says she has nightmares every day of the rape – and even attempted to take her own life.

She became anorexic, dropping to around six stone in weight, and used alcohol to numb her pain.

The mum says she was drinking around one box of wine – the equivalent of up to four bottles – a night.



Allison had always dreamed of becoming a nurse, but says this was also ruined by Siddall, as she was never able to return to school.

She struggles to let people close and says she has “destroyed” every friendship a few months in.

Allison said: “When I had my first glass of wine, I found that it numbed the pain, and I continued down that line.

“It was a blackout to make me forget and not have the nightmares. I can’t form a relationship, so I am just alone.”

Things came to a head four years ago when Allison sought help for the alcoholism, and her doctor reported the rape to police.

Officers came to her door and she told them everything that happened.

According to Surrey Police, when interviewed, Clive Siddall responded “not true”, and “no way” to the allegations put to him.

He was charged in April 2024 with one count of rape, one count of indecent assault on a girl under the age of 16, and four counts of indecent assault on a girl under the age of 14.

Following a trial at Kingston Crown Court in March, a jury found him guilty of all six offences.

Siddall, formerly of Oxted, Surrey, was sentenced at Guildford Crown Court on July 14 to 12 years in prison.



Though relieved to see him behind bars, Allison says she feels guilty that she hadn’t been able to get him convicted sooner – and fears her monster dad my have hurt other girls.

She said: “I wish I had done this years ago. Back then nobody listened or really cared.

“I feel a tremendous amount of guilt because if I was stronger back then I could have pushed someone to help.”

You're Not Alone EVERY 90 minutes in the UK a life is lost to suicide It doesn’t discriminate, touching the lives of people in every corner of society – from the homeless and unemployed to builders and doctors, reality stars and footballers. It’s the biggest killer of people under the age of 35, more deadly than cancer and car crashes. And men are three times more likely to take their own life than women. Yet it’s rarely spoken of, a taboo that threatens to continue its deadly rampage unless we all stop and take notice, now. News.title: One dead and seven injured after driver plows car into crowded restaurant
News.content:
DINER HORROR One dead and seven injured after driver plows car into crowded restaurant







Next

ONE person has been killed and seven injured after a driver drove into a crowded restaurant on Saturday morning.

The driver, identified as a 93-year-old woman, plowed into brunch diners eating on the terrace at Meg’s Grill in Lavallette, New Jersey, just after 11am.

Lavallette Police believe the driver had been trying to park when they hit the gas pedal instead of the brakes, sending the Buick Encore crashing into the eatery.



The vehicle went through the outdoor eating area and into the building.



A 56-year-old woman from Toms River was killed at the scene, News 12 New Jersey reported.

The driver sustained minor injuries and all other victims were taken to hospital.

Their conditions and extent of their injuries are not known at this time.

News.title: Royal Navy pilot, 31, killed when helicopter crashed into Channel ‘after commander mistakenly switched off two engines’
News.content:
CHOPPER TRAGEDY Royal Navy pilot, 31, killed when helicopter crashed into Channel ‘after commander mistakenly switched off two engines’







Next

A ROYAL Navy pilot died in a helicopter crash after his commander mistakenly switched off two working engines during a night training exercise, an inquiry has found.

Lieutenant Rhodri Leyshon, 31, plunged into the English Channel when the Merlin helicopter lost all power off the Dorset coast on September 4, 2024.



The tragedy unfolded as the aircraft operated alongside the aircraft carrier HMS Queen Elizabeth.

An investigation has now found that a series of errors left the crew fighting to keep the helicopter in the air.



At 8.46pm, a rubber component inside one of the Merlin’s three engines split, causing it to spiral out of control.

Warnings flashed up in the cockpit but failed to identify which engine was affected.

The crew mistakenly believed the other two engines had failed, prompting the commander to switch them off.

The decision was made without the required confirmation from a second crew member.



The remaining faulty engine then revved so violently that its safety system shut it down.

The aircraft was suddenly left without any engine power and plunged into the sea.

The impact snapped off the tail and flipped the helicopter upside down.

While the commander and an aircrewman managed to escape, Lt Leyshon was seriously injured and unable to get out.

A rescue operation was then hampered by a series of further failures.



A senior officer aboard HMS Queen Elizabeth ordered a second Merlin to prepare for the rescue without realising it had no winch.

The aircraft could only hover over the wreckage as survivors remained stranded in the water.

The carrier’s main rescue boat was also unable to launch because of a sensor fault affecting its crane.

A second boat was eventually deployed, setting off at around 9.02pm.

The two surviving crew members were pulled from the water, but Lt Leyshon was not found for almost two hours.



He was later pronounced dead in hospital.

His devastated mother, Mary Scourfield, said: “I know that he would have done everything within his power to get the helicopter back.

“It is therefore heartbreaking to see that he was put into this situation.”

The inquiry found that the crew had initially planned to land on the moving carrier, a manoeuvre investigators said would “almost certainly” have succeeded.

The inquiry made 44 recommendations covering engine maintenance, cockpit warnings, pilot training, rescue equipment and crash survivability.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Lt Leyshon’s father, Tim, said: “We believe that he was let down by people and systems beyond his control.”

Colonel Mark Johnson, commanding officer of the Commando Helicopter Force, described Lt Leyshon as a “consummate professional and a shining light with a bright future”.

News.title: New 3.2million sq ft ‘masterplan’ in UK’s ‘poshest’ area is revealed with new riverside homes and shops
News.content:
Next

A NEW 3.2million sq ft “masterplan” for the next phase of development at an iconic UK attraction has been revealed.

The plans will see commercial, residential and cultural venues built on the riverside neighbourhood.



Battersea Power Station could be set to see the continuation of its major development as architects have submitted plans for its next phase.

The original masterplan debuted over 15 years ago, but has now been updated by Studio Egret West and submitted to Wandsworth Council by the Battersea Power Station Development Company (BPSDC).



The revamped proposals include plans for up to 3.2million sq ft of residential, commercial and leisure space that will complete the second half of the development

Its revision follows feedback given at a public consultation this summer with the new plan said to reflect how people work and spend their time.

Plans for the remaining 16 acres of the neighbourhood will include a range of commercial spaces, new housing, cultural and leisure venues.

Buildings are set to be constructed as smaller clusters, rather than larger development blocks, and will be encircled by a network of streets, laneways, courtyards and passages.

Sightlines also form part of the plans, so residents and visitors can have a direct view of the power station.

The proposal also includes a new cultural venue dubbed the “Third Generator” set to bring together the arts, music, fashion, food, education and sport.



Work has already begun on Prospect Place South which will bring 300 new homes, 65,000 sq ft of commercial space and a community hub to the site.

It will also see the completion of the pedestrianised high street Electric Boulevard.

James Saunders, CEO of BPSDC, said: “The last decade has seen events like Covid-19 and digital integration into everyday life blur the boundaries between work, living and leisure time, all fundamentally changing how we interact with cities.

“Responding to this, our refreshed masterplan seeks to place community and connection at the core of Battersea Power Station.

“From green spaces, to expanding London’s cultural scene, championing business innovation, creating new homes and delivering thousands of new jobs, our proposals for the next chapter of Battersea Power Station will build upon our existing successes and create a future-proofed neighbourhood that London can be proud of.”



David West, founding director at Studio Egret West, said: “The revised masterplan builds on the success of the first half of the Battersea Power Station story, creating opportunities for more homes, workplaces, retail and leisure including a new hybrid cultural venue.

“The future phases will be more permeable, inclusive and intriguing, with an expanded network of playful, artistic and biodiverse public spaces.

“The refreshed vision is also deliberately flexible, leaving room for serendipity, while remaining responsive and resilient to what we’ve learned from the journey so far. It’s about commerce, culture, community and curiosity working in harmony.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The council are set to make a decision on the new masterplan proposal at a later date.

The area is known to be one of UK’s ‘poshest’ areas with celebrities and royals calling it home and even a local corner ship selling wine for over £3,000.

News.title: Nearly 100 can’t return to homes after ‘deliberate’ fire leaves seafront hotel ‘unsafe’ – as pictures reveal devastation
News.content:
Next

A HUGE blaze at a seafront hotel has forced nearly 100 people from their homes amid fears the building is “unsafe” – as shocking images reveal the devastation.

Fire crews descended on the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone, Kent on Saturday with cops suspecting the fire may have been started deliberately.



Kent Fire Service said it is believed the inferno started in the basement of the property as 26 fire engines raced to the scene in the early hours.

Around 280 guests and hotel staff were evacuated with local residents warned to avoid the area and to “close all windows and doors”.



Dramatic images show the devastation inflicted on the hotel with charred rubble seen strewn across the floor along with blackened walls and hanging debris.

Burnt out cars were also pictured in the basement and lined up outside the venue after the flames tore through the lower levels of the building.

Now, the local council has been forced to evacuate 90 residents from nearby Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace.

It follows safety inspectors’ concerns that the intensity of the fire at the hotel weakened the building’s structure, Folkestone and Hythe District Council said.



Folkestone’s housing team is working to arrange alternative housing for affected residents while the hotel undergoes further assessments and any required works to make it safe.

Chief executive Susan Priest said on Saturday evening: “This has been an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes.

“The extent of support of organisations including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks.”

Emergency services swooped on the hotel at around 1am on Saturday with 26 fire engines on the scene at the height of the incident.

Fire crews wearing breathing apparatus battled the blaze as shocking photos showed flames bursting from the underground level of the hotel with black smoke pouring into the air.



The hotel overlooks Folkestone’s harbour and has 550 rooms, according to the Britannia Hotels website.

A number of guests were assessed by paramedics at the scene with one taken to hospital with minor injuries – no other injuries have been reported.

Levi Shaw, 19, told The Sun he was staying on the 10th floor of the hotel with his girlfriend and two friends at the time, calling it an “absolutely terrifying experience”.



“We had a lovely day and then when we got to settling down at 1am, we were awakened by the fire alarm and red flashing lights.”

The teen said they were “rushed out of bed” and evacuated away from the smoke.

He said: “We sat down on the wall near the fountains and every so often all we heard as a bang, then saw a huge orange flames where I’m guessing multiple cars set alight.”

“The police, fire and hotel staff were all amazing and got everyone out as quick as possible”.

Kent Police released a statement on Saturday evening saying they were treating the blaze as “suspicious” as detectives appeal for information.



“Enquiries into the circumstances are underway and officers now believe the fire may have been caused deliberately,” the force said.

Meanwhile, Kent Fire and Rescue service said this morning that “operations are now complete” but road closures remain in place.

A spokesperson for Britannia Hotels Group said: “We are fully co-operating with Kent Police and supporting their investigation into the circumstances surrounding the fire.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We remain in close contact with all relevant authorities and will provide any assistance or information required as their inquiries continue. In the meantime, the safety and wellbeing of our guests and team members remains our priority.”

Anyone who may have witnessed the incident or might have relevant CCTV or dashcam footage from the area, particularly from 10pm on Friday to 12.30am on Saturday, is urged to call Kent Police on 01843 222289 quoting 46/155727/26.

News.title: Thousands of foreign criminals remain in the UK FIVE years after they should have been deported
News.content:
STILL HERE Thousands of foreign criminals remain in the UK FIVE years after they should have been deported







Next

NEARLY 7,000 foreign criminals who should have been deported from the UK are still living in the country FIVE YEARS after they were released from prison.

Fresh figures obtained by The Sun reveal the number of overseas offenders still in Britain more than half a decade after they should have been removed has doubled in just four years.

Under new laws, any non-British or non-Irish citizen sentenced to at least 12 months’ imprisonment in the UK is subject to automatic deportation.



But many foreign offenders released back into the community then appeal against their deportation by claiming a breach to their right to a family life under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).



A Freedom of Information response reveals 6,945 foreign criminals who are subject to deportation remain on Britain’s streets more than five years after their custodial sentence ended.

That figure has doubled since 2022, up from 3,460, according to previous Home Office figures.



Hundreds are suspected to have exploited delays in their deportations by putting down roots in the UK, which makes it much more difficult for them to be removed after marrying or having children born and brought up in Britain.

In 2025, it was revealed Albanian criminal Klevis Disha appealed his deportation by claiming it would be “unduly harsh” as his son “did not eat the type of chicken nuggets available abroad.”

Meanwhile, it was revealed last month that a Romanian national, known only as Mr Hirtie, was convicted of wounding with intent, and sentenced to 39 months imprisonment.



But he also avoided deportation on Article 8 grounds because of the ‘psychological impact’ separation would have on his partner.

Other overseas offenders claim they will suffer inhumane or degrading treatment in their home country if they were returned.

Nigerian criminal Gift Oladele successfully fought a deportation case on human rights grounds after he was jailed for a sexually motivated attack in 2022.

The 24-year-old was allowed to remain in Britain but then went on to rape a teenager on her way home from a night out in Wrexham just two years later.

Oladele was jailed for 17 years in April 2026.



The Sun also exposed a Jamaican rapist who said he did not know having sex with a sleep woman was wrong, could not be deported because he claimed he would be targeted in his native country for being bisexual.

The 41-year-old man was branded a “danger to the community” by the Home Office, but a judge ruled that he allowed to stay in the country on the basis of his sexuality.

Our probe also found a further 5,002 foreign criminals remain living in the community after leaving prison between 2 – 5 years ago.



And another 5,433 overseas offenders are back on the streets after being released up to two years ago.

Recent Home Office data shows that 21,294 offenders are still living in the UK despite facing deportation in June 2026. That figure has more than tripled in a decade from 5,928 in June 2016.

Chris Philp MP, Shadow Home Secretary, said: “Foreign criminals living in our communities should be deported.

“Every foreign criminal we cannot deport is someone who could threaten the community. We have seen near-daily stories of vile and heinous crimes being committed by foreign criminals.

“The public are furious that we cannot deport those with no right to be here, and they are right to be furious. That is why the next Conservative Government will leave the ECHR so we rapidly remove foreign criminals.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

A government spokesperson said: “Over 11,700 foreign criminals including murderers and rapists have been removed since the last election.

“Any foreign national who receives a prison sentence in the UK is referred for deportation at the earliest opportunity and will be barred from ever returning.”

News.title: Where on earth is Samba? How UK’s beloved escaped capybara has evaded capture for 6 MONTHS dodging drones & sniffer dogs
News.content:
Next

SEARCH teams have scoured rivers, sent up thermal-imaging drones and called in sniffer dogs – but despite their best efforts, the hunt for the UK’s most infamous escapee has now entered its sixth month.

There have been more than 150 reported sightings of the four-legged fugitive – whose disappearance has made headlines across the globe.



Samba, a one-year-old capybara, vanished from Marwell Zoo on March 17.

Her disappearance has seen her earn celebrity status and inspire an entirely new genre of internet memes.



These include hilarious AI-generated pictures of Samba riding bikes, eating Nando’s, attending football matches and travelling on planes.

In a Houdini-esque manoeuvre, she broke out through a small gap in her temporary enclosure alongside her sister, Tango.

But while Tango bottled the escape, Samba managed to evade keepers, before setting off into the Hampshire countryside.

Punters at a pub quiz in nearby Owslebury couldn’t believe their eyes when they saw the world’s largest rodent saunter past the following day.



And by the end of the first week, there were numerous sightings of Samba, with search teams supported by drones and sniffer dogs.

A dog walker spotted her relaxing on the banks of the River Itchen in the Colden Common area, a couple of miles from the popular zoo.



Several seconds of mobile phone footage shows Samba sunning herself, before the elusive semi-aquatic herbivore plunges into the water.

Capybaras are capable of holding their breath for up to five minutes and can reach speeds of roughly 20mph on foot.

Marwell Wildlife chief executive Laura Read is said to have spotted the rodent in dense foliage less than 24 hours later.

Camera traps were then installed in the Twyford area, roughly three miles from Samba’s home.



The Sun joined the search for Samba several days later, sending reporter Eleanor, who had been armed with binoculars and a large net.

But even we couldn’t find the South American critter, which have been known to grow to more than 5ft and weigh 12st.

Zoo spokeswoman Sarah Berry said at the time: “The biggest risks she faces are people and roads.



“She has plenty of fresh water, vegetation to eat and places to find shelter and rest.

“She would be fine until next winter, but we are obviously doing everything we can to retrieve her as soon as possible.”

Another possible sighting on the river sparked excitement on April 23, but it was not confirmed to be Samba.



A fortnight later, another camera trap was installed along Highbridge Road, which stretches over the body of water.

By May, Marwell confirmed it had received some 150 potential sightings of the runaway rodent -most of which turned out to be muntjac deer.

The zoo later sent out dozens of staff to look for footprints and droppings in the Brambridge area after a number of alleged sightings in June.

In July, Ripple – a seven-year-old capybara – arrived at Marwell, sending shockwaves across the country.

The plant-munching creature had been transferred from Blackpool Zoo.



But Marwell insisted Ripple was not a replacement for Samba – and confirmed the search was still ongoing.

And, just last month, photographic evidence of Samba in the wild was sent to keepers.

The lead was described as “very promising”.

Samba seekers can keep up to date with the latest on the Marwell Zoo website.

An appeal on the page reads: “Please do keep a watch out when walking or driving in the local area.



“Check ponds or local waterways as capybaras love to spend time in water.

“Samba is likely to be more mobile at night but may also be seen sunbathing on the banks of the river on sunny days.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We’re incredibly grateful to everyone who is helping us search for Samba.

“If you believe you may have seen her, please take a photo, send it to 07436 167401 and include the What3Words or Google Maps location.”

News.title: Inside the ghost towns of Route 66 with rotting relics 100 years after historic highway opened
News.content:
LEFT TO ROT Inside the ghost towns of Route 66 with rotting relics 100 years after historic highway opened







Next

ROUTE 66 is one of the most famous highways in the world but more than 100 years on from its grand opening, the road is now home to dozens of ghost towns and rotting relics.

Rotting wooden signs, rusting roofs, collapsing buildings and abandoned motels all untouched for decades can be found littered across the 2,448-mile stretch of road.



Hundreds of once-thriving towns sitting along Route 66 have since been left abandoned and unused for decades, when the arrival of the Interstate crippled towns relying on traffic from the iconic highway.

The road stretched all the way from Illinois to California and crossed over eight states.





It would take a whopping 40 hours to drive from one end to the other in a single sitting and for most roadtrippers can last for up to three weeks.

First opened up on November 11, 1926, Route 66 was given the iconic nickname the Mother Road, but has since been split into fragments after being decommissioned in 1985 for modern interstate highways.

One of the most dramatic downfalls along Route 66 is Eldorado Canyon, in Nelson, Nevada, a nearly-deserted relic of the Gold Rush era.

The sacred grounds once epitomized America’s Wild West with the area plagued by greed, murder, and untold lost riches.



Sat just an hour from the extravagant and always packed out Las Vegas Strip, the canyon is far from its former glory today.

Tires are scattered around the dusty lands, and rusting old cars nestled away inside wooden garages have replaced people in the area, with census data from 2020 revealing that just 22 people live in Nelson.

At the heart of the canyon is the abandoned Techatticup Mine which closed in the mid-1940s, but is being revived by a couple who are breathing new life into these historical sites.



Their stretch of the canyon road is now a pit-stop for filming crews, roadtrippers, content creators, and wedding parties looking for an alternative venue.

Tony Werley and his wife Bobby, bought the land in the 1990s and moved in with their children.

“It may be wild, but it’s our home,” Tony told travel writer Toby Skinner.

Around two hours south of Eldorado Canyon lies another town that is frozen in time and still pays homage to its wild west roots.

The town of Oatman, found in the Black Mountains of Mohave County, Arizona, is yet another once-booming mining town that went bust and was deserted by those who thought they would make their fortune.



Now, it’s a classic tourist stop with daily Wild West gunfight shows, authentic saloons, and hundreds of burros, or wild donkeys, that roam the streets of the town and outnumber people roughly 10 to 1.

They are living reminders of Oatman’s history, as the burros arrived with prospectors of the town to help with the mining.

However, when mining was stopped in 1942, the burros were abandoned, but unlike the people, they kept Oatman as their home.



Over 200 miles east are the ruins of the Twin Arrows Trading Post and the ghost town of Two Guns, Arizona.

After opening in the 1940s, the Twin Arrows Trading Post was a popular stop along the Mother Road with two gigantic arrows directing drivers to the rest stop for gas, food, and the souvenir shop.

Now, the buildings are collapsing, only one arrow remains, and the area is covered in graffiti, much of it pointing to conflict with the Indigenous community, with phrases like “stolen land” and “land back” daubed on what is left of the place.

Just 11 minutes from there is the abandoned town of Two Guns which is said to be a hub of paranormal activity, and a place where treasure was once buried.

It was a thriving stop along Route 66, popular with visitors for not only its gas and food, but also its small zoo that once stood there.



Now, you can see the ruins of the mountain lions enclosure, the skeleton of the burned-down gas station, and a crumbling “welcome” sign that epitomises the town’s demise.

Also in Arizona along the historic road is the abandoned Truxton Canyon Training School, also known as the Valentine Indian School, which was built in 1903 to force Native American children to assimilate.

It closed down in 1937 and you can still see the abandoned brick schoolhouse, its decrepit basketball court and rusted merry-go-round.

The officially-registered Historic Place is now owned by the Hualapai Indian Nation which plans to rehabilitate it as a community center and tribal offices.

Meanwhile, a seven-hour drive east will take you to Cuervo, New Mexico, a town founded in 1901 that was killed off when it was literally split in two by the I-40 which replaced Route 66.



Crumbling and abandoned homes and businesses on either side of the highway, a small church, and a gas station are all that is left of the once-busy railroad and cattle stop.



Just 80 miles down the road, is the next ghost town of Glenrio which straddles the New Mexico/Texas border which was once packed with filling stations, motels, and cafes until the I-40 diverted the traffic away in the 1970s.

Unlike the other abandoned parts of Route 66, Glenrio is one of the few where many of the buildings are still intact and give more of an impression of what it would have once been like.

In 2007 it was put on the National Register of Historic Places featuring 17 abandoned buildings, and the old Route 66 roadbed.

According to visitors, the sound of the nearby Interstate traffic only highlights the eerie silence of the abandoned town.

If you keep going east on the I-40 for about 180 miles, you will end up in Texola, Oklahoma.



This living ghost town on the Texas/Oklahoma border has a population of around 40, and you can still see the abandoned historic stone jail with just one roo, and a 1930 Magnolia Gas Station among the derelict buildings.

Many of these shells are left scattered with retro cars and s.

In the 1930s, The Great Depression and the Dust Bowl left the town largely deserted, as farmers fled to other regions, but Route 66 helped keep it alive.

RECOMMENDED STORIES



However, once again, the arrival of the I-40 was the final nail in the coffin for the tiny town.

The iconic Mother Road that endures as a lasting icon of Americana celebrates its centennial on November 11 with a slew of activities taking place nationwide to celebrate the historic road.

News.title: Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC
News.content:
Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly-worded response to his claims about King Charles.

That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Speaking to the Mail on Sunday, Earl Spencer accused the King of psychological manipulation over the palace's statement.

"It is not every day you wake up to find you've been gaslit by the King," he said. "It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I'd lied without the King being able to deny what I'd said".

Journalist Richard Kay, who had been close friends with Diana, also wrote in the newspaper on Sunday that in the week between her death and funeral, Earl Spencer had told him of a "furious row" with Charles.

"It was 'about the boys', but he was reluctant to go further," said Kay, adding that Earl Spencer said the then prince had been "utterly pathetic".

However, speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House on Sunday, Dame Julia Cleverdon, a trusted aide and friend of the King, said the claims about his response to Diana's death did not reflect "the language or the behaviours of a man I've known for 40 years".

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".

Dame Julia said: "To say that the Prince of Wales was elated and somehow took any pleasure... he was as if a 10-tonne truck had fallen on him.

Her own husband had died a fortnight before Diana and she said Charles "could not have been more supportive, loving, concerned about the children and interested".

News.title: Watch: Diana's brother says press has 'cancerous influence' on Harry and Meghan's lives
News.content:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC that there are similarities between the way his sister Diana, Princess of Wales and the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been treated by the press.

He said Princess Diana was "brought low" by press criticism of her and that it is a "pity" to see echoes of that in Harry and Meghan's lives now.

He added that people should learn from Princess Diana's example, and that for anyone being "destroyed daily" by the tabloid press, it must be a "cancerous influence" on their lives.

The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, will be available on iPlayer from 16:00 and broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday.

News.title: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder
News.content:
Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.

In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.

Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe.

"The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.

News.title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
News.content:
Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.

The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.

Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy.

"Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said.

The policy would cost about Â£2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding."

In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from Â£3 to Â£1, and reduce rail fares by 10%.

He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs.

Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already.

"Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them."

News.title: Sex and dating for the sandwich generation - Sharon Horgan on her latest comedy Youth
News.content:
Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe and Motherland.

Now, with her latest show Youth, Horgan puts the spotlight on 50-something women, imbued with her trademark tightly balanced mix of hilarity and pathos.

The HBO Max series sees Horgan's character, Alex, gamely attempting to juggle a stressful publishing career while looking after a teenage son and elderly parents. She's part of the so-called sandwich generation, those in midlife who have to juggle caring responsibilities for old and young while often working, too.

And that's not all - Alex is also back in the dating game following a divorce.

I'm curious to know how much of Youth is based on Horgan's own experience. The star is divorced and has two daughters.

"We've all got kids who are kind of adults now and parents who are getting older and ailing in some cases. There is a chunk of my life in there, anâ¦ autobiographical element for sure. But the good thing about writing autofiction is that no one really knows which bits are real and which bits aren't, I guess, except the people [in it]!"

The hit writer, producer and actress mulled over the idea for Youth before going on to make Apple TV's Bad Sisters, coming back to it after the dark comedy ended.

The 56-year-old says she was keen to "write about this particular time in a woman's life... through the lens of a mother of a son".

Horgan wanted the story to be "post-divorce and "menopause adjacent".

"And I wanted it to be a comedy, you know? Because there's a lot that's very funny about our bodies failing!"

But it's not just her comedy chops that have gained her a loyal following - a big factor in Horgan's success over the last 20 years or so is the authenticity she brings to her work.

"I spent a lot of time trying to make it as real and as accurate as possible and trying to put in my faults as a parent and mistakes as a woman, my own sort of anxieties and insecurities," she says.

"I try to put all that in thereâ¦ and hope that's a universal feeling because it's really madly important to me that women, especially, watch it and see themselves reflected back."

She says that Youth "felt like the next stage on" from her popular sitcom Catastrophe.

The series, which first aired in 2015 on Channel 4, followed the lives of 40-somethings Sharon and Rob (played by Horgan and Rob Delaney), a couple who got together suddenly after their brief transatlantic fling resulted in pregnancy.

"This [show] feels part of the same trajectory, almost, which was fun and really helpful when it came to trying to figure out what the tone was, although I hope it's kind of doing its own thing," Hogan explains.

News.title: 'People forget we exist': Why older LGBTQ+ people fear losing identity
News.content:
As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisation in 1967 to the first same-sex marriages in 2014.

But now she says this important part of her identity is frequently overlooked due to her age.

She's part of England's older LGBTQ+ community, which a new report suggests often experiences poorer health, more limited finances and greater social isolation than the wider older population.

The report, from the Centre for Ageing Better, says without specialist support, this growing demographic could be forced "back into the closet" when accessing care, warning they may even delay getting the care they need because of concerns about homophobia.

Adam Porter, a housing development manager from the LGBT Foundation charity, says he regularly meets older members of the community in exactly that situation.

"It's very common for people to hide things if they have a carer visiting their home, for example hiding their wedding photos or taking down a trans flag," he says.

"In the case of someone moving into a care environment, that means hiding who they are in their own home, for what could be the rest of their life."

He says he has been "horrified" by some of the stories he has heard meeting older LGBTQ+ people, including some who have had carers offer to "pray for them" regarding their sexuality.

Porter is part of the team behind Kindred House, a first-of-its-kind LGBTQ+ social housing scheme for over-55s, set to open in Manchester next year.

News.title: Trump escalates media fight after week of setbacks
News.content:
The president's frustration at the media, however, came after a week of setbacks in which major institutions handed him a series of losses across his agenda.

First, the Supreme Court blocked his plan to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms. This prompted Trump to lash out at the court's justices including those he had appointed. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," he said.

The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, then raised interest rates after Trump had spent months arguing they should be cut. This was followed by a judge ordering his administration to give 30 days' notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center arts venue in Washington DC after the president warned it could be "ripped down".

These headlines, combined with approval ratings that recently sunk to record lows for his second term, suggest Trump is facing challenging political headwinds.

His latest attack on the press, however, raises clear legal questions.

The First Amendment to the US Constitution forbids Congress from "abridging" the freedom of the press. It is language that courts have long interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.

All three targeted news outlets have promised to file lawsuits challenging Trump's decision.

Although the breadth of this move is unprecedented, it is far from the first time the Trump administration has attempted to limit or deny access to the White House to members of mainstream media outlets.

In his first term, the administration revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press credentials, setting off a legal battle that was ultimately resolved in the journalist's favour. It also temporarily suspended the pass of a reporter who had a heated argument with White House adviser Sebastian Gorka â a move that also was subsequently blocked by the courts.

Last year, the White House banned reporters for the Associated Press from participating in the president's press pool - which allows media outlets access to smaller in-town and travelling presidential appearances - because the newswire service would not follow Trump's move to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

That dispute also led to a protracted - and yet to be fully resolved - legal battle, prompting the White House to change press pool rules to drop the guaranteed spot for all wire services.

News.title: 'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
News.content:
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.

It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isaiasâs displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.

In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.

Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.

The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.

It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.

"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.

"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."

In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.

After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.

Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.

"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.

"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"

Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.

Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.

"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."

Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.

All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.

The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.

Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.

At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.

The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.

Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.

Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.

As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."

News.title: Homes evacuated over fears fire at seaside hotel weakened building's structure
News.content:
Speaking to the BBC, John Dighton, who was evacuated from Pavilion Court, said he was told to leave his flat at about 19:00 on Saturday.

The 50-year-old said: "We don't know how long we will be out for but we have grabbed stuff for a couple of days.

"The worst thing is the not knowing. We are at a hotel over the road from the flats."

Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.

He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying.

"We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions."

Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel.

The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm.

"We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin.

"We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was."

The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said on Saturday: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks.

"This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes."

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner loses moral high ground after tax exile, Labour chair says
News.content:
The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt".

Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return.

When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile".

Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects".

Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do."

"Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said.

Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules.

News.title: Man rearrested after missing mum's remains found
News.content:
A 56-year-old man has been rearrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and further arrested on suspicion of murder after human remains were identified as a missing mother-of-three.

Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.

Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham, London, on 12 August after bones were found in shrubland damaged by a fire a week earlier.

The man, from Southampton, first arrested in 2020, has been released on conditional bail. Another man, also 56 and from Southampton, was released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder.

News.title: Strictly returns with new hosting trio as celebrities find out dance pairings
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting line up.

Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut on Saturday, taking over from long-running hosting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left the show last year.

A fresh cohort of famous faces â including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips â also stepped onto the ballroom floor for the first time.

During the launch show, it was revealed which professional dancers they were paired with.

Stepping out onto the ballroom floor after a huge all-cast opening dance routine, Willis said presenting Strictly was a "genuine honour".

"Josh, you've got moves," proclaimed Radebe, a former professional on the show. While Widdicombe added that it was "a little bit overwhelming" but he was "delighted" to be there.

In a first for the show, celebrity and pro pairings were revealed via three dance routines. It functioned as a musical chairs of sorts, in which the contestants switched partners until the music was paused, and a couple was announced.

News.title: JLR suppliers call for shift to aerospace
News.content:
Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs.

The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production.

JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

News.title: Maddy Cusack 'more than a number on a shirt' as anniversary falls during inquest delay
News.content:
Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun.

Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad".

But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers.

An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July.

But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records.

It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming".

"It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"They're very difficult days."

News.title: Tens of thousands of fridge freezers left at docks as household collections suspended
News.content:
People have reported storing broken fridges and freezers in their gardens for months because some council collections have been suspended.

It follows the closure of specialist treatment facilities and a wider shortage of capacity to process cooling appliances, the Local Government Authority (LGA) said.

Recycling company Unimetals, which had dozens of sites in the UK, filed for liquidation in 2025 leaving tens of thousands of fridge freezers at Newport Docks.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working to manage the capacity shortages.

Almost a quarter of Welsh councils say they have suspended household collections of fridge-freezers due to a shortage of space at disposal sites.

Cardiff is one of these and Lee Young, who lives in the city, has been trying to get rid of his broken fridge-freezer for two months.

"I tried to take it to the recycling centre in July but was told it wasn't accepted. Someone said the council would collect it, but they won't either."

It has been sitting in his back garden ever since and he does not know when council collections will resume.

News.title: Michael Marra announced as new Scottish Labour leader
News.content:
He went on to thank his opponents, Joe Fagan and Monica Lennon, and praised them for their ideas about how the party needed to change.

He said: "Joe argued for a politics rooted in people and place, for less control in the centre and more control for local communities. That should be the case in our country and in our party.

"Monica was right to say we need to reconnect with the trade union movement that birthed the Labour party.

"Her record delivering change through parliament is also a template for how Labour should behave in opposition â robust in our criticism of the SNP, yes, but also making our own change."

Marra continued: "Scots know what we are against. They can't tell you what we are for... Social justice. Eradication of poverty. Good work. Good housing. Good public services. The good life for working people. An economy where everyone has a fair chance in life, which redistributes power, wealth and opportunity."

News.title: Celtic v Rangers LIVE: Gers add to Hoops misery with second Old Firm win in a week
News.content:
( Getty )

Celtic failed to get revenge over Rangers as they lost 1-0 in the first Old Firm clash of the Scottish Premiership season, for a second defeat at the hands of their bitter rivals in a week

The Gers powered to an impressive 3-0 victory in the League Cup quarter-finals at Ibrox last weekend, and followed that up with another dominant display, although the scoreline was closer this time around.

Ryan Naderi slammed home a rebound on 33 minutes for the decisive goal and completed a week that has surely given Derek McInnes lift-off after a difficult start to life in Glasgow.

Away fans are banned from matches between the Old Firm teams in the Premiership and League Cup this season, so Celtic Park was exclusively green and white but that didn’t help Martin O’Neill’s side, who also endured a deflating defeat to Ferencvaros in the Europa League in midweek and have now lost three on the spin with the clouds of crisis beginning to gather over Parkhead.

News.title: Five children a day killed or injured by explosives around world – as AI and drones increase threat
News.content:

The growing use of drones and artificial intelligence in conflict is exposing children to new threats at a time when more than five a day are already being killed or injured by explosives around the world.

Children accounted for nearly half of civilian casualties from landmines and explosive remnants of war between 2020 and 2025, according to new research by Save the Children (STC). More than 12,000 were killed or injured.

Now, rapidly evolving military technology is changing civilian exposure to conflict at a time when rights groups say the international norms designed to protect children and their families are being weakened.

Air-launched explosives, including from attack drones, accounted for around two-thirds of incidents of civilian harm last year globally, with health workers carrying out medical procedures by phone light to avoid attracting their attention, STC said.

In Ukraine, drone attacks on schools increased by 358 per cent last year, while drone attacks accounted for the vast majority of child casualties in Sudan in the first months of this year.

Khaleel, 10, was playing football near a school in Gaza when the ball rolled into an area containing an explosive remnant of war. When he went to retrieve it, an explosion left him with shrapnel wounds to his face, both eyes and one ear.

He has since suffered severe vision loss, persistent pain and hearing problems, and struggles to read the board at school or play with other children.

“Seeing him covered in blood and unable to open his eyes was one of the most painful moments of my life. He is my only son after many years of waiting, and watching him suffer has been devastating,” his mother, Mona, 42, said.

Mona and Khaleel’s names have been changed for their safety.

STC also highlighted Gaza as an example of a new phase in modern warfare, in which drone surveillance, AI-supported targeting and other unmanned systems are being used at an alarming scale in densely populated areas.

open image in gallery Khaleel, 10, was seriously injured by an explosive remnant of war while playing football near a school in Gaza. He suffered multiple shrapnel injuries to his face, eyes and ear ( Save The Children )

AI technology has already changed how wars are fought, bringing the time it takes to identify targets from tens of minutes to, in some cases, seconds. Its growing use in warfare also raises concerns about how decisions to use force are being made, particularly when children and other civilians are present.

In a report published on Thursday, the UN’s top human rights body said they had found “reasonable grounds” to believe the US committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in Minab, that killed at least 177 civilians. US officials have previously confirmed that AI was used during the operation to process intelligence and assist analysts in identifying targets. The US department of defence has investigations into the incidents ongoing, but the US has denied committing war crimes. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement, “The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime.”

Speaking during a visit to Imperial College London’s I-HUB innovation centre also on Thursday, Harry, the Duke of Sussex, pledged his commitment to children injured in conflict, saying that “whilst children continue to suffer, I will keep working to ensure they can live life to the full”.

“Children should not be exposed to conflict. They should not be losing limbs to blast,” he said.

The university hosts the Centre for Paediatric Blast Injury Studies, which has pioneered prosthetic technology and long-term rehabilitation techniques for children who have suffered blast injuries.

It comes as monthly child casualties in Ukraine have reached a four-year high, according to Unicef, while they have also surged in Sudan in recent months.

In June, a report by an independent United Nations inquiry found that Israel’s ongoing killings of children in Gaza after a truce was called in its war against Hamas could amount to genocide. It said that Israeli military operations have continued causing “unprecedented death, injury and trauma” to Palestinian children. Israel has repeatedly denied any suggestion it has committed war crimes inside Gaza.

“Governments must ensure that the laws and protections designed to keep children safe evolve with changes to warfare,” said Claire Sanford, conflict and humanitarian director at STC UK. “Children’s rights and safety must remain at the centre of decisions about how emerging technologies are developed and used.”

News.title: Man charged after driver attacked and thrown off bus in Telford
News.content:

A man has been charged after a bus driver was allegedly attacked and thrown off a bus that ploughed into several vehicles.

Officers were called at around 6.37pm on Friday to Court Street in Madeley, Telford, West Mercia Police said.

The bus driver was treated for minor injuries by paramedics.

No-one else is believed to have been injured.

Ali Balhad, aged 33, has been charged with aggravated vehicle taking, assault, attempted grievous bodily harm, driving a motor vehicle dangerously, robbery, theft from a store, threats to kill, and three counts of criminal damage.

Balhad, who is a Yemeni national and who is believed to have been in the Telford area for around a week, has been remanded in custody and is due to appear before Telford Magistrates’ Court on Monday, police said.

Great Britain wrapped up a straightforward victory over Ecuador to book their place at the Davis Cup Finals in November.

After singles victories for Arthur Fery and Toby Samuel on Saturday at London’s Copper Box, Henry Patten and Neal Skupski clinched the tie at the earliest opportunity with a 6-3 6-4 win against Gonzalo Escobar and Diego Hidalgo in the doubles rubber.

Britain therefore join three-time defending champions Italy, Canada, Czechia, South Korea and Austria in booking their spot for the eight-team event in Bologna.

It is the first time Leon Smith’s side have reached the quarter-finals since 2023, when they were beaten by Novak Djokovic’s Serbia in Malaga.

Whoever they draw – and as a non-seed they could find themselves up against the likes of Italy or Spain – they will face a much stiffer test than that provided by Ecuador.

The South American outsiders gave their all to the task in the hope of repeating their famous victory in the competition at Wimbledon in 2000 but were outclassed by Smith’s men.

Britain are the leading nation in men’s doubles and it would have been a huge upset had world number one Patten and new US Open champion Skupski not prevailed.

open image in gallery Henry Patten, right, serves at the Copper Box (John Walton/PA) ( PA Wire )

They had played together only once before – Patten’s sole previous appearance – in a tie against Canada two years ago but gelled quickly, breaking serve at the first opportunity.

There was a moment of contention on the first point of the second set when umpire Marijana Veljovic ruled that Escobar had hit a volley while leaning across the net, awarding Britain the point.

The Ecuador duo put their anger aside to hold serve but a return winner from Skupski earned them another break in the ninth game, and Patten served out the victory.

“We’re very, very happy to get it done in the first match,” said Patten. “I think we played a good one.”

A sustained polling boost for the new government is fuelling speculation that Andy Burnham is considering an early general election, as a fall in popularity for Reform UK continues.

The governing party has remained consistently above Nigel Farage’s party for approval since Mr Burnham’s coronation in July, when Labour overtook Reform for the first time since March 2025.

The new leadership has also hit the ratings of Zack Polanski’s Green Party, which has seen a drop in support over the past few months.

The government has said that it does not intend to call an early election. However, Labour sources told The Independent last week that the by-election to replace Sir Keir Starmer in Holborn and St Pancras is being seen as a test run for the possibility.

The former prime minister announced that he would be leaving parliament earlier this month after resigning as prime minister and Labour leader to make way for Mr Burnham.

Mr Polanski has confirmed that he will stand as the Green candidate for the seat next month, in what will be a key test for the new government.

Opposition parties also appear to be preparing for the country to go to the polls early, with Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey having revealed a manifesto working group has already been formed.

“We don’t normally do it this early,” he told The Guardian.

Meanwhile, Reform sources have suggested Mr Burnham could be convinced to call an early election depending on the outcome of the London by-election.

They told The i that if Labour’s candidate beats Mr Polanski “convincingly”, he could be dismissed a “dud” and convince Labour that the progressive vote was uniting behind them once again.

A Tory source also told the paper a victory over the Greens in Holborn and St Pancras could “tempt” the prime minister into an early vote.

“[Burnham’s] whole thing is to consolidate the left,” they said. “If he continues to constrict the Green vote then it will tempt him into an early election whilst the right remains split.”

Under Sir Keir’s leadership, polling showed that Labour began to lose support from left-leaning voters over issues such as Gaza and welfare spending.

This coincided with a boost to the Greens, which recorded a high of around 14 per cent approval in April this year, based on an average of top pollsters, compared to a Labour low of 19 per cent in the same month.

Pollsters have broadly forecast that Labour will win the contest, taking a nearly 50 per cent majority in the seat in 2024.

However, the picture has changed since. The Greens took three London councils from Labour at the local elections earlier this year, and took its share of seats in Camden – home to Holborn and St Pancras – from one to 11 at the contest, while Labour held overall control.

Will Labour call an early election?

There are clear upsides for Mr Burnham in calling an early election, particularly if Labour holds the seat of Holborn and St Pancras.

The new prime minister has pledged sweeping changes. However, having secured the role with just 24,000 votes from the people of Makerfield – and after running uncontested to be Labour leader – his opponents have argued that he does not hold a mandate from the nation to pursue his agenda.

A general election victory would inarguably grant this, plus an extra two years to deliver the policies he has begun to set out.

Under present rules, the latest the next general election can take place is in 2029.

A sustained polling boost for the new government is fuelling speculation that Andy Burnham is considering an early general election ( PA Wire )

Polling would suggest that it would also be an inopportune time for two of Labour’s key political opponents – Reform and the Greens – given dropping support for both parties.

Reform’s approval now sits at its lowest in 20 months, at an average 24 points, and the Green’s at 10 points from 14 in April.

The Conservatives meanwhile have begun to plateau at around 20 points, and the Lib Dems at around 11.

However, polling expert John Curtice has poured doubt on Labour optimism in the face of these trends, telling The Independent last week that there is still a chance for Reform UK to become the biggest party at a nationwide contest.

“The numbers are just not there”, he said.

Labour disastrous local election results – where it lost 38 councils – saw it drop support in places where they were previously the strongest party, Mr Curtice explained. This pattern means Reform could “still do perfectly well in terms of seats.”

Mr Burnham has also been “dying [to become PM] for years”, Mr Curtice added.

“Holding an election now means risking three years to gain two. It’s a bad deal.”

Piers Morgan has hit out at Ed Sheeran for “bowing to the mob” during his Philadelphia concert after the singer tearfully addressed the controversy around Macklemore’s removal from his tour.

On Saturday, the British singer-songwriter took to the stage for the first time since Macklemore announced that he had been fired from Sheeran’s Loop tour over his pro-Palestine comments at an earlier gig. The rapper claimed that Robert Kraft – the CEO of Kraft Group who owns Gillette Stadium – personally called Sheeran to say he would not be allowed to perform at the venue, while Sheeran later responded by stating he would not be drawn into a public debate about the Gaza war and that it was “the promoter’s decision” to remove Macklemore.

After all of Sheeran’s remaining support acts withdrew from the tour earlier in the week, the singer appeared to read from an autocue as he apologised to his fans at last night’s concert. “I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes. I’m so, so sorry. I don’t want to disappoint fans,” he said. “I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore. What happened in Israel, and at the music festival on October 7th was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate.”

Now, broadcaster Piers Morgan has spoken out about Sheeran’s concert speech, saying that the singer looked like “some bullied puppet” reading from the autocue.

Ed Sheeran dropped Macklemore from his tour last week ( PA Wire )

“I agree with Ed Sheeran’s overview of the Israel/Hamas war (Oct 7 terrible, Israel response disproportionate) but I wish he hadn’t bowed to the mob and felt forced to say it publicly, especially reading it off an autocue like some bullied puppet,” the outspoken journalist said on X. “He needs better advisors.”

Others commented on Sheeran’s apology, including presenter Richard Bacon – who said that the singer is “a good person with a good heart”.

“He’s a bloke trying to do his job, his way who got caught in a mincer movement. The chess pieces shifted against him,” he continued in a tweet. “It was bad luck. He is decent. Obviously.”

While earlier on Saturday, Jeremy Clarkson defended Sheeran, writing in his column in The Sun: “He literally said nothing at all and, for that, his fans are trying to offload tickets for his ­forthcoming tour, his support acts have all walked and, from what I hear, even his band is ­refusing to play with him.

“They want him to sound off on ­Palestine, and because he’s not really that sort of person, the keyboard warriors have sent him to Coventry.”

During Saturday’s show, Sheeran gave his personal views on the Gaza situation, saying: “My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilian loss and loss of children’s lives. And the systemic injustice we’re seeing unfolding the West Bank cannot be overlooked.”

He also said that he went ahead with the show as honouring his commitment to his fans is “completely central to who” he is.

The gig was pushed back to the later time of 8pm from 5:30pm ET due to Sheeran’s support acts quitting, while pro-Palestine protesters positioned themselves outside of the venue.

Just hours earlier, Saturday Night Live UK mocked Sheeran in a sketch, which depicted the singer as “sitting on the fence” as war broke out between humans and artificially intelligent robots. “I don’t like to take sides. I don’t want to alienate any of my fans – humans or robots,” cast member Annabel Marlow said as Sheeran, complete with ginger hair, guitar and tattoos.

“A lot of my tickets are bought my scalping bots. Sometimes when it comes to conflicts, the bravest thing you can do is to say nothing at all.

Sheeran is next due to perform on Saturday 25 September at Kraft’s Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts.
