Sports.title: Bournemouth v Liverpool: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
As for Liverpool , Iraola is still picking at his back-four – ultimately, he doesn’t have full-backs he can rely on, so it’s likely he’ll be flicking through options until he does. Similarly, his midfield is going to remain unbalanced until it isn’t. Dominik Szoboszlai, of course, is a mainstay, but there’s not much pace and control around him; Alexis Mac Allister is scoring goals currentl, but doesn’t offer enough else, while Florian Wirtz is getting more chances than a Monopoly champion. We see flashes because he’s extremely talented; the question is whether he’s quick enough, of foot and thought, or robust enough, to regularly impose himself in “this league”. Our collective sense seems far closer to no than yes.

I don’t imagine Rose spent too long sweating over his team. Kluivert is a miss, and of course Junior Kroupi is long-term injured, but otherwise, his team is pretty settled. Adam Scott, who we might’ve thought would leave in the summer, stayed, and has started the season in excellent form. His ball-carrying is exceptional and he offers height in both boxes; if he can develop his passing, especially shirt, punched through the lines, he might develop into an all-round monster.

Also kicking-off at 2pm: Man City v Sunderland and Leeds v Palace. We’ll keep you updated with any goals that go in; I’m really looking forward to seeing how Daniel Farke’s men get on after their Monday-night dematerialisation of Newcastle.

It’s interesting that, for all the money in the Premier League , many of the best players, especially attackers, are in Spain, Munich and Paris. If you consider Vinicius, Bellingham, Mbappe, Lamine Yamal, Raphinha, Oliseh and Kane, the Prem doesn’t have superstar that equivalence and only Bruno Fernandes is remotely close to that company in terms of being among the world’s best in his position. Nor are there that many Prem players who might have the potential to hit a similar level.

Andoni Iraola, meanwhile, is still searching for his best blend – for any blend, really. He leaves out Victor Munoz, Ryan Gravenberch and Kostas Tsimikas, with Alexis Mac Allister, Milos Kerkez and Cody Gakpo coming in.

Marco Rose makes one change to the side that sorted Sociedad in midweek, Justin Kluivert replaced by Ryan Christie. He’s not in the sqaud at all, so presumably is injured.

There have never been as many brilliant footballers in the world as there are now, there has never been as much money anywhere as there is in the Premier League now, and the use of data has never been as sophisticated; for those reasons, Premier League fixtures have never been as hard to predict nor of such high average standard. Every team has players good enough to hurt every other team.

Bournemouth v Liverpool offers a case in point. Andoni Iraola left Rayo Vallecano to join a team with a ground capacity of 11,307, who have won precisely no top-level honours, then used their scouting systems to attract players of calibre from clubs of similar or greater size. He then moved to Anfield, spending insane amounts of money on attackers the summer after Arne Slot did exactly the same at cost of his job, and yet it’d be no surprise whatsoever if his old club take the points today.

Thus far, the richer clubs have retained their advantage over the course of a season – having the best players, rather than merely brilliant players is enough to win them sufficient marginal games to keep reaching the Champions League – but, as we’ve already seen this weekend at Brentford and Brighton, week to week, they are prone to being out-thought and out-played. Might this be the season that their talent ID – for managers as well as players – is so good, that next, we see it backed in the market with Champions League money?

Both Bournemouth and Liverpool have made iffy starts to the season, learning new systems following a World Cup summer with squads built to someone else’s specifications, both much better going forward than backwards. And both will want a win to see them off into the international break, fearful of the grim deal sitting with a defeat for a fortnight entails. Which for us, means only good things – this should be a terrific tussle.

Kick-off: 2pm

Sports.title: Zidane’s next move as France coach may reveal the wizard behind the curtain | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Even in his playing days, Zinedine Zidane seemed unknowable. As a manager, the sense of distance has only grown. He won three Champions Leagues with Real Madrid without ever giving a sense of what his idea of football looked like.

France are perhaps the most perplexing football country: a squad that teems with such talent that a B team would be serious contenders at a World Cup, that reached three major finals under Didier Deschamps with a sense of unfulfilment, a team that progressed but rarely entranced, or at least didn’t until this summer’s World Cup, when they attacked with gusto and ended up overrun in midfield by Spain.

On Friday, the two come together as Zidane, for the first time, leads France in their Nations League fixture against Turkey, an enigmatic coach leading a mercurial squad.

Zidane is one of five coaches to have won the Champions League on three or more occasions, ranking alongside Bob Paisley, Pep Guardiola and Luis Enrique and behind only Carlo Ancelotti. He is the only manager to win three successive Champions Leagues and yet few would consider him one of the game’s elite coaches. In that spell he won one La Liga title.

He left five days after the third of those Champions League successes, vaguely citing the club’s need for change. Like so much else in his career, his motivations were opaque. But he returned the following March after the inglorious reign of Julen Lopetegui and Santi Solari’s attempt to pick up the pieces. He won another La Liga title in the two full seasons that followed.

How to assess a coach in the modern world? Two league titles in four full seasons. Three Champions Leagues in his first two and a half seasons. In another age, in another country, that would have marked Zidane as indisputably elite, but in Spain in the past decade? Domestically, his achievements feel about par.

View image in fullscreen Zinedine Zidane was viewed at Real Madrid as a head coach who let his star players like Ronaldo and Gareth Bale just be. Photograph: Matt West/BPI/Shutterstock

Madrid and Barcelona win everything, so for a Madrid coach to win half the league titles available is essentially what would be expected. But he lost eight of his first 100 games, a record. His side scored in a record 73 consecutive games. They won a joint-record 16 La Liga games in a row. They won a record 13 successive away games.

They are stats that seem unanswerable, but their accumulation has the opposite effect to that which might be expected. Zidane’s Madrid, in his first spell, were crushingly dominant. But were they dominant because of his genius or did he appear a genius because of their dominance? What comes to matter, then, is not the how many, but the how. Did Madrid win with dashing football of fitting elegance? To which the answer is, again, a shrug: they were fine.

Those three Champions League wins in a row, equally, offer surprisingly little evidence for Zidane’s greatness. Madrid have always had a tremendous capacity for achieving European success in the shadows, as though they are the default, the club that wins when nobody else is quite inspired enough to do so. Rarely has that been felt as acutely as in 2016, when they beat Roma and Wolfsburg, then edged by Manchester City on penalties in the semi-final thanks to a Fernando own goal before beating Atlético Madrid on penalties in an unmemorable final.

The following year was more impressive: the extra-time surge against Bayern and Cristiano Ronaldo-inspired demolitions of Napoli, Atlético and Juventus. But 2018 was a return to curiously ordinary success. Yes, Ronaldo and Luka Modrić were often brilliant, but there was also carelessness, notably in the quarter-final win against Juventus when they let a three-goal lead slip before a late penalty rescued them. Victory over Liverpool in the final came after a shoulder injury sustained by Mohamed Salah in a challenge with Sergio Ramos, a terrible error by a possibly injured Loris Karius and a Gareth Bale wonder goal.

View image in fullscreen Didier Deschamps was successful as head coach of France, but his side rarely captivated Photograph: Martin Meissner/AP

It was hard to isolate any one moment in the success that could definitively be assigned to Zidane’s coaching genius. He didn’t create the midfield three of Casemiro, Modric and Toni Kroos. He didn’t find some new role for Ronaldo or Bale. Perhaps Zidane was some elite player whisperer, coaxing them to habitual greatness, but it was hard for an outsider to tell. Being Zidane, he was inscrutable, a cipher into which observers could read whatever message they wished.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Real Madrid coaches often run into a similar problem. They have great players. Great players do great things. Philosophies and structures always seem subservient to their talents. Ancelotti, like Zidane, has often been underappreciated, seen as somebody who essentially lets the players be. That is probably unfair and, even if it were not, perhaps that, too, is a skill. After all, plenty of coaches at Real Madrid have not been able to let the players express their innate superiority.

At the very least, it can be said that Zidane has an aura. Even those who accused him of being little more than a pair of hands clapping on the touchline must acknowledge that some hands are more authoritative than others. That may turn out to be an essential quality with France, a national team that became notorious between their two World Cup triumphs for ill-discipline, with the scandals of Seoul in 2002 and the strike at Knysna in 2010.

Whatever doubts there may be about whether Deschamps’s caution was counterproductive – until at the last, in that semi-final against Spain, he wasn’t cautious enough – over his 14 years in charge he prevented the sort of breakdowns of discipline that had undermined his predecessors, despite some extremely challenging situations.

Perhaps this is not such a troubled or troublesome France squad as some of the past decade have been, but that Zidane has taken the unusual step of banning the press from covering the arrival of players at their Clairefontaine base suggests he is eager to make a bid for control early.

His squad features a number of new faces. This is not continuity Deschamps. In the greater autonomy national coaches have compared with their club counterparts, perhaps, with France, the true nature of Zidane the coach will emerge and the great enigma will develop a face.

Sports.title: ‘We miss her the same every day’: Olivia Cusack on her late footballer sister Maddy
Sports.content:
Olivia Cusack says her sister, the late Maddy Cusack, is on her mind every single day and she is determined to ensure her “legacy lives on” three years after the former England youth international midfielder’s death.

Olivia, together with family and friends of Maddy, walked 29 miles from Bramall Lane, Sheffield United’s home, to their family’s home in Horsley, near Derby, on Saturday to raise funds and awareness. Maddy’s loved ones are still enduring a “frustrating and confusing” wait for answers about the circumstances surrounding her death on 20 September 2023.

An inquest into the death of the 27-year-old Sheffield United player was adjourned again in July and has been scheduled to resume on 7 December, after fresh evidence came to light. Cusack, a former England Under-19s international, was the first player to appear in 100 matches for Sheffield United’s women’s team.

Olivia says Saturday’s walk, “Bringing Maddy Home”, was motivated by some of the evidence the inquest heard. “After the inquest we wanted to bring her home from Bramall Lane, back to our family home,” she says. “Many people know Maddy as the professional football player and the name on the back of her shirt, the number, the colours she wore, the club she was associated with.

“But I felt in the inquest it was lost that she was a person, she wasn’t an object that we were discussing. She’s a person, she’s a family member of ours [and] a person that’s sometimes been lost within the chaos surrounding her death really, so that’s the notion behind the walk. To claim her back, bring her home and protect her.”

A minute’s applause will be held before kick-off at Sunday’s Women’s Super League 2 fixture between Newcastle and Sheffield United. Discussing that anniversary, Olivia says: “We miss her the same every day, as I will on Sunday. The anniversary is always something that creeps up on us. It’s very emotional and it’s a time where we just reflect, but we do so much throughout the year so she really is at the heart of pretty much every single day. Not a day that goes by where we don’t think about her.

View image in fullscreen Sheffield United and Maddy Cusack’s family paid tribute at Bramall Lane shortly after her death. Photograph: Richard Callis/MB Media/Getty Images

“There can be days when you just feel absolutely drained and you know you don’t quite know what the right thing to do is, but I think the way that we just get through it is that we remember who she was as a person. She loved her life, she loved trying new things and just enjoying life’s simple pleasures, we try and embody that on every day, not just the anniversary.

“I really do encourage people to, as difficult as it can be sometimes, share the photos, share the memories, bring her up in conversation wherever you can, talk about her, and between all of us, you know, her legacy will live on.”

The family have already endured eight full days of evidence, after the hearing belatedly began on 29 June, but the discovery of additional documents led the proceedings to be paused until December. The coroner apologised to the family for yet another delay. The case had previously been set to start being heard on 5 January 2026 after additional postponements in 2025.

“It’s been really difficult,” Olivia said of the delays. “It’s not something that any of us anticipated to happen. It’s very confusing and it can be very frustrating, the length of time it’s taken, it can be difficult to work that out and to know how you should be feeling and the process of it. However, we know that for the right outcome it has to be taken seriously. They need the time to come together and really get an outcome.

“It feels as though she can’t be at peace until it’s finished. And I do feel that’s quite upsetting to think about and to work through. It needs to come to a conclusion.”

View image in fullscreen Maddy Cusack was also remembered during the Premier League match between Sheffield United and Newcastle. Photograph: George Wood/Getty Images

Olivia said she would “channel Maddy’s energy” during Saturday’s 29-mile walk, when a group of about 15 family and friends travelled in the reverse direction to another fundraising walk in February 2024 from Pride Park to Bramall Lane.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

This time they set off from Sheffield at 5.30am. A fundraising page for the walk had surpassed £1,100 as of Saturday afternoon. Olivia described that tally as “incredible – £1,000 is just amazing, it’s more than I ever expected. Particularly with it being Maddy’s anniversary, it’s going to be very much a mental challenge as well as a physical one, so it gives you that extra motivation to make the people who’ve donated proud.”

The money is being raised for the the Maddy Cusack Foundation, which is helping a range of causes targeting women’s and girls’ football and “letting girls be seen within sport”.

“We provided Derby County Community Trust with a series of bursaries for girls and families who struggle with the financial prospects of becoming dedicated to their football. It’s a helping hand for any child that needs that extra sort of funding, taking away the barriers that they might face.”

The foundation has also partnered with the Stockport County defender Ben Osborn’s organisation Elite Football Development, which aims to inspire young people through sport and education.

“They work with girls and boys but we sponsor the girls’ side of things, which is focused around post-16 study, and allows girls to gain qualifications alongside being able to train and live the life of a professional footballer. We were really keen to get involved in this as Maddy was really passionate about education.”

Sports.title: Hayen must worry about his Burnley future but fans’ fears are existential
Sports.content:
The greatest moments of Burnley’s history were beamed on to a big screen before kick-off at Turf Moor, accompanied by famous lines of commentary. The final one, the moment promotion was sealed under Scott Parker in April 2025, was soundtracked by: “Burnley are back in the big time.” That feels a long time ago now, with a return to the Premier League a remote prospect.

Burnley appeared to have this game against Derby sewn up, leading through Zeki Amdouni’s first-half header, but a stunning stoppage-time strike from the Rams’ substitute Mohammed Fuseini soured the Turf Moor mood. It means Burnley’s winless home league run could now reach a year, the Clarets last tasting victory at Turf Moor on 18 October. Their last win in any competition in 90 minutes was on 11 February.

The draw left Nicky Hayen, the under-fire head coach, under scrutiny, though the majority of fans will direct their anger towards Alan Pace, the chair, given the financial problems and off-field turmoil that have plagued the club during a disruptive summer.

Hayen vowed to fight for his future and revealed he would talk with Pace, though could give no assurances he will remain in charge for the next game at Watford on 10 October after the extra-long international break. “I can understand the fans are angry after a start like this, it’s not what they want to see from their team or from myself,” he said. “It’s my responsibility. But I’ve always shown resilience and I’m always going to fight. We need this [international] window to change a lot of things.”

View image in fullscreen Mohammed Fuseini celebrates scoring a late equaliser for Derby. Photograph: Alfie Carling/PPAUK/Shutterstock

In his programme notes before the game, Pace called for fans to “unite and show togetherness”, after they had chanted for his removal during the home defeat by Bristol City a fortnight ago. There was some early encouragement for Hayen’s team as they sought to make early inroads against Derby. Although a lack of thrust in the final third was evident at times, Burnley made the breakthrough via Amdouni’s forehead, the forward peeling around the back post to nod home Lucas Pires’ corner.

Hayen, who was managing Haverfordwest County in the Welsh Premier League four years ago and was not Burnley’s first choice to replace Parker, celebrated. Having been accused of muddled selections in his tenure so far, he had made some brave calls, dropping the club captain, Kyle Walker, and struggling goalkeeper Max Weiss, and recalling Marcus Edwards, who had been jettisoned after featuring in the campaign’s opening two games.

Those decisions were nearly vindicated, right up to the moment Fuseini pounced, leaving Hayen to bear the brunt of more fan criticism. “It is really difficult [to take],” he said. “You saw the reaction of the players after the game, sitting on the ground, disappointed. We wanted to give the fans the win, I wanted this for them, I can accept their frustration. I want to give back to the fans, I feel we can give back a lot. You saw we were close, we wanted to do it just before the international break.”

View image in fullscreen Zeki Amdouni sprints off to celebrate his goal for Burnley. Photograph: Alfie Carling/PPAUK/Shutterstock

The break may represent a chance for Hayen, if he remains, to regroup, though for Pace and the board there remain unanswered questions about the £142m of external debt the club owes, as well as the £81m owed by his firm ALK Capital to the club itself after a leveraged buyout in December 2020. Comparisons with the Glazers’ takeover and ownership of Manchester United have been made. James Holroyd’s recent departure, after 15 months as chief executive, feels reflective of the worsening malaise in the boardroom. Holroyd previously worked under the Glazers at United.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Despite two promotions under the current regime (and three relegations) the Clarets’ financial situation has deteriorated, with some fans now harbouring genuine fears of total extinction if debts are not repaid. Parachute payments may help for a time, but Burnley no longer have the cash reserves they boasted in their debt-free era before Pace and ALK when they enjoyed five successive seasons in the Premier League under Sean Dyche. Such stability now feels a world away and problems are spilling on to the pitch. Money has been spent on transfers, with squad turnover high in recent seasons, but there was particular concern when the £20m sale of Zian Flemming was not reinvested in a new striker, with 39-year-old Jamie Vardy hastily arriving on a free transfer after the transfer window had closed.

Hayen ushered on Vardy and loan signing Largie Ramazani to retain a counterattacking threat against Derby late on, as Burnley hung on. But with a slender lead going into stoppage time, their confidence appeared brittle. Goalkeeper Grégoire Coudert had been forced into a couple of late interventions after Ryan Hedges should have equalised for Derby on the hour mark.

Then, just when it seemed Burnley’s winless streak would be broken, the rocket from Fuseini snatched two points away, leaving them bottom of the Championship. “It’s hard to take,” said Hayen. “It’s frustrating.”

Sports.title: Andros Townsend avoids injury after bizarre pitch roller incident in Thailand
Sports.content:
The former England winger Andros Townsend has joked Stoke away “wasn’t so bad after all” following a bizarre incident in Thailand where he was run over by a pitch roller.

The ex-Tottenham and Crystal Palace attacker Townsend currently plays in Thai League 1 for PT Prachuap and made headlines on Saturday night when a clip emerged on social media which showed the 35-year-old being taken out before a fixture at Pattani.

Townsend was warming up when a member of staff at Pattani appeared to lose control of the pitch roller and it crashed into the 13-cap England international. The left leg of the Prachuap player briefly got stuck under the vehicle, but he did feature off the bench late on in the 3-0 win.

Regular ITV pundit Townsend later took to Instagram to make light of the incident, referencing one of his recent posts in which he contrasted a sun-drenched Thai away trip with previous visits to Stoke’s windswept stadium.

Townsend said on his Instagram story: “It turns out Stoke away wasn’t so bad after all. Swipe to see why.”

Another post described Townsend as ‘The King of Memes in Thai League history’ and he replied “trust me” with four laughing emojis.

Sports.title: ‘They deserved to win’: Mikel Arteta left humbled by Brighton defeat
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta admitted Arsenal were taught a lesson by free-scoring Brighton as their 100% start to the season was abruptly ended on Saturday. Not since 10 May 2023 – 1,224 days ago – when the same opponents won 3-0 at the Emirates Stadium had the Premier League champions lost by three goals. But they were second-best throughout as Pascal Gross, Charalampos Kostoulas and Chema Andrés rounded off a comprehensive victory.

“They deserved to win the game and it’s a big lesson for us,” said a disappointed Arteta, who felt his players were not their usual combative selves. “From the first throw-in you could sense it, it was so clear.

“We put ourselves in trouble one time, two times, three times and we need to get out of that much quicker than that. That’s one of the biggest lessons that we have to take from the game.

“We knew how tough it was going to be and the first thing we had discussed was about the first part. If you don’t get out of that first part as winners, it will be extremely difficult to dominate the game and to have any probability of winning the game. At this level, it’s extremely important to respect and to understand [that] before anything else.”

Quick Guide How do I 

Asked whether this was a wake-up call after nine straight league wins that included them being crowned champions for the first time in 22 years in May, Arteta said: “For us it’s crystal clear. We knew and we talked for two days about what we have to do here. We played the fourth away game in a really short period of time.

“We know what it takes to win every single match and we know what it’s going to take to win against Leeds when we come back. That’s not a surprise, but it doesn’t take away the disappointment and emotional state we have”

Brighton have recorded victories over the reigning champions in the past three seasons and with 16 goals from five matches are all but certain to go into the international break as the division’s top scorers. Fabian Hürzeler compared the 35-year-old Gross to “a good wine” after he was instrumental in the win and praised his team’s collective efforts.

“Everyone has this mindset today: ‘I need to defend first and we defend as a team,’” he said. “We wanted to approach this game by getting small wins. Everyone speaks about a goal is a win, but a small win can be the first throw in, the first corner, win the first header, win the first tackle.

“If you win these small steps, if you celebrate them individually as a win then you can grow into the game. Then you can gain bigger and bigger wins.”

Sports.title: European football: Rosenior taunts Strasbourg fans who ‘insulted family’
Sports.content:
Paris FC extended their unbeaten start to the Ligue 1 campaign, beating Liam Rosenior’s old charges Strasbourg 2-1 in a match marred by abusive chants towards the Englishman from visiting fans.

The game was halted in the second half as Rosenior was targeted by his former supporters. There were also ugly scenes after the final whistle as Rosenior motioned to remonstrate with the away fans and had to be pulled away by his players.

He said later: “A small section of the fans, and I want to stress that it was only a small section, because Strasbourg is a fantastic club, were disrespectful. They insulted my family. My bench was very angry. So, for me, celebrating like that was obviously sending a message. I won’t say anything more about this.”

Goals from Ilan Kebbal on 18 minutes and Pablo Pagis 12 minutes into the second half were enough for the capital club to add a third win to their two draws so far this campaign, despite conceding a late own goal by Moustapha Mbow.

The game between Lyon and ⁠Stade Rennais was also disrupted after ⁠Lyon ​fans ‌displayed an ‌offensive banner ‌directed at their rivals St Etienne. Lyon were leading 2-0 ‌through two goals from ​Ernest Nuamah when the banner ⁠was unveiled, prompting ​officials to ​suspend ​the match ​briefly ‌before ​play ​resumed. They went on to win 4-0.

Lautaro Martínez rode to Inter’s rescue as the Serie A champions fought back from 2-0 down to force a 2-2 draw at Roma, in a meeting of what had been the last two sides with 100% records.

Manu Koné’s double had given Roma a 2-0 lead at half-time but for the second time in a week Cristian Chivu’s side, inspired by Martínez, showed mettle as the champions fought back from such a deficit.

View image in fullscreen Lautaro Martínez celebrates after scoring a second goal for Inter. Photograph: Danilo Di Giovanni/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

After the announcement earlier in the day of the death of Sandro Mazzola at the age of 83, both sides paid homage to the former Inter and Italy playmaker prior to kick-off, with the Nerazzurri also sporting black armbands.

Roma raced out of the blocks as Koné sent them ahead with less than six minutes on the clock when he readjusted his body well to rifle home Nahuel Molina’s knockdown.

The champions had bounced back from being 2-0 down inside the opening 16 minutes at home to Udinese to emerge 5-3 winners on Monday. But Inter were not at the races for most of the opening period at the Stadio Olimpico as Paulo Dybala twice threatened to double the hosts’ advantage.

However, just as Inter slowly seemed to be waking up, Koné had the ball in the net again when he tucked in from close range at the back post on 37 minutes. His celebrations were initially cut short by the assistant’s flag before the video assistant referee intervened and, after a lengthy review, Davide Massa pointed to the centre circle as the 25-year-old skipped off in delight after notching the sixth Serie A goal of his career.

Martínez halved the deficit less than a minute after the interval with a scuffed finish from Thuram’s pull-back that just crept perfectly into the side-netting of Mile Svilar’s far post.

Just as the match appeared to be petering out going into the final 10 minutes, a sudden goalmouth scramble saw Svilar make a sharp save before Martínez headed on to the bar under pressure. Inter, however, managed to recycle the ball and it came back to the Argentinian inside the box and this time he made no mistake as he controlled with his thigh and arrowed a finish past the Serb to ensure the spoils were shared.

View image in fullscreen Roma supporters hold up scarves during their match against Inter. Photograph: Ciro De Luca/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Lazio joined their city rivals Roma and Inter on 13 points after beating bottom-side Venezia, who remain pointless, 2-0. A 51st-minute Mattia Zaccagni penalty, coupled with a Tijjani Noslin goal on the hour, was enough to earn Gennaro Gattuso’s team a fourth win from five outings.

Barcelona maintained their ⁠100% record this season with a 3-1 La Liga ⁠victory over Sevilla, as captain Raphinha scored a hat-trick ⁠to continue his remarkable start to the campaign. Sevilla opened ⁠the scoring after 18 minutes ​through a ‌Youssouf Fofana header, ‌but Barcelona hit back with ‌a Raphinha strike four minutes later.

Seven minutes into the second half, Raphinha headed in a Lamine Yamal cross and the pair combined again ​as the Brazilian completed his hat-trick in the 69th minute, his 12th league goal in ⁠seven games this season. Barcelona are ​provisionally ​six points clear ​at the top of ​La Liga, with ‌second-placed Real ​Madrid, ​who have a game in hand, playing Atlético Madrid on Sunday.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Maximilian Beier’s 70th-minute winner secured Borussia Dortmund a 1-0 victory at Stuttgart as they moved to the top of the early Bundesliga table. Beier tapped in from Jobe Bellingham’s low cross to send Dortmund to the summit for the first time since May 2023, a run of 1,212 days since they threw away the title with a final-day home draw against Mainz.

View image in fullscreen Maximilian Beier (centre) celebrates with teammates after scoring Borussia Dortmund’s winner against VfB Stuttgart. Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPA

The victory also marks the first time in a decade Dortmund have won their opening four league matches. “Sounds good to me,” Beier told Sky Germany. “We’ll take that.”

Earlier, Freiburg had missed a chance to return to the top of the Bundesliga after being held to a 2-2 draw at Eintracht Frankfurt. Bayern Munich’s ruthless 7-0 win over Union Berlin on Friday had put them top overnight.

Several new members of Jürgen Klopp’s 44-man Germany squad shone on both sides in a see-sawing encounter. Frankfurt’s Younes Ebnoutalib finished off a lovely team move to score 10 minutes in, two days after a surprise first call-up.

Derry Scherhant, another of Klopp’s lesser-known new additions, levelled for Freiburg, but Jonathan Burkardt edged Frankfurt back in front. Scherhant created a second for Yuito Suzuki to grab Freiburg a point and leave them level with Bayern on 10 points.

Mohamed Salah scored a hat-trick and set up another ⁠goal as Trabzonspor thrashed Galatasaray 4-0, handing the ⁠defending champions their first defeat of the Turkish Super Lig season.

Salah opened ⁠the scoring in the fourth minute, running through from midfield and finishing calmly, ⁠before he turned provider to set up Noah ​Saviolo, who struck ‌from inside ‌the penalty area in the 39th. Salah added a ‌third in the 44th minute with a clinical finish from a Franculino Dju assist. He completed his ‌hat-trick in the 80th minute, running more than half the length of the ​pitch unchallenged to score with a trademark side-foot finish.

Galatasaray’s coach, Okan Buruk, was sent to the stands in the 71st minute while Lesley ⁠Ugochukwu was shown a red card in the ​87th. Trabzonspor are fifth in the table with 10 points from six games, three points behind Galatasaray.

Sports.title: Tottenham outcast Richarlison takes to social media to send pointed message to club just hours after Spurs' latest Premier League defeat
Sports.content:
Tottenham outcast Richarlison takes to social media to send pointed message to club just hours after Spurs' latest Premier League defeat

Exiled striker Richarlison has been making his presence known amid Tottenham's poor start to the new Premier League season, posting on Instagram hours after their defeat to Aston Villa.

Richarlison was set to depart north London this summer but a move never materialised, and the Brazilian has now been kept out of Tottenham's first-team squad.

In the latest twist to what is turning out to be a protracted saga, Richarlison took to social media on Saturday within hours of Tottenham's 3-2 defeat to Villa to post videos of himself training.

He captioned the video of him undertaking drills: 'The focus remains'. His second post was another video of him undergoing sprint training, accompanied by the caption: '35.4km/h - I broke my record'.

Richarlison's future in north London has become increasingly uncertain after a proposed transfer to Brazilian side Vasco da Gama fell through last week.

He hasn't made a matchday squad in the top flight since the opening-day defeat to Brentford, while he was also left out of Roberto De Zerbi's squad for their away loss to Liverpool in the third round of the Carabao Cup earlier this week.

Richarlison took to social media on Saturday within hours of Tottenham's defeat to Villa to post videos of himself training

De Zerbi has stood firm on Richarlison's absence, saying on Monday: 'At the start of this season, I spoke to him (Richarlison) many times to convince him to stay and he didn't want to

Earlier this week Richarlison shared a screenshot of a social media post about his omission and accompanied it with the message 'Why?' and a tearful sad-faced emoji

His absence has been compounded by Tottenham's lack of goals this season, with Spurs scoring only their first two league goals of the campaign against Villa on Saturday through Conor Gallagher and Jan Paul van Hecke. However, they came too late to influence the result as Tottenham lost 3-2.

On Tuesday, Richarlison shared a screenshot of a social media post about his omission and accompanied it with the message 'Why?' and a tearful sad-faced emoji.

De Zerbi has stood firm on Richarlison's absence, however, saying on Monday: 'At the start of this season, I spoke to him (Richarlison) many times to convince him to stay and he didn't want to.

'I can't go every day to pray for him to stay.

'What I have done at the beginning of this season has been to speak with him and to propose an extension of the contract. If he said, 'no thank you,' I finished my job.

'I know what happened in the last 45 days. It's not right if I explained. It's not my behaviour. The relationship, the problem is between the player and the club.'

Richarlison also had a proposed £35million deadline-day transfer to Everton collapse after the forward failed to agree personal terms with the Toffees.

He was subsequently left out of Spurs' Premier League squad amid a dispute between him and the club over the remaining nine months of his contract, according to BBC Sport.

Richarlison, Spurs' top scorer with 11 Premier League goals last season, remains in north London and trains with De Zerbi's squad, except when they are undertaking tactical work.

The 29-year-old signed for Tottenham from Everton in 2022 for £60million.

Sports.title: Inside Burnley's shocking decline under Alan Pace's ALK: The humiliating sponsor fiasco, why highly-respected CEO quit the Clarets, club staff aghast at changes behind the scenes and the 'ominous shadow' of debt leaving supporters terrified
Sports.content:
Inside Burnley's shocking decline under Alan Pace's ALK: The humiliating sponsor fiasco, why highly-respected CEO quit the Clarets, club staff aghast at changes behind the scenes and the 'ominous shadow' of debt leaving supporters terrified

The threat of mutiny has long been simmering away at Turf Moor. And earlier this month, as Burnley threw away a lead against Bristol City, extending a barren run at a ground in which they have now not won a league game in nearly a year, the fury of a despairing fan base finally boiled over.

Boos thundered around the stadium. Clarets striker Armando Broja got into an angry confrontation with a disgruntled fan in the car park. No one was immune to the ire, and certainly not owner and chairman Alan Pace who bore the brunt of the chanting.

You expect he may well suffer it again if Burnley flounder against Derby on Saturday as they return to Turf Moor rooted to the foot of the Championship with one league win in the last 328 days and none since February. The last time they were in this division they won promotion with 100 points. How far away those days feel now.

Not just because of the dismal football they are having to endure, and the precarious position that’s put them in, but for the ever-growing list of questions for which they are so rarely given answers.

Why did the club wait until relegation before sacking Scott Parker? Why did they wait 71 days to appoint Nicky Hayen and start pre-season without a manager? Why did they sell top scorer Zian Flemming on deadline day with no replacement lined up, and why did they only receive £20million for a player with 11 top-flight goals in a summer when Premier League clubs spent £3.5billion?

Why did they have to drop shirt sponsor Finotive One, a self-titled ‘trading ecosystem’, on the eve of the season? And why, after all that, has the club’s chief executive James Holroyd just left his position after little more than a year in charge?

Pace promised an ‘exciting journey’ when he bought the club in December 2020. That’s certainly one way of putting it. And all of this against the backdrop of that leveraged buy-out, one akin to Manchester United under the Glazers, that used Burnley’s own money to turn a once debt-free organisation with £80m in the bank into one with £13m cash in the coffers, according to the last accounts, and £142m of debt casting an ominous shadow.

No wonder it’s starting to turn toxic.

Burnley owner Alan Pace (centre) has been the subject of fan ire at recent games amid worries about the Clarets' performance on and off the pitch

Nicky Hayen's side slumped to a 2-1 defeat at home to Bristol City a fortnight ago. They have not won a league game at Turf Moor in 2026

Holroyd’s arrival was seen as a huge coup for the club, a man steeped in experience having spent 14 years at Manchester United following another 14 years at adidas.

One former colleague described him to Daily Mail Sport as ‘incredibly serious and incredibly methodical about his work’. A man who spent the best part of three decades working for just two companies was out of his third one after just over a year.

Burnley confirmed his departure to Daily Mail Sport and said that Holroyd had ‘decided to step down to pursue a new challenge’. He will continue to work at the club as part of their Burnley In The Community department but is no longer involved on the commercial side of the business.

‘It's been an honour and a privilege to serve this great club,’ said Holroyd. ‘There's a pride and a resilience that runs through Burnley that you feel from the moment you arrive. That's what makes this such a difficult decision, but it's why I'll keep supporting the incredible work being done by BFC in the Community.

'I want to thank Alan and the board for the opportunity to serve this club, and the staff and supporters for making me feel truly part of the Claret family.'

Daily Mail Sport understands the embarrassing and expensive Finotive One fiasco, where the club dropped their shirt sponsor after just 42 days despite a star-studded launch that featured investor and former NFL star JJ Watt, England cricket legend Jimmy Anderson and Arnold Schwarzenegger, and replaced all purchased shirts free of charge, played a part.

Burnley refused to confirm the reason why the sponsorship ended but it’s understood Finotive One failed to meet its payments.

Sources also told Daily Mail Sport that difficulties had arisen in Holroyd and Pace’s working relationship and the Finotive One debacle did nothing to ease matters. A parting of the ways was decided to be best for all concerned.

The club dropped their shirt sponsor after just 42 days despite a star-studded launch that featured investor and former NFL star JJ Watt (right)

Holroyd has been replaced on an interim basis by Amy Wells, who was head of HR, and director of strategy and transformation Nathan Kavanagh.

Sources suggested Holroyd found the chairman too hands-on, a complaint echoed to Daily Mail Sport by other former members of staff, with one saying employees often felt they were not trusted to get on with their job.

Most of the staff who were in place when Pace's ALK took over are no longer there, many leaving within a year, leading to a sense among those close to the club that they cannot recognise the one they once knew.

‘These were local people, where the club meant everything to them, and one by one you saw them leave,’ said one former member of staff.

There’s a feeling that the sense of community and togetherness that forged a spirit able to take Burnley into Europe has been eroded.

Pace has spent money, and appointed two good managers in Vincent Kompany and Parker, but fans struggle to connect to an ever-revolving door of players they see as mercenaries as the club bounces between the Premier League and the Championship. None of them they see as personifying the famous ‘Legs, Hearts, Minds’ motto emblazoned on Sean Dyche’s request on a wall at the training ground.

The overwhelming sense among the fanbase now is that the last two promotions have papered over the cracks and the fissures are growing too wide to fix.

Manager Hayen is already under pressure and facing questions about his future and whether he’s been told defeat by Derby could spell the end. ‘Not at the moment,’ he said. ‘They didn't tell me this can be my last game. It can be, I don't know.’

Kyle Walker addressed staff this week to tell them that the players were doing everything they could to fix things.

Manager Nicky Hayen is already under pressure and facing questions about his future and whether he’s been told defeat by Derby today could spell the end

Midfielder Reo Hatate looks pained during Burnley's draw at Wrexham last week

So much of it, though, comes back to the money. The £142m debt from the most recent accounts for the 2024-25 promotion season, the interest on bank loans of up to 12 per cent, the £36m of net interest payments over the last five seasons when there was none before the takeover.

The £9.5m taken in ‘management fees’ under the current ownership, ones that jumped from £1.5m to £4m after relegation. The transfer debt of £95m that was just £3m four years ago and takes the club’s total gross debt to nearly a quarter of a billion. The near £40m sale of incoming transfer fees to London-based firm Fasanara Capital. And why Velocity Capital, ALK’s investment arm, still owes the football club around £81m.

Under the previous ownership, made up of local businessmen, Burnley were famously debt-free, cash rich, and one of the most profitable clubs in Premier League history. Dyche worked miracles on a budget as he established the Clarets in the Premier League and took them into Europe.

Now, according to respected finance blog Swiss Ramble, Burnley’s external debt of £142m last year was the fourth highest in England behind only Tottenham and Everton, who have built new stadiums, and the Glazers’ United.

‘There’s a few of us who have been querying the leveraged buyout model of Alan Pace for a few years,’ football finance expert Kieran Maguire tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘It’s reliant on Burnley regularly being in the Premier League for the broadcast cash flows, when its matchday income is only seven per cent of total revenue.

‘The concerns are that the club has £75m of short-terms loans, £30m of long-term loans, has sold players but has sold the transfer instalments from the sales and owes £94m in unpaid transfer fees. Under those circumstances they will struggle to borrow more and, if they do, will have to pay punitive interest rates.

‘It therefore could come down to whether or not Alan Pace has (a) the cash and (b) the desire to provide funding himself.’

Kyle Walker addressed staff this week to tell them that the players were doing everything they could to fix things

Sources suggested outgoing CEO James Holroyd found Pace too hands-on, a complaint echoed to Daily Mail Sport by other former members of staff

In response to questions about Burnley’s financial position, the club told Daily Mail Sport that the latest set of accounts, due to be submitted to the Premier League by October 31, ‘will give a more accurate picture of the current position’.

Those accounts are expected to show a fall in both debt and how much is still owed by Velocity to the club.

The management fees, meanwhile, are understood to be payments to non-full-time Burnley employees, such as consultants, for their services. The increase is thought to be due to performance-related bonuses.

The worry for Burnley, especially after such a torrid start to the campaign, is what happens if they don’t go up again this time. They are only getting two years of parachute payments instead of three as they came straight back down last season.

The £35m settlement Everton were forced to pay for breaking financial rules in the season Burnley were first relegated was a lifeline, but it remains uncertain whether the Clarets will ultimately receive it after the Toffees appealed against the decision.

Concerns have been raised, too, about whether Burnley will become a side dish as Pace and ALK expand their multi-club model. They have already purchased Spanish side Espanyol and are believed to be eyeing up Club Leon in Mexico.

In the most recent meeting between the club and its independent supporters association, the group was told, according to the latest newsletter, that ‘while EPL TV money is still available to the club, we will remain the priority’.

‘The question does remain what happens in the circumstances where the club is not quickly re-promoted to the EPL and the parachute money comes to an end,’ the newsletter continued.

There’s a feeling that the sense of community and togetherness that forged a spirit able to take Burnley into Europe under Sean Dyche has been eroded

Burnley have not been outside the top two divisions in more than a quarter of a century. They may well no longer exist had they not beat Leyton Orient on the final day in 1987 to stay in the Football League. Supporters worry that their status as a modest town club, surrounded by big cities, will make it even harder to fight their way back up.

‘There’s a feeling that we could be the next Leicester,’ said one source. The deeper fear, of course, is whether they could also become another Bury and be the first Premier League team to go bust.

The club, for now, are not in immediate danger of that and plans are said to be in place should the worst happen. But the longer Burnley remain outside the top flight and, heaven forbid, fall through the divisions, the more difficult it will be to keep on paying the piper.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick takes another swipe at referees after Erling Haaland's derby goal following huge VAR blunder - as Man United boss tells Howard Webb his apology 'doesn't mean an awful lot'
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick takes another swipe at referees after Erling Haaland's derby goal following huge VAR blunder - as Man United boss tells Howard Webb his apology 'doesn't mean an awful lot'

Michael Carrick says the apology from referees’ bosses for the VAR blunder over Erling Haaland’s goal in the Manchester derby ‘doesn’t mean an awful lot’.

Howard Webb, the head of Pro Ref, admitted the error after Haaland’s winner for Manchester City at Old Trafford last weekend was allowed to stand, even though his teammate Enzo Fernandez was in an offside position and clearly interfering with play.

Webb has blamed ‘tunnel vision’ for the mistake and stood down VAR officials Matt Donohue and Blake Antrobus until after the international break.

Carrick insists he still has faith in the system, but believes the best Manchester United can hope for now is that the marginal decisions will even themselves out over the course of the season.

‘Listen, one-off things can happen,’ he said as United prepare to return to Premier League action at Fulham on Sunday. ‘At the time it was a pretty big one, we know that. I don't think I need to go over that.

‘Yes, I've got faith in it, of course. It’s the system that we work towards and that we use, so the apology doesn't mean an awful lot.

Michael Carrick says Howard Webb's apology over Erling Haaland's goal 'doesn't mean a lot'

Enzo Fernandez was allowed to interfere with play before the goal in a huge VAR blunder

Webb has blamed 'tunnel vision' for the mistake and temporarily stood down the VAR officials

‘I can appreciate it and I respect them for putting their hands up and saying “we got that wrong”. It happens.

‘Moving forward, we just have to deal with what's thrown in front of us. Maybe we get one or two decisions on the back of how it balances out; percentages or law of averages or whatever that may be.’

Carrick has urged his players to put the controversy behind them and focus on recovering from a poor start to the season after losing half of their six games in all competitions.

‘That was a pretty big one to take and had a huge impact on that game, and that's why it was particularly tough,’ he added.

‘It can have an impact in that moment of time – it can have a big impact – but we can't let it have an impact on the rest of the season. That's for us to get back to winning ways as soon as possible.’

Sports.title: England set to rest Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson for T20 Australia tour as new coach Stephen Fleming sets out ambition to lead Test side to world No 1
Sports.content:
England will use a second-string bowling attack during the Twenty20 section of their upcoming tour to Australia in a bid to keep their Test artillery fresh for Stephen Fleming's debut series in South Africa in December.

In a first sign of how England's job share between Fleming and limited-overs coach Brendon McCullum will work, plans have been drawn up to rest Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson from the five T20 matches Down Under.

Although the trio will travel to Australia for the three one-day internationals taking place between 13-18 November - a year out from the World Cup in southern Africa - they are likely to be offered a period of rest before hooking up for an official warm-up fixture between 9-11 December, ahead of three Tests in South Africa.

It would mean Sonny Baker, Saqib Mahmood and Jamie Overton taking on greater seniority for a team that returned to the top of the Twenty20 rankings in completing a 3-0 whitewash of Sri Lanka at Emirates Old Trafford on Saturday.

'Right through the schedule we will look at what the priorities are and how we are able to manage the key players and personnel so that English cricket has the best opportunity to succeed in those times,' McCullum said, of trying to balance resources leading up to next summer's Ashes and the World Cup.

'How do we make sure we have got the best players available for that stuff? We will see, probably the fast bowlers in particular given a bit of a freshen up leading into that Test series, so therefore the T20s may be an area where we can introduce some new talent, which will be important for us as well, to keep growing our talent base in that space.

Plans have been drawn up to rest Jofra Archer (left) and Gus Atkinson (right) from the five T20 matches down under

It is a first sign of how England's job share between England's new Test coach Stephen Fleming (right) and limited-overs coach Brendon McCullum (left) will work

'We will work it out. We will do what we think is right to ensure everyone has the best opportunity to succeed and that will include, at times, having to sit guys out.'

Despite McCullum's talk of drafting in new talent, 38-year-old Richard Gleeson remains amongst the most effective English pacemen in the shortest format while Brydon Carse, 31, also enjoyed a good Hundred competition. His availability will depend on the outcome of a Cricket Regulator probe into a late night incident in Derby last month.

Meanwhile, Baker, who at 23 is at the other end of the career spectrum, took the man-of-the-match award in Manchester after completing a series analysis of 11.5-2-44-6 and was 'walking a foot taller on the back of it,' according to McCullum.

England will now focus on moving further up the one-day standings by winning a three-match ODI series versus the Sri Lankans starting in Chester-le-Street on Tuesday. Harry Brook's team are currently seventh, one place behind their opponents.

Fleming marked his unveiling as England coach on Saturday by setting himself the goal of toppling Australia as the world's No 1 Test team.

Speaking at Emirates Old Trafford, the 53-year-old nominated emulating the unique achievement of Andy Flower in taking an England team to the summit - staying there for 12 months from August 2011 - as the primary goal of a job he began with a tour of county cricket earlier this week.

'I would love to be in charge of the No 1 Test team in the world. That would be my aspiration,' Fleming said.

'The marquee events - the Ashes - are something I can't wait for. As a New Zealander, I have watched and loved the Ashes all my cricketing life, so to be part of that is an absolute highlight. I can't wait for that.'

'I would love to be in charge of the No 1 Test team in the world. That would be my aspiration,' Fleming said

Those five matches next June and July represent Fleming's first home series in charge, and he will hope to have narrowed the 24-point chasm by then between the Australians and an England side currently languishing in mid-table - the 3-0 whitewash of a poor Pakistan earlier this month, overseen by captain Joe Root and interim head coach Marcus Trescothick representing a first series win since 2024.

Fleming's family and business commitments meant he was slow out of the blocks, after being appointed in July and some will even argue it's a false start, as he will honour his contractual obligations as a commentator with Sky in his homeland for four T20 matches between New Zealand and India next month before heading to South Africa for his first assignment this December.

As a coach it is T20 that he is associated with, following 18 years in charge of Chennai Super Kings at the Indian Premier League, but he was 'kissing coaches' heads' at four County Championship fixtures this week, reacquainting himself with the English domestic game, having captained Nottinghamshire to the title in 2005, and was quick to remind people of his influence on New Zealand's cricket as a player.

'My DNA was based on Test cricket. I am inherently a red ball lover, and that was where I learned strategy, leadership, captaincy, the nuances of the game,' he said.

'If anything, I moulded myself into the white ball world based on man management and strategy and leadership.'

One of the relationships he developed at Chennai was with Ben Stokes, and although the pair caught up at Chester-le-Street on Thursday, Fleming was quick to dismantle suggestions of England's ex-captain launching a sensational comeback against Australia next summer.

'My view – when a player decides to retire it's a big decision and I have the utmost respect for that decision so that's where it sits,' he said.

Stokes was, however, along with Fleming's compatriot and close friend McCullum, the subject of praise for creating a template for Test cricket in this country to which he will look to add pragmatism.

Of comparisons in style to McCullum, Fleming said: 'I'll bet on the favourite and he'll bet on the longest odds possible.'

Adding: 'It depends which timeline you want to talk about but for me, the way they changed the nature of Test cricket was quite remarkable. I have a huge amount of respect for the courage that took. Obviously the last 12 months it hasn't evolved as they would have liked, or the fans would have liked, but as a lover of cricket I was very impressed with how the team went about it.'

Among the changes Fleming says he would like to instill, creating a new 'identity' for the team, is greater discipline both on and off the field, vowing to bowl overs quicker in a bid to avoid World Test Championship points penalties and improve image following a spate of alcohol-related incidents.

Unable to comment on the news that Carse has avoided charges following a police investigation into a Derby nightclub incident due to an ongoing secondary probe by the Cricket Regulator, Fleming did offer guidance on the conduct he expects within the squad he inherits.

'If you want an example, a great example of how to behave as an international cricketer, Joe Root is it,' he said.

Sports.title: Ex-Chelsea manager Liam Rosenior sparks heated on-pitch melee after taunting former club Strasbourg as he claims fans 'disrespected my family'
Sports.content:
Ex-Chelsea manager Liam Rosenior sparks heated on-pitch melee after taunting former club Strasbourg as he claims fans 'disrespected my family'

Paris FC manager Liam Rosenior's exuberant post-match celebrations against former side Strasbourg incited a scuffle between the coach and Strasbourg players.

Rosenior's Paris FC beat Strasbourg 2-1 at home on Saturday. The English coach, who spent 18 months at Strasbourg prior to joining Chelsea last year, could be seen pointing his finger, slapping his chest and raising his arms towards the travelling fans after the final whistle.

Within moments, Strasbourg players walked over to confront Rosenior before members of the Paris FC squad sprinted over to lend support to their manager. A shoving match between the two sets of players ensued, with Rosenior in the middle of the fracas.

After the match, Rosenior said that his enthusiastic celebrations had been a result of being provoked by sections of the Strasbourg fanbase, who he claimed had insulted his family.

The 42-year-old said: '(There was a small part of the Strasbourg) support who disrespected my family. I understand the context of what they were saying. My bench were visibly upset.

'I want to make this very clear: a small section. Strasbourg is a fantastic football club, with great people who work for the club, and great people who support the club.

😳 Scène surréaliste à l’issue de la défaite du Racing à Jean Bouin.



Insulté pendant la rencontre, Liam Rosenior est venu narguer les supporters strasbourgeois. Lucas Hogsberg est venu lui dire d’arrêter avant des échauffourées dans la confusion. #RCSA #LeClubRacing pic.twitter.com/RHE3cQj4e6 — CLUB RACING (@LECLUBRACING) September 19, 2026

The English coach slapped his chest and raised his arms towards the Strasbourg fans after the final whistle

A shoving match between the two sets of players ensued, with Rosenior caught in the middle of the fracas

'For me to celebrate in that way was a message. A message to a group of people who never wanted me to be successful at that club. But I'm not going to say any more than that.'

Rosenior also addressed the incident in a post-match interview with Ligue 1+.

'The people in the club (Strasbourg) who know me know I've always been respectful, I've always wanted the best for that football club,' he said. 'I still do want the best for that football club.

'But when I heard the chants - I understand French, I understand the context, the language - that's a step too far.

'It's a wonderful football club, it's a great city, it's a club with great tradition, I've always protected those traditions.

'So for me to celebrate in the way that I did was for many reasons. Many reasons.'

Paris FC clinched a deserved win at the Stade Jean-Bouin through goals from Ilan Kebbal and Pablo Pagis, despite conceding a late own goal by Moustapha Mbow.

It was another step in a positive start to the season, with Paris FC having won three and drawn two of their opening five matches to sit third in Ligue 1, two points behind table-toppers Monaco.

Sports.title: Tottenham make pre-match facilities for visiting teams less hospitable, Donald Trump's links to the darkest levels of sport and plans for Ryder Cup to be held in Bolton accelerate: INSIDE SPORT
Sports.content:
Tottenham make pre-match facilities for visiting teams less hospitable, Donald Trump's links to the darkest levels of sport and plans for Ryder Cup to be held in Bolton accelerate: INSIDE SPORT

Tottenham are pulling out all the stops in an attempt to make their new stadium less hospitable for visiting teams.

Those who previously travelled to the shiny facility were treated to a dressing room along with no fewer than four separate rooms in which to prepare.

However, it has been noticeable that some of the rooms have now been locked on matchdays, bringing the facilities offered in line with their Premier League rivals.

The decision is thought to have been made by senior leadership, with the backing of manager Roberto De Zerbi.

Plans for the Ryder Cup to be held in Bolton, first revealed by Daily Mail Sport in 2021, appear to be gathering pace. New Prime Minister Andy Burnham is known to be behind the proposals, while Greater Manchester Combined Authority have already green-lighted £60m for a key new road around the site, in Hulton Park.

Officials are now waiting to hear if they have been chosen as the venue for the UK's bid for the event in 2035.

Tottenham are pulling out all the stops in an attempt to make their new stadium less hospitable

If the Trump family's investment into the Enhanced Games, alongside their shameless involvement in the Gianni Infantino scheme to plunder the soul of world football was bad enough, along comes an even more bizarre case with links to the highest and darkest levels of world sport.

The hugely influential Russian oligarch, Umar Kremlev, who is close to president Vladimir Putin is widely reported to have covered the cost of Donald Trump Jr's recent wedding.

Kremlev is also the president of the Olympic-ostracized International Boxing Association and is desperately seeking high level connections to get back in favour with the IOC.

And while the Trump family are now claiming it will all be paid back, their portfolio of wealth generation schemes from the darker side of sport continues to grow.

There is a buzz among publishers about a book at the early stages of being written by former West Ham midfielder and maverick manager Martin Allen.

Allen, better known throughout football as 'Mad Dog', has been putting down the stories from a playing and managerial career stretching back more than four decades.

Umar Kremlev, who is close to president Vladimir Putin is widely reported to have covered the cost of Donald Trump Jr's recent wedding

Among the many tales there is understood to be a sensitive episode from Allen's past that will require careful legal consideration before publication. Allen won't discuss the details, saying only: 'I've got plenty of stories.' The book is still at an early stage, but it would appear that Mad Dog has rather more to tell than the usual well-worn dressing-room autobiography.

There were raised eyebrows at Southampton when officials watched the Jose Mourinho documentary on Netflix.

In one revealing section, former Chelsea captain John Terry reveals that Mourinho obtained a video of a Bolton Wanderers training session, before the two were to play each other.

'It was just like – wow, who gets footage from someone's training ground? I am actually still not sure where he got the footage from!'

Saints are waiting to hear the FA's punishment for their role in Spygate, having been thrown out of last season's play-offs by the EFL after an intern was caught filming a Boro session from behind a tree.

Sports.title: Former Premier League star jokes Stoke away 'wasn't so bad after all' after being RUN OVER by a pitch rolling machine at half-time during match in Thailand
Sports.content:
Former Tottenham and Everton winger Andros Townsend was bizarrely run over by a roller as he was warming up for a game in Thailand. The ex-England man-turned pundit, 35, is plying his trade in the Far East, having joined PT Prachuap in the summer transfer window. Over the break, he was in the United States covering the World Cup for ITV, and made headlines for some of his diet choices during the tournament. Incredibly, though, on Saturday, he narrowly avoided serious injury when he found himself under a pitch roller while he warmed up at half-time. Footage showed the driver of the roller struggling to control the vehicle, with Townsend kicking a ball away, not looking in that direction, and the crowd gasped. The roller then hit Townsend, and he fell to the floor, with the roller literally going over his legs and lower body. 🚨Andros Townsend got lucky to avoid injury during warmups in the Thai League pic.twitter.com/ctEOycMZcF — Polymarket Sports (@PolymarketSport) September 19, 2026 Andros Townsend was bizarrely run over while warming up for a game in Thailand on Saturday Townsend went viral during the World Cup for his bizarre diet, which includes eating raw meat Incredibly, he walked away unharmed, and came on as a substitute late on in his side's 3-0 win. He would later share a video of the incident to his Instagram page. He joked on his Instagram story: 'It turns out Stoke away wasn't so bad after all. Swipe to see why.' Another post described Townsend as 'The King of Memes in Thai League history' and he replied 'trust me' with four laughing emojis on his profile. PT Prachuap – based in Prachuap Khiri Khan province, 150 miles south of Bangkok – appeared to have leaked Townsend's arrival two weeks before he joined when they asked if anyone had a three-bedroom house available for the player to live in. They are the 17th club of his career. Townsend made 29 appearances for Kanchanaburi Power last season, scoring three goals. He has previously played for Spurs, Newcastle, Palace and Everton, and moved to Thailand after a short spell with Turkish side Antalyaspor. Townsend making the move comes after he worked for ITV as a co-commentator during the World Cup. The ex-England winger went viral at the tournament for his unconventional diet – which includes eating raw steak. He released a slew of videos promoting his all-natural diet including the steak, sardines and boiled eggs on a plane. Townsend's aim was to stay healthy while staying in hotels throughout the tournament, while being denied access to cooking facilities and facing the constant temptation of fast food. 'Never let your circumstances dictate your health,' he says. Townsend claims to have been eating raw meat for four years, dating back to his time when he was in the Premier League and would have had access to industry-leading dietary advice.

Sports.title: Man Utd, Liverpool and Chelsea have questions to answer in best of the rest race
Sports.content:
Arsenal endured what they hope will be a blip at Brighton on Saturday afternoon, but even in spite of that 3-0 reverse, they and Manchester City will still go into the first international break as the Premier League's top two.

After four games the two teams, who have battled it out for the title in three of the past four seasons, had perfect records. Four wins from four.

Arsenal have been tipped by some to retain their Premier League crown with relative ease. They've hardly been out of second gear. City, despite their mass overhaul on the pitch and in the dugout, could provide more of a challenge than some expected before a ball was kicked.

The bookies have Arsenal favourites at 11/10 to win the title, City just behind at 8/5. The next best after that is 20/1, which tells its own story of how the Premier League is shaping up.

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

But the battle to be best of the rest could prove one of the most intriguing subplots of the season, even if it is only five weeks old. The so-called top six may remain from a financial point of view, but rarely have we seen them finish in the top six for some time.

Last season saw the bulk of the big hitters come to the fore, and those who didn't generated excitement with some of their decisions over the summer. But already things aren't necessarily shaping up as we'd expected.

‌



Arsenal's loss at Brighton aside, they and City have looked levels above the rest. So if third is the new first, who might land that spot come May?

Liverpool

Andoni Iraola took on the challenge of whether he could step up a level having continually outperformed his resources at Bournemouth. At Liverpool he's had to deal with the weight of expectation and a squad, which whilst expensive, lacks balance and still has obvious flaws.

View 4 Images Florian Wirtz has come in for criticism from some quarters (Image: Images)

Bradley Barcola became the third £100million plus player to arrive at Anfield in the last 12 months, following Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak. And yet Liverpool appear a side boasting stellar individuals struggling to become a collective.

‌



Defensively they can be got at and plans need to be made for life after Virgil van Dijk. The lack of an obvious holding midfielder remains and finding a position for Wirtz, which doesn't harm the team, is becoming more of an issue.

Three draws already has underlined their issues, the only win coming over Ipswich. Iraola has claimed the team cannot yet do what he's asked, in pre-season he claimed they couldn't do it for long enough. His Bournemouth success owed to huge buy in from the players, and huge work rate. Failure to get those could make things problematic.

Man Utd

However frustrating it's been at Anfield though, it is nothing compared to what's going on at Old Trafford. Before the season started many had the Red Devils in the mix for the top four, at the very least.

The loss in the Manchester derby will have stung, not least because Pro Ref admitted the winning goal shouldn't have stood. But the failure to take advantage of City's red card highlighted a lack of a killer instinct. The good will from last season's rise to third spot under Michael Carrick has largely disappeared, even if there is a desire from the fanbase to see one of their own succeed.

‌



View 4 Images Man Utd have won just once in the Premier League this season (Image: Martin Rickett/PA Wire)

The opening-day loss to Hull was an eye opener and, even in the demolition of Ipswich, United still conceded twice on their own patch. Choosing to not add defensive reinforcements in the summer looks a massive blunder and the midfield doesn't, currently, look like a unit that has had £150m spent on it.

Carlos Baleba is yet to make his debut, but it's a stretch to think he can solve their problems alone. An inability to manage games or keep goals out looks set to plague Carrick's team for months, unless something changes soon.

Chelsea

Two games in, despite games being somewhat chaotic, the Blues looked to be upwardly mobile. Xabi Alonso, of all the new managers in the top flight, has the most pedigree owing to his Bundesliga success with Bayer Leverkusen.

‌



They acquitted themselves well enough at Arsenal, even if they did lose from a winning position, but the results since have showcased, had their been any doubt, that this is a team still very much learning. Hull taking a point from Stamford Bridge came before the damaging loss at Brentford.

In Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer they'll always offer a threat in the final third, but like some of their rivals they lack overall balance throughout the team.

View 4 Images Chelsea's defence has been a major issue in the opening weeks of the season (Image: Getty Images)

Enzo Fernandez wasn't replaced on deadline day, leaving a notable void, and Alonso can ill afford for the Blues to concede at the rate they are. Shipping 12 goals in five games gives them the worst defence in the top flight.

‌



An outsider

Aston Villa? Brentford or Brighton? Before a ball had been kicked you may have looked at Tottenham as a top four contender, not now. Newcastle already flirt between being a good side and one that will frustrate, but they are embarking on a new era.

As the table stands going into the international break its the Seagulls, fresh off their Arsenal demolition job, that sit third. They and Brentford can both bask in the glory of 3-0 wins against some of the Premier League's elite for the next few weeks, even if their managers will no doubt get their focus fixed on what's to come, not what's happened.

Both are terrifically coached, with a sprinkling of star quality. Brentford must be wise to the fact Mamadou Sangare could be on the radar of Europe's top dogs before too long.

Villa showed signs of clicking into gear on Saturday lunchtime, but a win over Tottenham is becoming less and less impressive with each passing week. Unai Emery has proven himself time and time again and their season will come down to how quickly his new players can gel and embrace his ideas.

‌



Tottenham off the back of spending £300m on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes and Omar Marmoush were an intriguing prospect, but already look as if they're more likely for relegation than European football.

Of course, fast starts are no guarantee of season-long form. Liverpool won five from five last year and were scrapping to make the Champions League after collapsing, so Arsenal or City could well be usurped from the top two positions they currently hold. But conventional wisdom, and recent history, suggests they're the benchmark the others are chasing.
