World.title: Amina Orfi set to become youngest Women’s Squash World #1 at age 19
World.content:
Egyptian squash prodigy Amina Orfi has made history by becoming the youngest player ever to reach World #1 in women’s squash – at just 19 years old.

Orfi clinched the top spot after winning the QTerminals Qatar Classic in a thrilling 3-2 final against compatriot Hania al-Hammamy, raising her total to 2,109 points and dethroning the world standings leader.

The reigning World Champion and four-time World Junior Champion survived a tense fifth-game decider to secure the title.

Speaking to Al-Ahram, Orfi acknowledged the final’s intensity and emphasized her resolve to hold onto the top ranking as she eyes gold at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

From surprise exits to marathon wins

Semifinal runs: Orfi swept America’s Olivia Weaver 3–0 to reach the final, while al-Hammamy outlasted Malaysia’s world #5 Sivasangari Subramaniam 3–2 in a marathon battle.

Early exits: Eight-time World Champion Nour al-Sherbini suffered a surprise 1–3 defeat against Malaysia’s Delia Arnold.

Withdrawals: Former World #1 Nouran Gohar—returning to the tour following a two-year maternity break—and Belgium’s Tinne Gilis both withdrew in the quarterfinals.

World.title: Egyptian physicist Ahmed Al-Gendy wins global Marie Curie Medal for nanotech cancer treatment
World.content:
Egyptian physicist Ahmed al-Gendy, an associate professor of physics at the University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP), has earned global scientific acclaim after receiving the 2026 Marie Curie Medal for his breakthrough work applying nanotechnology to cancer treatment.

Conferred by the Sweden-based International Association of Advanced Materials (IAAM), the prestigious award honors groundbreaking research in advanced materials science.

Al-Gendy was chosen for his pioneering contribution to magnetic nanomaterials and their targeted application in oncology.

The UTEP’s College of Science formally announced the honor across its official platforms, celebrating the milestone.

A second major honor from the IAAM

The recognition marks al-Gendy’s second major distinction from the International Association of Advanced Materials in just two years, following his receipt of the IAAM Advanced Materials Award in 2024.

Securing back-to-back honors from the international body reflects the scientific community’s interest on his research into magnetic nanostructures.

Targeting solid tumors with magnetic nanoparticles

The award coincides with the publication of new research by al-Gendy’s team in the journal Acta Biomaterialia.

The study details the development of specialized magnetic nanoparticles engineered to directly target and destroy solid tumors when activated by an alternating magnetic field.

World.title: William V.S. Tubman Jr., 93, Son of Liberia’s Longest-Serving President, Dies
World.content:
Monrovia – William V.S. Tubman Jr., son of former President William V.S. Tubman and son-in-law of President William R. Tolbert Jr., has died at 93.

Mr. Tubman was born in 1933, the son of William V.S. Tubman, who served as Liberia’s president from 1944 until his death in 1971 — the longest tenure of any Liberian head of state. He was also the son-in-law of his father’s successor, President William R. Tolbert Jr., having married Tolbert’s daughter, Wokie.

Known widely as “Shad,” Tubman became a public figure in his own right early in life. In the 1950s, his father’s influence saw him named head of the country’s Congress of Industrial Organizations, and he went on to serve as a senator during both the Tubman and Tolbert administrations.

Though born into one of Liberia’s most powerful families, Mr. Tubman often spoke of his life in terms of struggle rather than privilege, comparing himself to the Biblical Moses — a man born into comfort who endured hardship before leading his people. In earlier years, he had publicly broken with his father’s positions and pressed for greater political inclusion of Liberia’s tribal population, straining his relationship with both his father and his father-in-law.

He survived the bloody coup of April 12, 1980, in which President Tolbert and much of the country’s governing establishment were killed. Mr. Tubman was attending an international conference in Norway and taking a stopover in New York when the coup occurred; he did not return to Liberia and reunite with his family until more than a month later. In the coup’s immediate aftermath, he retained a measure of popularity among ordinary Liberians, and rumors persisted — never substantiated — that he had ties to the ruling military council.

In later years, Mr. Tubman was affiliated with the Reformed United Liberia Party (RULP).

Funeral arrangements have not been announced.

World.title: Liberia: Suspected Narcotics Shipment From Malaysia Under Testing at Roberts Airport Amid Growing Trafficking Concerns
World.content:
Photographs reviewed by FPA show the consignment arrived packed across multiple DHL “GoGreen Plus” cartons, each marked with recommended-weight guides and shipping labels citing waybill number 96 5091 8255.

A 202.5 kg shipment declared as botanical powder, coffee and candy — sent from Malaysia and cleared through Roberts International Airport customs — is now being tested for narcotics after drawing suspicion, FrontPageAfrica has learned. The development adds to a year marked by escalating cocaine seizures that have placed Liberia at the center of West Africa’s trafficking corridor.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – Liberian authorities are testing materials recovered from a shipment that arrived at Roberts International Airport (RIA) via DHL from Malaysia to determine whether it is narcotics, according to documents obtained by FrontPageAfrica Saturday.

FrontPageAfrica has been informed that Liberian investigators are working with US authorities as part of ongoing probe into the recent wave of drug busts in Liberia.

Paperwork in possession of FPA shows the shipment — declared as “Botanical Powder, Coffee, Candy,” weighing roughly 202.5 kg — was sent by Dynamic Ace Global Sdn Bhd of Selangor, Malaysia, and consigned to a Tan Gouet Gerard at an address on Fiamah Coleman Avenue, Monrovia.

Photographs reviewed by FPA show the consignment arrived packed across multiple DHL “GoGreen Plus” cartons, each marked with recommended-weight guides and shipping labels citing waybill number 96 5091 8255. Shipping labels further indicate the consignment was broken into multiple pieces — one carton examined was marked “Piece 3/9,” with an individual weight of 22.5 kg against a total shipment weight of 202.5 kg, suggesting the shipment arrived as nine separate cartons rather than a single package. Inside, the goods were packaged as ordinary consumer wellness products: boxes of “Aceguard” — an herbal immune-support powder branded under the “Dynace” label, sold in sachets — sat alongside foil pouches of “Triple Root Coffee,” an arabica blend infused with ginseng-style root extracts, and slim cartons of “Rocenta,” described on its packaging as a botanical drink mix featuring lotus and other herbal ingredients. On paper, the shipment reads as a routine consignment of herbal supplements and gourmet coffee.

Records show the Liberia Revenue Authority assessed the shipment at RIA’s collectorate on September 18, 2026, and it was released after $437.65 in duties, levies and GST were paid in cash — before the material apparently drew suspicion.

Records show the Liberia Revenue Authority assessed the shipment at RIA’s collectorate on September 18, 2026, and it was released after $437.65 in duties, levies and GST were paid in cash — before the material apparently drew suspicion.

Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency and local customs officials are yet to confirm at what stage the parcels were flagged and what triggered testing.

A separate document obtained by FPA — a Laissez-Passer issued by police in Danané, Côte d’Ivoire, dated September 9, 2026 — records travel clearance for an Ivorian national heading to Liberia; its connection to the shipment, if any, is unconfirmed.

Context: A Year of Escalating Busts

If confirmed, this would be the latest in a string of major narcotics interceptions that have put Liberia at the center of West Africa’s cocaine-trafficking corridor this year:

• June 8, 2026 — LDEA and joint security intercepted 198 compressed plates of cocaine (about 237.6 kg) hidden in six cargo boxes at RIA, bound for Europe via Brussels Airlines, valued at an estimated US$19.2 million. • Late June–July — Lawmakers summoned LDEA, immigration, customs and airport officials over the case; five suspects were eventually charged. • July 22, 2026 — Security forces raided a warehouse in Duazon, Margibi County, detaining two foreign nationals in what was then called the country's largest cocaine haul. • July 21–23, 2026 — Police announced an even larger seizure: nearly four tonnes of cocaine, worth an estimated $317 million. • August 19, 2026 — Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor was arrested and later remanded in custody in connection with what officials called one of the biggest drug busts in Liberia's history, alongside two Croatian nationals and a Ukrainian national.

Civil-society groups have repeatedly flagged Liberia’s growing role as a transit hub for cocaine moving from South America toward European and Middle Eastern markets, and criticized a pattern where seizures are heavily publicized but prosecutions stall.

This developing story will be updated as more information becomes available.

World.title: Liberia: LNP Launches New Recruitment Drive, Betting on Numbers and Reform to Rebuild Public Trust
World.content:
Inspector General Gregory Coleman told recruits Friday that the force is currently at a roughly 21-to-79 ratio of women to men and is targeting 33 percent female representation, framing the goal as part of the reform agenda under President Joseph Nyumah Boakai’s administration.

Inspector General Gregory O.W. Coleman has launched a new Liberia National Police recruitment exercise, framing it as central to nearly two decades of post-war security sector reform. The drive echoes past campaigns going back to a 2007 UNMIL-backed push for female recruits, and revives familiar goals: closing the police-to-population gap, replacing an aging workforce, and lifting women’s representation toward a 33 percent target from the current 21 percent. Coleman also pledged the process would be merit-based and free of bribery, as the force seeks roughly $12 million to add 1,500 officers ahead of the 2029 elections.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia- Liberia’s police force is opening its doors to a new generation of officers, with the Liberia National Police (LNP) launching a recruitment exercise this week that officials describe as central to consolidating nearly two decades of security sector reform.

Speaking at the launch, Inspector General of Police Gregory O.W. Coleman told an audience of government officials, international partners, security sector representatives and civil society leaders that the drive is not simply about growing headcount. “Our objective is not simply to increase the size of the police service,” he said. “It is to strengthen an institution that is already serving the Liberian people and make it more representative, inclusive, accessible, responsive and effective.”

A FORCE STILL REBUILDING

The LNP’s story is inseparable from Liberia’s post-war history. Formed in 1956, the force was gutted during back-to-back civil wars that ended in 2003, and much of its modern rebuilding took place under the United Nations Mission in Liberia (UNMIL), which helped restructure and retrain the LNP alongside Liberian authorities in the years that followed.

That rebuilding produced a string of recruitment drives. In 2007, UNMIL and the LNP relaunched a campaign specifically targeting female applicants, after the force fell short of a 3,500-officer recruitment goal. At the time, then-LNP Director Beatrice Munah Sieh — the first woman to head the force — pointed to a persistent obstacle: “The Police remain unattractive to the public due to low salary, incentives, and negative perceptions.” UN officials framed the push as part of a broader democratic transformation, with then-Deputy Special Representative Luiz Carlos da Costa arguing that “sustainable peace is founded on the bedrock of a genuinely democratic law enforcement agency.”

Nearly two decades on, the LNP has grown into a force of roughly 4,100 officers operating 151 stations nationwide, contributing personnel to UN peacekeeping missions in South Sudan and taking on a widening set of responsibilities — from gender-based violence response to counter-narcotics and, increasingly, cyber-enabled crime.

OLD PROBLEMS, NEW URGENCY

But many of the same pressures that drove earlier recruitment pushes remain. Coleman has told lawmakers the force needs roughly $12 million to recruit and train 1,500 additional officers, citing manpower shortages that officials want addressed before the 2029 general and presidential elections. In late 2024, Coleman also announced a shift in recruitment strategy — enlisting officers from within their own counties rather than assigning Monrovia-trained recruits to rural posts, a practice he said had proven ineffective because transferred officers “end up struggling to return to their families.”

Officials are casting the recruitment drive as one piece of a larger institutional rebuild that also depends on training, logistics, welfare systems and accountability structures — pieces that outside donors have historically helped fund.

That county-based approach echoes through this week’s launch remarks, in which Coleman singled out Liberia’s police-to-population ratio as a priority. Rural and hard-to-reach communities, he said, stand to benefit most from a larger, more locally rooted workforce, while an aging cohort of veteran officers approaching retirement adds urgency to building a pipeline of new recruits who can absorb their institutional knowledge before it is lost.

GENDER AT THE CENTER

If the 2007 drive marked the LNP’s first major push for female recruits, this exercise sets a firmer benchmark. Coleman said the force is currently at a roughly 21-to-79 ratio of women to men and is targeting 33 percent female representation, framing the goal as part of the reform agenda under President Joseph Nyumah Boakai’s administration.

Coleman was careful to frame gender-responsive policing as more than a recruitment target. It means, he said, recognizing that “women, men, girls and boys may experience crime, violence and insecurity differently,” and removing the barriers — including harassment and discrimination within the ranks — that keep women from applying, staying and rising through leadership.

GUARDING AGAINST CORRUPTION

Coleman also used the launch to draw a hard line against a problem that has dogged public hiring processes in Liberia before: the buying and selling of positions. “No applicant should pay money to secure a place in the Liberia National Police,” he said, warning that anyone caught selling recruitment forms, exam results or job offers would be investigated. Candidates, he said, will be assessed strictly against published requirements — character, education, physical and medical fitness.

WHAT COMES NEXT

Officials are casting the recruitment drive as one piece of a larger institutional rebuild that also depends on training, logistics, welfare systems and accountability structures — pieces that outside donors have historically helped fund. Coleman thanked international partners for continued support and said Liberia is looking to deepen that cooperation on training, infrastructure and technology as the new recruits move through the pipeline.

Whether this drive succeeds where earlier ones fell short of their targets may hinge on the same issues officials flagged nearly twenty years ago: pay, working conditions and public perception of the job. For now, Coleman is appealing directly to the next generation of applicants, urging “qualified women and men of good character” from every county to come forward — a call that will be tested in the weeks ahead as recruitment offices open and the force works to convert launch-day rhetoric into filled positions.

World.title: Global Governance Initiative: Towards a More Inclusive and Equitable Global Order
World.content:
Siafa G. Sheriff

President

Liberia-China Friendship Organization

Introduction

The twenty-first century is characterized by rapid globalization, technological advancement, economic transformation, and increasing interdependence among nations. At the same time, the world faces complex challenges, including armed conflicts, climate change, poverty, inequality, food insecurity, public health emergencies, terrorism, economic instability, and the rapid development of artificial intelligence. These challenges do not respect national borders and cannot be effectively addressed by individual countries acting alone. They require cooperation, dialogue, coordination, and collective action at the international level.

By Siafa G. Sheriff President Liberia-China Friendship Organization

In this context, the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) provides an important framework for thinking about how countries can work together to address common global challenges. The initiative emphasizes principles such as fairness, justice, equality among nations, multilateral cooperation, peaceful coexistence, consultation, and shared responsibility. It also highlights the need to make global governance more representative of the interests of developing countries and the Global South.

Understanding Global Governance

Global governance refers to the rules, institutions, agreements, and processes through which countries and other international actors cooperate to manage issues that affect the global community. Unlike national governments, there is no single world government. Instead, global governance is carried out through international institutions, treaties, regional organizations, governments, civil society, businesses, and other stakeholders.

Organizations such as the United Nations, African Union, World Bank, International Monetary Fund, World Trade Organization, and other multilateral institutions contribute to global governance. These institutions provide platforms for countries to discuss international problems, establish common rules, promote development, and resolve disputes.

However, the international system has evolved significantly since many of these institutions were established. The growth of developing economies, the increasing population of Africa, technological transformation, and changes in global economic and political relations have created calls for reforms that better reflect contemporary realities.

The Importance of the Global Governance Initiative

The Global Governance Initiative is important because many global challenges require collective solutions. Climate change, pandemics, international financial instability, food security, cyber threats, and technological development cannot be effectively managed by one country.

A more effective system of global governance should therefore encourage countries to cooperate while respecting national sovereignty and differences in political systems, cultures, histories, and levels of economic development.

Another important aspect is representation. Developing countries have often argued that their influence in major international institutions does not correspond with their population, economic potential, or contributions to global affairs. Strengthening the participation of developing countries can make international decision-making more inclusive.

The initiative therefore supports the idea that global governance should be based on consultation rather than unilateral decision-making and that countries should have opportunities to contribute to the formation of international policies.

Africa and Global Governance

Africa has a vital role to play in the transformation of global governance. The continent has abundant natural resources, a large and youthful population, expanding markets, and significant potential for economic growth and innovation. Africa is also increasingly important in discussions concerning climate change, food security, energy, migration, peace, and international development.

Nevertheless, African countries continue to face challenges such as poverty, inadequate infrastructure, limited access to technology, debt pressures, unemployment, and insufficient development financing. These challenges demonstrate the importance of stronger international cooperation.

The African Union can play a significant role in coordinating African positions on global issues. Greater unity among African countries can strengthen the continent’s ability to participate effectively in international negotiations and advocate for reforms that reflect African priorities.

Africa should not simply be a recipient of international development assistance. It should be an active partner in shaping international policies and contributing solutions to global challenges.

China, Africa, and Global Governance

China-Africa cooperation provides an important example of South-South cooperation. Over the years, China and African countries have expanded cooperation in infrastructure, trade, education, healthcare, agriculture, technology, and cultural exchanges.

The Global Governance Initiative places emphasis on strengthening cooperation among countries and addressing common challenges through dialogue and consultation. Within this framework, China-Africa cooperation can contribute to development and international cooperation.

African countries can benefit from cooperation in areas such as infrastructure development, industrialization, digital technology, agricultural modernization, education, and skills development. At the same time, African countries bring their own experiences, resources, markets, and perspectives to international cooperation.

Such cooperation should be based on mutual respect, shared interests, equality, and the development priorities of participating countries.

Global Governance and Sustainable Development

Global governance is closely connected to sustainable development. The Sustainable Development Goals emphasize the importance of eliminating poverty and hunger, improving health and education, promoting decent work, protecting the environment, and reducing inequality.

Achieving these goals requires international partnerships. Developing countries often require financing, technology, technical expertise, and capacity-building support to implement ambitious development programs.

For African countries, international cooperation can support infrastructure development, renewable energy, healthcare systems, education, agriculture, and digital transformation. A more equitable global governance system should therefore create opportunities for developing countries to access the resources necessary to achieve sustainable development.

Peace and International Security

Peace and security are fundamental components of effective global governance. Armed conflicts can destroy infrastructure, disrupt economies, create refugees, and undermine development.

The Global Governance Initiative emphasizes the importance of dialogue, consultation, peaceful coexistence, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Countries should use diplomatic mechanisms and international institutions to resolve disagreements whenever possible.

For Africa, strengthening regional peace and security mechanisms is particularly important. The African Union and regional organizations have an important responsibility in preventing conflicts, supporting mediation, and promoting stability.

At the global level, stronger cooperation among major powers is also necessary to address international security challenges and prevent disagreements from developing into wider conflicts.

Technology and Global Governance

Technology is transforming the global economy and society. Artificial intelligence, digital platforms, biotechnology, cybersecurity, and other emerging technologies create enormous opportunities but also raise new governance challenges.

Developing countries must have opportunities to participate in the digital economy. Closing the digital divide requires investment in internet connectivity, digital infrastructure, education, research, and technological skills.

Global governance should encourage responsible technological development while ensuring that developing countries are not permanently left behind.

The Role of Youth

Youth participation is essential to the future of global governance. Africa has one of the world’s youngest populations, making young people important stakeholders in the continent’s development.

Young people should be encouraged to participate in international exchanges, education, entrepreneurship, technology, diplomacy, peacebuilding, and cultural programs. People-to-people exchanges can also promote mutual understanding among countries and civilizations.

Youth should therefore be viewed not only as beneficiaries of development but also as partners in creating solutions to global challenges.

Conclusion

The Global Governance Initiative provides an important framework for strengthening international cooperation in a rapidly changing world. Its emphasis on fairness, equality, consultation, multilateralism, peaceful coexistence, and shared development responds to many of the challenges facing the international community.

For Africa, the initiative offers an opportunity to strengthen the continent’s participation in global affairs and ensure that African perspectives are better represented in international decision-making. China-Africa cooperation and broader South-South partnerships can contribute to development, technology, infrastructure, education, health, and people-to-people exchanges.

The future of global governance should be based on cooperation rather than confrontation, dialogue rather than isolation, and partnership rather than exclusion. By strengthening international institutions, increasing the participation of developing countries, supporting sustainable development, promoting peace, and empowering young people, the international community can work toward a more inclusive and equitable global order.

The success of global governance ultimately depends on the willingness of nations to recognize their shared responsibilities and work together to address challenges that affect humanity as a whole.

World.title: ICE Deports Former Liberian Combatant Accused of War-Era Atrocities
World.content:
Photo credit: Fox News

Monrovia — A former Liberian combatant accused by U.S. authorities of involvement in killings, torture and the recruitment of child soldiers during Liberia’s civil wars has been deported from the United States to Liberia after nearly two decades in the country.

According to an exclusive report by Fox News, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) deported Amos Sheik Massaquoi, 55, to Liberia on August 11, 2026, following years of immigration proceedings in the United States.

Massaquoi is believed to have served as chief bodyguard to Maj. Gen. Daniel Chea, a former leader in Charles Taylor’s National Patriotic Front of Liberia (NPFL).

According to ICE, Massaquoi is believed to have ordered or participated in extrajudicial killings, torture, arbitrary arrests and detentions, forced labor and the recruitment of child soldiers during Liberia’s civil wars between 1989 and 2003.

The allegations have been attributed to U.S. authorities and are not presented here as judicial findings against Massaquoi.

ICE Chicago Field Office Director Frank Padula said the agency would continue pursuing people suspected of human rights violations committed abroad.

“If you are a confirmed human rights violator and you believe you can hide in the United States, you are mistaken,” Padula said, according to Fox News.

He added that ICE would “pursue, arrest and remove” individuals who committed atrocities abroad and prevent U.S. communities from becoming a refuge from accountability.

Nearly Two Decades in U.S.

Massaquoi legally entered the United States in August 2006 but was authorized to remain only until November 6 of that year.

He remained in the country beyond his authorized stay until Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) arrested him in Maryland in August 2019 for being unlawfully present in the United States.

An immigration judge subsequently granted him bond, and he was released less than two months later.

ICE’s Baltimore office took Massaquoi back into custody on April 1, 2025, after authorities said he had failed to comply with the conditions of his release. An immigration judge ordered his removal the following month.

Fox News also reported that Massaquoi received specialized military training at an academy in China in 2004, a year after the end of Liberia’s second civil war.

ICE Human Rights Investigation

The investigation into Massaquoi was supported by ICE’s Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center, which investigates individuals suspected of human rights abuses and war crimes who attempt to enter or remain in the United States.

According to ICE, the agency has arrested more than 520 people for human-rights-related violations since 2003 and removed 1,178 known or suspected human rights violators. The agency said it has also prevented more than 415 suspected human rights violators and war-crimes suspects from entering the United States.

HSI Maryland Special Agent in Charge Akil Baldwin said Massaquoi was believed to have been involved in acts including killings, torture, forced labor, unlawful imprisonment and the recruitment of children into armed conflict.

“If it is confirmed that an individual has engaged in such bloodshed anywhere in the world, then you have no place in the United States,” Baldwin said, according to Fox News.

Liberia’s Civil War Legacy

Liberia endured two civil wars between 1989 and 2003, with widespread killings, displacement and other abuses committed by multiple armed groups.

The United Nations has estimated that nearly 250,000 people were killed, most of them civilians, during the conflicts.

Massaquoi’s reported deportation comes against the backdrop of longstanding efforts to document and address atrocities committed during Liberia’s wars.

Charles Taylor, who led the NPFL rebellion before becoming president of Liberia, was later convicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone for aiding and abetting crimes committed by rebel forces in neighboring Sierra Leone. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison.

World.title: Beyond the $1B Milestone: Liberians React to Historic Revenue Gains, Demand ‘Real Impact’
World.content:
Monrovia – Over the past few days, FrontPage Africa reporters have traveled across Liberia — from the market corridors of Monrovia and Paynesville to the trading cities of Kakata in Margibi County and Gbarnga, Bong County — sampling the views of ordinary Liberians on the government’s announcement that domestic revenue has crossed US$1 billion for the first time in the country’s 179-year history.

By Selma Lomax, Francis G. Boayue and Jaheim T. Tumu.

It is a number the Boakai administration has treated as a historic achievement, and by the raw arithmetic, it is. Revenue has climbed from about US$612 million in 2023 to US$699 million in 2024, US$848 million in 2025, and now past the billion-dollar mark this year, with the government targeting US$1.3 billion by year’s end.

Finance Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan on Tuesday delivered the news in Harper, Maryland County, while President Joseph Nyuma Boakai followed with a special national address titled “One Billion, One Liberia,” crediting Liberia Revenue Authority Commissioner General James Dorbor Jallah and a newly digitized tax system for the surge.

But numbers announced in a presidential address travel slowly, if at all, into the daily lives of the people meant to benefit from them. That is the gap FrontPage Africa set out to measure directly — not through additional statistics, but through conversations with the market vendors, business owners, single mothers and commuters who make up the tax base the government is now celebrating.

What they described, almost without exception, was a billion dollars they cannot see, cannot spend, and in several cases, do not entirely trust the framing of. Even Minister Ngafuan himself seemed to anticipate this reaction, telling communities in the Southeast that revenue should be judged not by what enters a government’s account, but by what enters the life of the citizen.

President Boakai, in his own address, went further, insisting the milestone must translate into support for market women, salary relief for civil servants, functioning classrooms for students, and steady medicine supplies for public hospitals.

That is a high bar for any government to set for itself, and it is precisely the bar Liberians are now holding the administration to. Health workers have already moved from words to organized demands — the Liberia Nurses Association is calling for a minimum monthly salary of US$500, and the Liberia Midwives Association has voiced similar hopes for greater investment in maternal health.

Minister Ngafuan has responded by urging patience while acknowledging the pressure is fair, telling those he met that scarcity must never be allowed to excuse indifference, even as the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning begins the delicate work of drafting the 2027 national budget under the weight of these expectations.

Outside the halls of government, however, the reaction has been less about competing budget priorities and more about a basic, recurring question: where, exactly, has this money gone?

From Kakata to Paynesville, the Liberians FrontPage Africa spoke with described an economy that looks unchanged by the announcement — prices that haven’t moved, exchange rate gains that haven’t translated into savings, and public services, from schools to hospitals, that remain as strained as ever. Their voices, gathered in their own words below, offer the clearest picture yet of how the billion-dollar milestone is actually landing across the country.

Yanga King, a businesswoman in Kakata, Margibi County, said her skepticism was sharpened by comments Ngafuan made suggesting the government had already been spending the revenue well before the public announcement — a detail she believes explains the timing and tone of the government’s messaging.

“The Government of Liberia announced about US$1 billion in revenue, but I think we, the Liberian people, are not feeling the impact or benefiting from this money. I listened to the Finance Minister today, and he said the government has been using this money since January of this year. That is just frustrating for us as Liberians.

“I believe the Finance Minister is a smart man. I think he is making this clarification that the money has been used to avoid future embarrassment, because people might say, in time to come, that when he served as Finance Minister, the government collected and announced this money, but the people did not feel its impact.

“Look at the situation in the schools, for example. Parents are unable to register their children because they do not have the money. The government says primary education is free, but there are not enough public primary schools here to accommodate all the students. As a result, parents are forced to send their children to private schools, even though they do not have the money to afford the cost.”

King’s account from Kakata was mirrored, almost point for point, by traders and residents interviewed in Monrovia and Paynesville — different towns, different circumstances, but the same underlying complaint about a milestone that has yet to reach the ground.

At Parker Paint Junction in Monrovia, Edith Wilson, a vendor, responded to news of the billion-dollar figure with a question of her own rather than a statement: “Who are they giving the $1 billion to?” she asked. Wilson said the cost of living keeps rising and prices of local goods continue to climb, describing conditions as no different from years when the national budget was in the hundreds of millions rather than the billions. “No improvement,” she said. “It’s from worse to worst.”

Patricia Sumo, a single mother, described the disconnect in the smallest possible terms — the difference between buying rice by the cup and buying it by the bag. “I’m not feeling nothing, no chance for me,” she said. “I’m still buying rice by the cup L$70, L$80 because I can’t even afford a bag of rice.”

Musu Gorlormator, a market seller in her 50s, said her living conditions are getting worse, not better, and tied her frustration to a personal loss — the death of her husband, which she attributed to inadequate care at the government-run John F. Kennedy Medical Center. “Citizens sick in the hospital and nurses are telling you no bed,” she said.

In Paynesville, Jerry Toe, a seller along the commercial corridor, focused his frustration on the exchange rate specifically, arguing that a stronger Liberian dollar means little if prices at the store never follow it down. “You drop the US exchange rate while prices in the stores remain the same,” he said. “What’s the difference?”

That same exchange-rate frustration was laid out at greater length by Fuku Joshua, another resident who has been closely watching the disconnect between currency movement and everyday costs.

“My take on the situation is that no commodity has been affected by the reduction in the exchange rate. The only thing that has changed is the value of the money itself. The rate has dropped, but nothing else has changed. Prices of goods and services are still the same. The price of gas is still the same, and other materials are also still the same. So, I really don’t understand why the reduction in the U.S. dollar exchange rate is not affecting the prices of other commodities.

“My recommendation to the government is that whenever the exchange rate goes down, we should also see a corresponding reduction in the prices of goods and services. If the rate is down, we should see the prices of basic commodities going down as well.

“Regarding the $1 billion reportedly raised by the Liberia Revenue Authority through taxes from January to September, I recommend that some of that money be used to empower ordinary Liberians. There are people who need support, including access to loans, to enable them to start businesses or pursue individual economic activities. This would help people become more self-reliant rather than depending entirely on government support.

“When it comes to spending the revenue on education, health, and job empowerment, I believe all three areas are very important. Education is important because in some parts of the country, students have to travel for three or four hours just to get to school. These are challenges that need to be addressed. Health is also important. When someone becomes sick, people sometimes have to travel for several hours to access medical care. Situations like these are very discouraging for our country. Therefore, the government needs to invest in education, healthcare, and job empowerment to improve the lives of the people.”

Peter Flomo questioned the emphasis placed on the US$1 billion milestone, arguing that Liberia’s natural-resource base gives the country potential to generate substantially more revenue.

He said the significance of the announcement should ultimately be measured by improvements in areas such as education, salaries, employment and basic living conditions.

Flomo also questioned the relationship between the revenue announcement and the government’s spending, noting that Finance Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan has clarified that the revenue is not sitting in a single account awaiting expenditure but is being used to finance government operations and programs.

The LRA itself has said the milestone should not be treated as an end in itself. Commissioner General James Dorbor Jallah has said the revenue authority’s performance should ultimately be judged by whether increased collections help finance development and improve public services.

Ngombu Kpawor, a Rehab Community resident, similarly welcomed the milestone but said Liberians would judge it by its effect on schools, hospitals and employment.

“We welcome the $1 billion revenue being raised, but again, we still have doubt as to whether that $1 billion can be used for the upliftment or the improvement of the life of our citizens,” Kpawor said.

He called for investment in public institutions rather than simply distributing money to citizens.

JU Henning Dempster said the government should focus on creating jobs and ensuring that increased revenue eventually improves household incomes.

“What government should do now is to see how the $1 billion can reflect on the local, the time trading,” Dempster said.

He said the milestone would have greater meaning for citizens if they could afford school fees, rent, food and other basic necessities more easily.

Elder Emmanuel Freeman, of Joe Bar Community, questioned whether US$1 billion should be regarded as sufficient given Liberia’s natural resources.

“One billion dollars is not changing lives and the situation in the country,” Freeman said.

He called for greater investment in processing Liberia’s natural resources domestically and expanding economic activity beyond the extraction and export of raw materials.

Freeman also criticized the continued gap between exchange-rate movements and consumer prices.

Not all the reactions gathered by FrontPage Africa were critical. Lavelah B. Kortimai, a motorcyclist, pointed to technical and vocational training programs, road construction, agricultural investment, and what he described as the deployment of 285 earth-moving machines as visible signs that the government is putting revenue to work.

“Everyone is not benefiting,” he said, “but at least some people are benefiting.” Bobby Smith, a local business owner, agreed, citing easier travel to the southeastern counties and a steadier supply of gasoline, rice, and other goods as proof the government is delivering on at least part of its promise — a point Ngafuan himself made during his own tour of the region, pointing to the newly paved road reaching Tappita and the National Transit Authority buses now connecting the Southeast to Monrovia, while acknowledging the area still needs better roads, schools, health care, jobs and transport.

World.title: Liberia: A Coalition of African Civil Society Groups Demands Control of Development Money. But Can They Afford to Say No to Donors?
World.content:
Nana Asantewa Afadzinu, executive director of the West Africa Civil Society Institute, speaks during the Africa at the Centre convening in Accra, Ghana. Credit: Africa at the Centre/WACSI

Summary

A coalition of African civil society leaders are pushing donors to give African organizations and communities more control over development money as traditional foreign aid shrinks. They are also looking to Africans to raise more funds themselves and restrain corrupt money flowing out of the continent.

A growing number of African organizations are rejecting funding agreements that they say do not match their needs.

Leaders say shifting control to African institutions will only work if those institutions are also accountable to the communities the money is meant to help.

By Tetee Gebro, gender and health correspondent with New Narratives

ACCRA, Ghana — When a donor offered money to an organization working in Kenya, it came with an opportunity to expand its work into more communities. For a small organization that needed funding, it might have seemed like an easy decision. It wasn’t.

The donor wanted the organization to expand quickly. The organization said the communities it was already working with needed deeper support before it moved elsewhere. So they made a tough decision.

“They respectfully denied the funding,” said Nafissatou Sene, senior manager of Portfolio Services at African Collaborative, an organization that raises money and funds for African groups working in health, education, gender justice, agriculture and livelihoods.

Sene declined to identify the Kenyan organization because she did not have permission to name it. She said its budget was small and it needed money, making the decision especially difficult, but in the end it decided it had no choice.

“We’re not going to take anything just because it comes our way,” Sene said of the organization’s position.

That kind of decision-making is what Nana Asantewa Afadzinu, executive director of the West Africa Civil Society Institute, said has too often been missing from development in Africa.

“For too long we’ve had development done to us,” Afadzinu said. “We’ve not been in the driving seats of deciding what the solutions should be to our own problems and resourcing them.”

The story has become an example of the kind of power a grouping of African civil society organizations gathered here for the first-ever meeting of African civil society leaders, say they want: the ability to decide what their communities need and insist that donors adjust their requirements to match the communities’ priorities rather than their own.

The three-day conference “Africa at the Centre: Leading Change, Shifting Power” brought together more than 200 civil society leaders, funders, policymakers and development experts from 30 countries, including Liberia. Organizers said decades of development assistance have left foreign donors with too much control over which African problems receive money, how projects are designed and how success is measured. They say this has led to failed projects, lack of accountability, talent diverted from entrepreneurship and job creation, dependency and corruption.

Now, as traditional foreign aid from rich countries shrinks, they are pushing for African organizations and communities to have greater control over development spending by demanding donors listen. But they are also looking to raise more funds from Africans and African governments, and to limit the amount of money that flows out of the continent in corruption and debt payments.

But some at the conference said their proposed solution raises another difficult question: if foreign donors give up power, who in Africa gets it? African governments and civil society organizations have their own problems with corruption, weak accountability and failure to listen to communities. Moving control of development money from foreign institutions to African ones will not necessarily put that power in the hands of the people the money is supposed to help.

Edwin Mende-Cole (far right), executive director of Youth Climate Change Liberia and participants at the Africa at the Centre convening in Accra discuss proposals for shifting greater control over development decisions to African organizations and communities. Credit: Africa at the Centre/WACSI

One Liberian at the conference, Edwin Mends-Cole, said he knows how difficult the first part of that equation can be. Mends-Cole, executive director of Youth Climate Change Initiative Liberia, said small civil society organizations often depend on donor projects to survive. Funding opportunities can be so scarce that organizations adapt what they do to what donors are willing to finance.

“It is hard to say realistically ‘I will not accept,’” Mends-Cole said.

Liberia’s dependence on foreign assistance extends far beyond civil society. World Bank data shows the country received about $563 million in net official development assistance and official aid in 2023, equivalent to two thirds of the national budget. A separate World Bank assessment found official development assistance averaged about 12 percent of Liberia’s gross domestic product between 2022 and 2024.

The limited income of the national government has meant major public services have been left to donors. Donor aid funds at least 50 percent of Liberia’s health sector, for example. But stories of corruption and mismanagement abound, and the government is no closer to standing on its own.

Mends-Cole agrees that donors need to better listen. He said he has seen what can happen when a local organization is able to challenge the way a donor wants to solve a problem.

In 2023, his organization worked on a project under the United Nations Development Programme’s Small Grants Programme to protect biodiversity and mangroves in the Mesurado wetlands. Mends-Cole said the proposed approach focused on educating communities about the need to stop destroying mangroves.

But some people were cutting the mangroves because they depended on them to make a living. Telling them about environmental protection without giving them another way to earn money would not stop the cutting, Mends-Cole said.

“We are on the ground,” he recalled telling the funder. “This approach will not work.” After discussions, he said, the project was changed to include alternative livelihoods.

Mends-Cole said local organizations demanding more power from donors must therefore be prepared to give communities more power too. Before designing a project, he said, organizations should first ask people what problem they need solved. They must be transparent and report to communities on how the funds are spent and results obtained, as well as donors.

West African Civil Society Institute’s Afadzinu said changing the system does not mean simply replacing foreign money. It also means changing who decides how that money is used. She said she wanted to see donors provide more flexible and core funding that allows African organizations to strengthen themselves instead of moving from one donor-designed project to another.

“Don’t help us to continuously depend on you,” Afadzinu said. “Help us to become stronger.”

African countries and organizations must also raise more of their own money, she said, including through local philanthropy, diaspora support, businesses and social enterprises.

Sene said African organizations may already have more power in their relationship with donors than they realize. One organization refusing money may have little influence, she said. Many organizations taking the same position could force donors to listen.

“We cannot give grants or funds to people who refuse to take it from us,” Sene said. “If everybody said no, what are we going to do with the money?”

She acknowledged that completely ending African civil society’s dependence on foreign funding is not realistic in the near future. The immediate goal, she said, should be changing the relationship.

Tendisai Chigwedere of the Flora Hewlett Foundation a Donor at the Convening in Accra

At least one international funder at the Accra gathering is already onboard.

Tendisai Chigwedere of the U.S.-based William and Flora Hewlett Foundation, which was a financial backer of the Convening, said philanthropy has historically held enormous influence because it controlled the money. She said Hewlett is listening to local organizations, giving them more control with long-term partnerships and flexible funding. The Hewlett Foundation said it awarded $631 million in grants in 2024, with nearly three-quarters provided as flexible funding.

“We don’t want you to be boxed into a project,” Chigwedere said. “Allowing you to have general operating support helps you build the institution, build the vision, and work on the agenda… to do the things you need to do.”

Changing how existing donors give money is only one proposal being discussed.

Wanjiru Kanyiha, network coordinator of the Global Public Investment Network, is pushing a model in which African countries would contribute to a common pool according to their ability and participate in deciding how the money is spent. The idea is summed up in three phrases: all contribute, all benefit, all decide.

Under such a system, Kanyiha said, a poorer country such as Liberia would not be expected to contribute as much as a wealthy country but would still have a voice in decisions and could receive more than it contributed based on need.

The model remains a proposal. It has not yet proved that it can replace or significantly reshape the current aid system. Supporters hope to have governments working around one or two pilots by the end of 2028.

After three days in Accra, the West African Civil Society Institute said it will temporarily steward the work after the meeting, coordinate follow-up and help participants continue developing ideas that emerged from the gathering.

In a post-convening reflection, Charles Vandyck, the Institute’s head of capacity development, acknowledged that transferring power from international organizations to African institutions alone would not transform development.

“Redistributing power is not about reversing hierarchies,” Vandyck wrote. “It is about building systems where power is shared, accountability is mutual, and agency is respected.”

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives .

World.title: The Price of a Vote: What Liberia’s Smallest UN Bill Says About Its Biggest Claims
World.content:
Monrovia – There is a number so small it barely registers on the ledger of a $3.45 billion organization: $34,000. It is the least any nation on Earth can be asked to pay the United Nations in a given year — a rate set aside for the world’s poorest countries, Liberia among them. And as of mid-September, it is a number Liberia has not paid.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

The amount is almost beside the point. What it represents is not.

By the United Nations’ own public accounting — the Committee on Contributions’ Honour Roll, updated as member states settle their books — Liberia’s regional neighbors have long since closed this chapter for the year. Côte d’Ivoire paid its assessment, a considerably larger $763,551 reflecting its bigger economy, back in March. Sierra Leone paid its own minimum-rate bill, $31,790, on September 9. Guinea followed five days later. As of September 14, 139 of the UN’s 193 members had paid in full. Liberia was not one of them.

It is tempting to read this as a story about capacity — a poor country simply unable to find $34,000. But that reading doesn’t survive contact with the rest of Liberia’s own record. The country met this same UN obligation on time as recently as 2017, paying $25,223 within the 30-day grace window. And at the International Maritime Organization, a separate UN body, Liberia has been anything but delinquent: in both 2024 and 2025, it settled dues of roughly $7.1 million — about 15% of that agency’s entire budget, a sum 200 times larger than what it now owes the UN’s regular budget — promptly and without incident. Liberia’s maritime registry is, after all, one of the largest in the world, and its government has clear institutional reasons to stay current there.

Which makes the lapse harder to explain as a matter of means, and easier to read as a matter of priorities.

That question of priorities sits uncomfortably next to the government’s own recent messaging. Officials have pointed to a milestone: domestic revenue, they say, has crossed $1 billion for the first time. A supplementary budget for FY2026 shows total receipts of $53 million, built on $48 million in World Bank budget support and a $5 million surplus over projections — money the government has been eager to publicize as evidence of fiscal turnaround. Whatever the merits of that broader claim, it is difficult to square a billion-dollar milestone with a $34,000 bill left unpaid to the institution whose Security Council Liberia currently sits on as a non-permanent member for the first time since 1961.

None of this rises to the threshold that triggers real consequences — Article 19 of the UN Charter, which strips a member of its General Assembly vote, only applies once arrears equal two full years of assessments, a bar of roughly $68,000 that Liberia has not yet crossed, and won’t for some time at this rate. There is no indication the country is being sanctioned or singled out. But symbolism has its own currency at the UN, and the Honour Roll — however minor a document it may seem — is precisely where that symbolism gets tallied, name by name, payment by payment.

World.title: Bembas and Tongas are not going anywhere – learn to coexist, says Nevers Mumba
World.content:
Former Republican Vice-President Dr Nevers Mumba has called on the Bemba and Tonga speaking people to end the growing hostility between the two groups. He said neither community is “going anywhere” and both must learn to live together as Zambians.

Speaking in an interview Dr Mumba said he chose to single out two of Zambia’s 73 tribes to be “razor-focused,” and that he was one of the two.

“Let me start with the Tongas. The Bembas are not going anywhere. So we have to find a way to live with each other, our children intermarrying and living in one country,” he said.

He then addressed his own tribe. “To the Bembas, my tribe, I want to be very clear. The Tongas are not going anywhere. They are not few, they are many, just like you are many as well. And both these groups are Zambian.”

Dr Mumba said Zambians needed to “mature” in the way they relate to each other.

“You can’t wish such a big tribe of the Tongas away just because you have a problem in your sleep at night. You can’t wish the big tribe of the Bembas to just disappear just because you think you have a problem with them. These are here to stay, and they’ll outlive you,” he said.

“We may not agree on everything, but we are one people. We belong to this country. And for this country to develop, we’ve got to agree to some kind of unity around the purpose of making our country a better place.”

The interviewer asked whether he was suggesting the two groups were not coexisting. Dr Mumba said the “vibes” he was picking up pointed to tension between them, though he said other tribes were also involved.

“Very few people say what I’ve said, but it is important,” he said.

He also spoke about recent attacks on Bemba Paramount Chief Chitimukulu, which he called “careless talk”. He said the chief had only refused to be pulled into partisan politics.

“All that Chitimukulu is saying is that, look, don’t make a politician out of me. Outside being a chief and a paramount chief, he’s like a statesman. He’s above parties and politics,” Dr Mumba said. “But there are politicians that want to make a politician out of him so that he speaks for them. And the chief is saying, no, that’s not me.”

World.title: Mpundu Accuses Tembo Of Betrayal As NRPUP Alliance Cracks
World.content:
Binwell Mpundu, chairman of the Tonse Alliance, has accused Ezra Tembo of betraying the people who built his political career, in a lengthy public statement describing recent developments within the coalition as painful and difficult to accept.

Mr Mpundu said he had spent a sleepless night trying to understand how someone could turn against people who stood by him when he had almost nothing.

“How can someone betray the very people who stood by them when they had almost nothing,” he asked. “People who picked you up when you were down, clothed you, supported you, gave you a platform, believed in you, and helped you rise to the position you occupy today.”

He said the National Restoration Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) rose quickly on Zambia’s political scene, gaining serious traction within a short period and eventually forming part of the alliance that went on to win the general election. He said that momentum has since been undone by internal disagreements that had already begun to surface within the coalition.

Mr Mpundu said his frustration was personal rather than political, describing the sacrifices he made through the ICHABAICE campaign, an initiative he had invested years building before setting it aside to support Mr Tembo’s bid in the Nyali constituency.

“I made sacrifices. I put aside my own political pursuits through ICHABAICE, something I had invested in for years. We gave our best to support the Nyali ticket,” he said. “We sacrificed time, resources, relationships and opportunities because we believed in what we were building.”

He said he personally looked for money, however little, to support Mr Tembo’s campaign. He also said he worked to convince Christopher Kangombe Junior, who had already carried out significant groundwork under ICHABAICE in Dag Constituency, to step aside and support Mr Tembo instead.

“When you remember those things and then find yourself on the receiving end of what feels like betrayal, it becomes difficult to process,” he said.

Mr Mpundu compared the experience to an earlier episode in the Patriotic Front (PF) involving Chabinga and Miles Sampa, saying this one felt different because it had touched him directly.

“I thought the Chabinga and Miles Sampa episode in PF was painful, but this one feels different because this time, it has touched me directly,” he said.

He posed a direct question to himself and, by extension, to Mr Tembo. “Without the people who stood by me, supported me, sacrificed for me and opened doors for me, would I have reached where I am today? And if the answer is no, then another question follows: why would I turn around and hurt the very people who helped me get there?”

Mr Mpundu said he needed time to process the situation, but maintained that outcomes in politics eventually reveal themselves.

“As I always say, time settles all matters,” he said. “Maybe this is simply the nature of Zambian politics. Maybe political survival comes with difficult decisions, shifting alliances and painful separations. But regardless of politics, I believe we should never forget the people who stood with us when the journey was difficult.”

He closed his statement with a direct message to Mr Tembo and a second figure he named only as Nonde.

“May you never lack in your lives. May you be blessed with abundance, and may you live long enough to see the full consequences, good or bad, of every decision made along this journey,” he said. “As for me, I will continue to believe that time settles all matters.”

Neither Mr Tembo nor NRPUP had responded to Mr Mpundu’s statement.

World.title: Release Mundubile and others, and call for an election rerun
World.content:
Zambia has reached a point where it has become dangerous to stand on the right side of the law when President Hakainde Hichilema is standing on the wrong side of it. The continued detention of Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and others has become a symbol of the risk now facing any Zambian who finds themselves on the dissenting side of political power.

Citizens can now be detained for prolonged periods while serious allegations remain under investigation, without those allegations being tested through judicial determination. Political proximity to power must never become the yardstick for justice.

Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu’s alleged crime is not treason. They never committed treason. The central political dispute surrounding them is their challenge to an election result the President does not want reopened.

They should be released unconditionally, and Zambia must call for an election rerun. If Mr Hichilema genuinely won the election, he would have nothing to fear from allowing the electorate to speak again. It would, after all, be the same electorate he claims voted for him.

A legitimate electoral mandate should not require the suppression of those who challenge it. One cannot perpetuate illegality by legitimising it. Mr Hichilema has not only managed to divide the country but has crippled its democratic institutions in the process.

If Mr Hichilema’s victory is legitimate, why was Mr Mundubile’s challenge not allowed to be determined by a court? If the treason and sedition allegations are legitimate, why are Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and others not being brought before a court for those allegations to be formally tested?

The statement from the Director of Public Prosecutions, Gilbert Phiri, that investigations into the treason and sedition allegations are still ongoing, raises further questions about the legal basis and duration of the continued detention. Because treason is a non-bailable offence, continued reliance on “ongoing investigations” without bringing the detainees before a court raises serious constitutional questions under Article 13 concerning the legality and duration of their detention.

This delay warrants an immediate writ of habeas corpus compelling the State to release the detainees. If Mr Hichilema genuinely believes he won a clean election, why should Zambia fear allowing the electorate to speak again? A president who genuinely believes he won a clean election does not need the political protection of an inaccessible court.

By Kanyanta Chanda Kapwepwe, Governance Analyst and Lecturer, Cape Peninsula University of Technology

World.title: Njapau Defends Invalidation Of IDs, Names HH’s Online Attackers
World.content:
Former Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD) Home Affairs deputy minister Grace Njapau said the Government should not be blamed for invalidating the national identity documents of people behind what she described as a vicious campaign to discredit it before the international community.

In a statement issued in Lusaka, Ms Njapau expressed sadness at what she called a continuing trend by politically disgruntled people of abusing cyberspace to target President Hakainde Hichilema. She named Emmanuel Mwamba, JJ Banda, Sishuwa Sishuwa and Lillian Mutambo, among others.

Ms Njapau said the perpetual use of vulgar language and hate speech, which she said had been consistently orchestrated by those individuals, was inimical to national unity and to the social cohesion that should bind Zambians regardless of ethnicity or political affiliation.

She described the behaviour as despicable and worrying, and said it reflected moral bankruptcy in people who, by virtue of their age and standing in society, were supposed to be role models for younger people.

“As a mother, I am concerned that our cultural values of respecting elders and those in authority are getting eroded. I’m deeply saddened that people who are politically disgruntled have resorted to relentlessly attacking President Hichilema through cyber space instead of promoting peace and national unity,” she said.

The former deputy minister went further. She said the Government should not be blamed for invalidating national identity documents for those behind a malicious campaign to discredit it in the eyes of the international community, saying necessary measures had to be taken in the national interest.

Ms Njapau said the gravity of the conduct of those whose national identity documents had been rendered invalid by the authorities called for drastic action. Their behaviour, she said, did not only border on dividing the nation but was also a serious threat to national security.

Her statement confirms that identity documents have been invalidated for people the Government accuses of discrediting it abroad. It does not say how many people are affected, which of those she named are among them, or under what legal process the documents were cancelled.

Ms Njapau said the opposition and President Hichilema’s opponents should accept that people from all parts of the country gave the United Party for National Development (UPND) a renewed mandate to govern for the next five years.

“As such, President Hichilema deserves to be respected and the decorum of his office protected from unnecessary attacks,” she said.

She urged Zambians to support the President and his administration, saying he had a clear vision to deliver development to all parts of the country. Mr Hichilema’s performance in his first term, she said, was self-explanatory, as shown by the milestones scored within a short time of assuming office.

Ms Njapau acknowledged that freedom of expression was a democratic right, but said it should be exercised with responsibility and only in the spirit of nation-building, not the opposite.

Her remarks come alongside a separate statement by the ruling party, in which UPND deputy media director Sikwindi Situla described Mr Mwamba as a renegade and “a wanted person in Zambia”, and accused Patriotic Front (PF) agents of feeding falsehoods to international election observers and journalists.

Ms Njapau maintained that the measures were taken in the national interest. Her statement did not set out how many people have had their documents invalidated or the procedure used.

World.title: Milenge targets 40,000 tonnes of maize by 2031
World.content:
Milenge District is targeting to produce more than 40,000 metric tonnes of maize by 2031, with over 4,600 farmers expected to benefit from the 2026/2027 Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

Milenge District Senior Agriculture Officer Baxter Musonda said achieving the production target would require farmers to adhere to recommended farming practices.

Mr Musonda said farmers should follow guidance provided by camp extension officers and other agricultural officials, particularly on improved farming practices.

He was speaking during the flag-off of the 2026/2027 FISP inputs.

Mr Musonda also cautioned FISP beneficiaries against selling their farming inputs after redemption, urging them to use the inputs for their intended purpose.

He said the district’s production target was in line with the Grow Zambia Agenda, which seeks to increase Zambia’s maize production to more than 10 million metric tonnes by 2031.

Government is supporting small-scale farmers through FISP to increase agricultural production, improve household incomes and contribute to national food security.

Meanwhile, Milenge Acting District Commissioner Chiluba Yamba said more than 4,600 farmers in the district would benefit from FISP during the 2026/2027 farming season.

Dr Yamba said FISP remained an important government intervention aimed at increasing agricultural productivity through the provision of subsidised farming inputs.

He said government remained committed to ensuring that farmers received farming inputs on time so that the programme continued to benefit intended beneficiaries, strengthen national food security and contribute to the broader objectives of the agricultural sector.

Mikula Ward Councillor Eric Kasongo urged FISP beneficiaries to safeguard their e-voucher codes to prevent unauthorised redemption.

Mr Kasongo also appealed to agro-dealers to stock a wider variety of approved agricultural inputs and other eligible items to give farmers more options when redeeming their e-vouchers, particularly when they have a balance after purchasing seed and fertiliser.

World.title: Mwense residents warned against politicising Govt programmes
World.content:
Mwense District Administrative Officer Philip Muonga has cautioned community members against politicising government programmes aimed at improving the livelihoods of citizens.

Mr Muonga said President Hakainde Hichilema had directed that all eligible beneficiaries of various government programmes should benefit regardless of their political affiliation.

He said this during the flag-off of the distribution of farming inputs under the 2026 Food Security Pack (FSP) in Mwense District.

Mr Muonga assured residents that all eligible beneficiaries would be considered under the programme, which he said was intended to benefit citizens across the district.

Under the social protection programme, 1,000 vulnerable but viable households in Mwense District are being targeted to improve household incomes and food security.

Mr Muonga also urged beneficiary households not to sell the farming inputs, saying his office had received reports of some beneficiaries engaging in the practice.

Meanwhile, FSP beneficiaries have commended government for promoting wetland farming in the district.

Kabelenga Katebe, who spoke on behalf of the beneficiaries, said the initiative had contributed significantly to improving household food security.

Mr Katebe said wetland farming had also helped improve household nutrition and contributed to efforts to address stunting.

He expressed gratitude to President Hichilema for the FSP inputs, saying they were helping households enhance food security.

“Wetland farming has also contributed towards improving nutritional status thereby helping in addressing stunting, we are grateful to the President for the FSP inputs, they really help in enhancing household food security,” Mr Kabelenga said.

World.title: Kapasa Makasa students sensitised on GBV, economic empowerment
World.content:
The Gender Division in Muchinga Province has conducted a one-day sensitisation programme for students at Kapasa Makasa University in Chinsali District on economic empowerment and gender-based violence (GBV).

Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary Brian Sichande, who officially opened the engagement, said government remained committed to continuously engaging young people on issues critical to national development, including GBV and economic empowerment.

Mr Sichande said the programme had come at an opportune time when government was placing emphasis on human capital development, economic empowerment, skills development, gender equality and the prevention of GBV.

He said the participation of young people in such programmes was vital because they constituted a significant proportion of the country’s population and were an important resource for social and economic development.

Mr Sichande said economic empowerment was fundamental to enabling individuals and communities to become self-reliant and contribute meaningfully to national development.

He said economic and social development could not be fully attained while GBV continued to affect individuals, families and communities.

The Deputy Permanent Secretary stressed the need to equip young people, particularly students in higher learning institutions, with knowledge on GBV prevention, available reporting mechanisms, referral pathways and survivor support services.

Meanwhile, Kapasa Makasa University Deputy Registrar Lillian Mukuka, speaking on behalf of university management, commended the initiative to equip students with knowledge on economic empowerment, capacity building and GBV.

Ms Mukuka said the knowledge and skills were important not only to students but also to their roles as members of the wider community and society.

She said capacity-building skills were essential to the development of all people, particularly young people.

Ms Mukuka said the knowledge acquired through the programme would enable students to better understand and critically assess situations in their lives compared to those who had not benefited from similar sensitisation programmes.

Meanwhile, students at Kapasa Makasa University welcomed the programme, describing it as important to their well-being in a rapidly developing country such as Zambia.

Emmanuel Tembo, a fourth-year Animal Science student who delivered the vote of thanks, expressed gratitude to the Gender Division in Muchinga Province for organising what he described as a timely and impactful programme.

World.title: World Vision closes Pemba programme
World.content:
World Vision Zambia has closed its Moyo Area Development Programme in Pemba District after investing more than 12.9 million United States dollars in Moyo Chiefdom over the past 17 years.

The programme, which commenced in 2009, benefited more than 30,000 people through interventions in health, education, livelihoods and child protection.

Southern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Gift Monde said the investments had made a significant impact on the lives of people in the chiefdom.

Mr Monde said the construction of Moyo Mini Hospital and maternity annexes at health facilities across the chiefdom was in line with President Hakainde Hichilema’s vision of bringing health services closer to the people.

“Government appreciates the contribution that World Vision Zambia has made towards improving the lives of people in Moyo Chiefdom. The investments in health, education and livelihoods have left a significant impact on the community,” Mr Monde said.

He said government would continue working with development partners to complement its efforts in improving service delivery and creating opportunities for communities to become self-reliant.

World Vision Zambia Associate Director of Programmes Betty Mbewe said the organisation was pleased to leave behind an empowered community with skills to sustain the gains made under the programme.

Ms Mbewe said the community had acquired skills in livestock management, gardening and savings, which would help residents continue improving their livelihoods after the programme’s closure.

She said World Vision had distributed more than 11,000 goats during the programme, contributing to an increase in the goat population in the area from less than 5,000 at the beginning of the programme to about 55,000.

Ms Mbewe said 175 savings groups had also been established, providing community members with opportunities to save, access small loans and invest in income-generating activities.

She thanked government and the people of Moyo Chiefdom for supporting World Vision’s development initiatives over the years.

Meanwhile, Chief Moyo pledged to sustain the gains made under the programme and ensure that the infrastructure and skills transferred to the community continued to benefit residents.

The Chief said the community would take ownership of the projects and work together to protect the investments made in the chiefdom.

The traditional leadership also called on community members to maintain the spirit of self-reliance and ensure that the benefits of the programme were passed on to future generations.
