World.title: Nigeria: Tinubu Meets Macron for Private Dinner in Paris
World.content:
According to Mr Onanuga, the dinner reflected the longstanding relationship between Nigeria and France.

President Bola Tinubu met French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday for a private dinner at the Élysée Palace in Paris.

It is the latest in the series of meetings and engagements between Nigeria and France since Mr Tinubu assumed office in 2023.

The president's Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, disclosed the meeting in a post on X on Friday. He also shared photographs of the two leaders at the French presidential palace.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

PREMIUM TIMES reports that the meeting took place while Mr Tinubu was in France during the second leg of his three-week annual leave in Europe.

He arrived in Paris on Monday after spending the first part of his leave in London.

According to Mr Onanuga, the dinner reflected the longstanding relationship between Nigeria and France.

In the post, he wrote, "French President Emmanuel Macron received President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for a private dinner Thursday night at the Élysée Palace, reflecting the enduring relationship between Nigeria and France and their shared commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation."

President Tinubu, in a separate post about the meeting, also said his conversation with Mr Macron reflects both countries' mutual interest in maintaining good relations and strengthening the existing partnership.

He also thanked the French president for his hospitality and friendship.

"It was a pleasure to share a private dinner with President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace in Paris. @EmmanuelMacron

"Our conversation reaffirmed the strong friendship between Nigeria and France, as well as our shared commitment to deepening cooperation and building a mutually beneficial partnership between our two nations," he wrote.

Photographs released from the dinner showed Mr Tinubu and Mr Macron together at the Élysée Palace, with another image showing Mr Tinubu, Mr Macron and France's First Lady, Brigitte Macron.

However, details of the interaction or any potential agreement between the two leaders were not provided.

World.title: Guinea: Guinea Bans France 24, Withdraws Jeune Afrique Correspondent's Accreditation
World.content:
Dakar — The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Guinean authorities to reverse Thursday's ban on France 24 after a presenter called President Mamadi Doumbouya a "putschist president" and to reinstate the accreditation of the pan-African weekly Jeune Afrique's Guinea correspondent Diawo Barry.

"By prohibiting France 24 from broadcasting and Jeune Afrique's Diawo Barry from working, Guinean authorities have shown their ruthless determination to silence independent voices and to intimidate other media outlets into self-censorship," said Moussa Ngom, CPJ's Francophone Africa representative. "Authorities must immediately reverse these decisions and refrain from further actions that erode press freedom and the public's right to information."

In its September 17 decision, the regulatory High Authority of Communication (HAC) said it had banned France 24 because it had failed to comply with its order the previous day "to immediately cease using terms deemed derogatory to the dignity of the Head of State and to make the required editorial corrections." The HAC also withdrew press accreditation for all the French state-owned channel's correspondents, special correspondents, and contributors in Guinea.

On Monday, a France 24 presenter used the word "putschist" while commenting on Doumbouya's visit to Ivory Coast.



Hours after the HAC's September 16 notice, France 24 added an online correction to the video's description, saying that Doumbouya had been "mistakenly labeled a coup leader."

"Having seized power in a coup on September 5, 2021, which overthrew President Alpha Condé, he was subsequently elected President of the Republic following the presidential election of December 28, 2025," the correction said.

France 24 told Agence France-Presse news agency that it had also apologized and corrected the error on air.

Also on September 16, the HAC revoked Barry's accreditation as Jeune Afrique's correspondent on the grounds that his coverage of news in Guinea did not meet the requirements of objective, neutral, balanced reporting.

The Guinean satirical newspaper Le Lynx, where Barry is publishing director, suggested that Jeune Afrique's September special report on Guinea, "Democracy under surveillance," had "ruffled feathers."

Jeune Afrique said that the HAC's decision had been handed down "without prior consultation" and was "not based on any specific allegation" to support its "vague" accusations.

Since Doumbouya took power, the HAC has introduced long-term and indefinite bans on numerous critical outlets and reporters. The whereabouts of journalist Habib Marouane Camara, who was seized by uniformed men in 2024, and of exiled journalist Mamoudou Babila Keita's elderly father, Elhadj Adama Keita, who was kidnapped in 2025, remain unknown.

Close 

CPJ's calls to request comment from the HAC went unanswered.

World.title: Nigeria: Niger State Imposes 24-Hour Curfew After Suspects Die in Custody
World.content:
The Niger State Government has imposed a 24-hour curfew across Minna, the state capital, as tension rises over the deaths of about 37 suspected illegal miners in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC).

The curfew takes effect immediately after Juma'at prayers on Friday, the government announced.

The government has also ordered the suspension of all mining activities in the state until further notice.

The directives are part of the state government's measures to address the prevailing security situation and restore safety across the state.



The government advised residents to remain indoors and comply fully with the curfew and other security directives until further notice.

The government also cancelled an All Progressives Congress (APC) rally scheduled for Minna on Saturday and suspended the NSCDC State Commandant, Suberu Aniviye, and his team.

Governor Mohammed Bago announced the measures during a press briefing in Minna on Friday.

He said the curfew was necessary to prevent a breakdown of law and order and to allow the government to manage the situation while investigations continue.

Background to the curfew

The deaths occurred after the NSCDC detained suspects arrested in connection with mining activities in the Ema Ushishi area of Niger State.

More than 37 detainees reportedly died while in custody, although the exact number and cause of the deaths have not been officially established.

The bodies were later moved to a mortuary, a development that heightened tension among youths and residents in Minna.

The incident triggered public concern and fears of possible protests or violence, prompting the state government to cancel the APC rally and impose the curfew.

Mr Bago described the deaths as tragic and unacceptable and said the government had begun steps to establish what happened.

He announced the constitution of a committee of inquiry to investigate the incident and determine the cause of the deaths.

Cause of death not established

The governor cautioned against concluding the forensic examinations, medical assessments, and autopsies.

He said possible causes being considered included suffocation caused by overcrowding in the detention facility and exposure to hazardous substances allegedly linked to illegal mining.

"There is no official root cause of these deaths yet. It is too early for anybody to conclude the root causes," Mr Bago said.

He said the state government was compiling a register of the deceased to identify and contact their families.

Mr Bago assured the victims' relatives that the government would engage with them and provide the necessary support during the investigation.

NSCDC commandant suspended

The governor announced the immediate suspension of Mr Aniviye and his team to allow for an impartial investigation.

He said the suspension was not a declaration of guilt but a measure to ensure that the investigation was conducted without interference.

The governor said the Director-General of the NSCDC, who is currently outside the country, had delegated his deputy to represent him in engagements concerning the incident.

He added that the state government had already met with the senior NSCDC official.

'We will probe deeply'

Mr Bago pledged that the government would investigate the incident thoroughly and ensure that those responsible for any wrongdoing were held accountable.

"Lives of human beings are lives of human beings. Such an unjust government will not tolerate any injustice, and we are going to make sure that we probe this thing deeply until we get to the root of this," he said.

He urged residents, particularly youths, to remain calm and obey the curfew.

Close 

"We are calling on all the youth to please stay away from violence. It is not going to bring about those who have died. It will rather cost us a lot at the end of the day," he said.

Mining suspended

The governor also ordered the closure of activities at the illegal mining site in Ema Ushishi.

He expressed concern over mining operations conducted without adequate technology, safety equipment and protective gear.

According to him, such practices expose miners to dangerous conditions and may have contributed to the incident.

The state government said it would continue to work with the NSCDC, the police, the State Security Service and other relevant agencies to establish the facts.

Mr Bago commiserated with the families of the deceased and declared three days of mourning in the state.

He said the cancellation of the APC rally was intended to allow the state to mourn the victims and focus on restoring calm and completing the investigation.

World.title: Africa: Hub Unconference to Tackle Ai's Growing Influence in Africa
World.content:
The Hub Unconference is set to return for its 12th edition in Harare next week, bringing together young Africans to debate the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies on society.

The two-day event, scheduled for 24 and 25 September at Harare Gardens, will run under the theme "Unruly Algorithms" and bring together students, creatives, journalists, policymakers, technologists and other digital enthusiasts.

Organisers said the gathering would examine how digital systems are influencing information, education, creativity and civic participation across Africa.

Rather than focusing solely on explaining artificial intelligence, this year's edition aims to explore how young Africans can influence and shape the technologies increasingly affecting their lives.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Hub Unconference Coordinator Takudzwa Musakasa said the organisers wanted to shift the conversation towards action and participation.

"We didn't want this year's edition to be just about what AI is doing to us, we wanted it to be about what we are going to do about it," Musakasa said.

He said the "Unruly Algorithms" theme would encourage young Africans to understand the systems influencing their lives, question how they were developed and take part in shaping their future.

The programme will feature panel discussions, masterclasses, debates, live podcasts, creative pop-ups and interactive showcases, with speakers from several African countries.

Among the speakers are Angela Kilisungu and Nkumi Mtingwa from Tanzania, Uganda's Antonio Kisembo and Samuel Eibu, Malawi's Willson Chivhanga, and Zimbabweans Darlington Chugumbu, Linda Mujuru and Joice Svotwa.

The programme will also feature a Canva masterclass led by Nicole Njanjari, as well as pop-up sessions involving organisations including Friendship Bench, Magitare Trust and Defend Defenders.

Participants from Uganda, Malawi, Tanzania, South Africa and Zimbabwe are expected to discuss ways African countries can strengthen control over their data and use it to promote transparency, civic advocacy and locally driven innovation.

Musakasa said bringing people from different sectors into the same space was central to the event's approach.

"We're bringing students, creatives, journalists, technologists and policymakers into the same space to question these systems, learn practical skills and imagine what a digital future shaped by us could look like," Musakasa said.

Close 

The organisers said the conference would provide an opportunity for participants to explore practical ways of engaging with emerging technologies while considering their wider social and civic implications.

The Hub Unconference is free to attend, although participants are required to register through the Shoko Festival website.

The event will take place alongside the country's annual urban culture festival, the Shoko Festival.

World.title: South Africa: Pressure Grows As Organisations Picket Outside Kempton Park Police Station
World.content:
A "Picket for Justice," backed by FEDUSA, Contralesa, SANCO and dozens of other organisations, is taking place at Kempton Park police station today from 8am.

The picket is part of a full day of action, including a march to Church Square and a meeting with runners at the Union Buildings, following at least nine women's deaths in Ekurhuleni since July.

A coalition of unions, traditional leaders and civil society organisations is holding a "Picket for Justice" outside Kempton Park police station today, demanding justice, accountability and action following a spate of women's killings in Ekurhuleni.

The picket, which began at 8am, is backed by a wide range of organisations, including FEDUSA, Contralesa, SANCO, the Civil Society Unmuted Coalition, Human Rights Institute of South Africa, and groups representing domestic workers and women across several provinces. One banner at the scene reads: "They can't kill us all."

The picket forms part of a broader day of action organised alongside the Office of the Deputy Minister for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities, Mmapaseka Steve Letsike, as part of the department's GBV and Femicide Response Programme.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Also today, a "Not in My Name" event is planned for 11am at Church Square, followed by a 3pm meeting with the Pretoria Runners group, marching from Sunnyside police station to the Union Buildings.

At least nine women's bodies have been found in and around Kempton Park and surrounding areas since July, most discovered near rivers or roads, with many showing signs of sexual assault. The most recent body was found in Dawn Park on 17 September.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has appealed to police to prioritise the investigations, and Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has announced a significant scale-up of Operation Shanela across the area, including a greater visible police presence and roadblocks.

This follows a week of protests across the country. Yesterday, around 200 people, including members of March and March and Operation Dudula, gathered in Kempton Park demanding answers from police.

In Cape Town, around 100 people held a silent protest outside the City Hall and a police station earlier this week, carrying placards reading "How many bodies?" and "Girls just want to live."

World.title: Algeria: Algeria Shifts Towards English As French Loses Ground in Schools
World.content:
Primary school pupils in Algeria are in for a change this year when, for the first time, the national curriculum will focus on English over French. The move follows a general trend across former French colonies in North Africa that are now prioritising English.

Algeria's 2026-27 school year kicks off next week with a change: a shift away from its usual focus on French as a second language.

Introduced in primary schools alongside French in 2022, from now on English will be the first foreign language children study.

Algerian education minister Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui announced in July that English classes would begin in the third year of primary school, when children are around 8. French lessons will follow a year later.



"In third year, only English will be taught," Saadaoui said.

Colonial baggage

The reform is part of a broader shift towards English in Algeria, where French remains closely tied to the country's colonial history.

In a paper published earlier this year, Algerian linguist Fadhila Leroul of the Mouloud Mammeri University of Tizi-Ouzou says the change can be explained not only by English's status as a global lingua franca, but because in the political context of former French colonies cutting ties from France, it steers Algeria "beyond the colonial legacy attached to French".

Algeria's history with France is long and tightly knit. Algeria was under French rule from 1830 to 1962, and was formally incorporated into France in 1848.

The French language was imposed everywhere from administration to formal education, but French was not accessible to just anyone. Arabic remained the language of the majority, while French was for Europeans and those with access to education.

According to Abu Bakr Khaled Saad Allah, an Algerian professor and researcher on higher education, this division made language deeply bound up with questions of national identity. Algerian writer Kateb Yacine, who wrote in French, once described the language as a "war trophy" taken from the former colonial power.

How a Nigerian town came to speak 'street French'

Following its independence, Algeria pursued policies to make Arabic the official national language. Arabic has been the country's primary language ever since, but for decades French remained prevalent in academia.

Algiers began toying with the idea of pushing English in the early 1990s, when primary school students were given the choice between English and French as a second language.

The plan was shut down and English was taken off the syllabus until 2019, when the minister of education put forward a plan to promote the use of English in universities. In 2022, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune announced that English would be introduced in primary schools.

The move coincided with a weakening of Algeria's relations with France. The relationship between the two countries has been tense since 2021 and, despite a period of rapprochement in 2023, worsened in 2024 after France declared its support for Morocco's sovereignty over the disputed Western Sahara.

The last word: why half of the world's languages could vanish this century

Regional shift

Both Morocco and Tunisia also took pains post-independence to cut ties to their former colonial power.

Morocco was a French protectorate from 1912 to 1956. Under Paris, French was the only language used for instruction. When Morocco got its independence, it steered the country towards policies of Arabisation to ensure Arabic once again took a central place.

The Moroccan government progressively introduced Arabic into primary education, but French remained the language of higher study, particularly in mathematics and science.

In the 2000s, the kingdom began to move towards a more multilingual model that supported both Arabic and French. At the same time, English was cementing its dominance as a global language - particular with younger generations.

One 2021 survey of 15-25-year-olds, commissioned by the British Council, found 40 percent of respondents believed English was the most important language to learn, compared to only 10 percent for French. As one participant said: "Everyone is turning to the English language because of its dominance on the internet."

By 2023, the Moroccan government began introducing English in public schools, where before it had been limited mainly to private institutions.

Close 

French overtakes Arabic to become world's fourth most spoken language

Tunisia was also a French protectorate from 1881 to 1956. The colonial rulers soon established a public education system that prioritised French, and it became the language of administration and economy. Those seeking access to higher opportunities therefore became bilingual in both French and Arabic.

After its independence, unlike Morocco and Algeria, Tunisia did not seek to cut out French from education and daily life. While it also pursued a policy of Arabisation, it maintained strong links with French education. The language of its former colonisers remained important in science, medicine, higher education, business and government.

But in contrast to its neighbours, Tunisia introduced English early on after independence as a foreign-language option in schools. Decades on, young people are increasingly choosing it.

In a 2020 Afrobarometer survey, around 68 percent of Tunisian respondents said English was the most important language for young people to learn. Only some 13 percent chose French.

World.title: Africa: Can Africa Turn Red Sea Rivalries to Its Advantage?
World.content:
A map of ports in the Horn of Africa.

analysis

Growing competition for African ports and security partnerships offers new leverage - if countries can avoid deeper geopolitical fragmentation.

Ongoing conflict in the Middle East exposes shifting regional geopolitical fault lines that are pulling African states into an emerging macro-conflict system anchored along the Red Sea.

This stems from several overlapping crises arising from US and Israeli military offensives against Iran and renewed Houthi attacks on shipping lanes, Saudi-Emirati competition across the Horn of Africa, and disputes amongst African states over sovereignty and regional influence.

Should these crises deepen and become self-reinforcing, the implications for African states across much of the Red Sea littoral could be dire.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The most recent US and Israeli offensive against Iran has added to these dynamics. Iran's retaliatory offensives against Gulf actors have called into question longstanding presumptions about the US' reliability in providing security for its traditional Gulf allies.

That in turn has precipitated more overt hedging strategies among regional powers, most notably the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Saudi Arabia. Their prior security coordination to counter Iranian influence has buckled under the weight of opposing conceptions of regional order and claims to regional leadership.

Abu Dhabi projects power through expansive investments in ports and infrastructure, and through ties to non-state armed actors and secessionist movements in Yemen, Sudan, Libya and Somalia. It has also deepened engagement with Israel since normalising relations with Jerusalem under the 2020 Abraham Accords.

Riyadh has sought to undercut Abu Dhabi's efforts by backing recognised central state authorities and building countervailing partnerships with like-minded regional actors. Its closer coordination with Egypt, Pakistan and Turkey points to its growing efforts to reinforce state-centric alliances, constrain the UAE and hedge against Abu Dhabi's close ties with Israel.

This fluid security environment raises the stakes for African states along the Red Sea, which can offer access to ports, airfields, intelligence and security partnerships.

Landlocked Ethiopia seeks sea access to reduce its heavy dependence on Djibouti. Somaliland's Berbera port appealed because the Emirati-owned logistics company DP World had already developed the port, an economic zone and a transport corridor to Ethiopia.

But since the controversial 2024 Ethiopia-Somaliland cooperation memorandum, Ethiopia and Somalia recommitted to each other's territorial integrity in the Turkish-brokered Ankara Declaration, agreeing to negotiate Ethiopian commercial sea access under Somalia's sovereign authority.

This has not, however, removed Ethiopia from Gulf competition. Turkey has become an important mediator between Ethiopia and Somalia, while the UAE retains deep commercial and political ties with Ethiopia and Somaliland.

Meanwhile, 2026 reports of UAE-linked training and logistics networks supporting Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF) from Ethiopian territory (which both Ethiopia and the UAE deny) have heightened regional tensions.

Africa's Red Sea States

Egypt, by contrast, controls the Suez Canal, has substantial military and naval capabilities and is strategically positioned at the Red Sea's northern end. Disruption around the Bab al-Mandab Strait directly hits Suez traffic and Egyptian revenues, while instability in Sudan and Somalia weighs heavily on Cairo's security interests.

Egypt's long-standing rivalry with Ethiopia has drawn Cairo into closer alignment with Saudi Arabia. Tensions have escalated since the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam was inaugurated in September 2025 and Ethiopia revived plans for three more dams on the Blue Nile.

Cairo has responded by working to undercut Addis Ababa, opposing Ethiopia's sea-access claims and unilateral control over Blue Nile waters, and bolstering ties with Eritrea.

Sudan's value to Gulf actors lies in both its war and its geography. Port Sudan is a crucial gateway for the weapons, logistics and personnel inflows sustaining the conflict. The UAE faces persistent allegations of backing the RSF, which it denies, while Egypt and Saudi Arabia have generally kept closer ties with the Sudanese Armed Forces.

Somalia's federal government decision in January 2026 to cut ties with the UAE was rejected by breakaway Somaliland and autonomous Puntland (and Jubaland), all of which have their own Emirati relationships. Turkey, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, however, have deepened engagement with the federal government.

Europe also has a role in this complex security landscape. The European Union (EU) maintains a substantial maritime presence through Operation ASPIDES, which protects commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, and Operation ATALANTA, which covers the Western Indian Ocean and parts of the Red Sea.

A July 2026 EU-Djibouti agreement on ASPIDES underlines European navies' reliance on African partners for access, logistics and onshore support.

In Somalia, the EU runs a civilian capacity-building mission and a military training mission, alongside anti-piracy initiatives. It is building maritime law enforcement and coast-guard capacity in Mogadishu, Somaliland and Puntland, with an emphasis on accountable security institutions and maritime governance.

This is a very different model of influence from the Gulf powers, who attach their support to greater access to ports, political patronage and strategic infrastructure in the Horn.

As African states along the Red Sea are pulled into the geopolitical orbit of rival Gulf powers, how sustainable are these partnerships and how might they change?

Gulf investment in ports, logistics, energy and other strategic infrastructure will probably continue, spurring deeper defence and security coordination. Commercial deals may become increasingly bundled with defence, security and intelligence commitments - a more compelling offer than anything Europe can provide.

The risk, however, is that African states become entrenched in rival security architectures and geopolitical alignments that narrow their room for manoeuvre.

Close 

This leaves Africa's Red Sea countries facing a policy dilemma. They could engage Middle Eastern powers through a coordinated approach that channels external competition towards a common development agenda. Or they could continue the current fragmented bilateral engagements that provide immediate investment, diplomatic backing and help with pressing security-related concerns.

But the short-term gains of bilateralism come at the expense of longer-term shared development and stability.

The African Union could help by assigning North and East African states a leading role in shaping the continent's engagement with Middle Eastern powers. Their proximity to the Red Sea and growing value to external players give them outsized access and influence that could be exercised on the continent's behalf.

The central question is whether Africa will harness this new value to advance shared development or allow it to deepen the continent's fragmentation.

This article was first published in Africa Tomorrow, the blog of the ISS' African Futures and Innovation programme.

World.title: East Africa: East Africa's Iconic Snow Peaks Face Imminent Extinction
World.content:
EAST Africa's iconic equatorial glaciers across three mountain peaks in Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania will soon disappear entirely, with new climate assessments predicting total extinction within three to five years.

According to the 2025 State of the Climate in Africa report, ice coverage on Mount Kenya Africa's second-highest peak has plummeted by 96 per cent over the past 115 years. The rapid retreat highlights a broader, unprecedented ecological shift affecting Mount Kilimanjaro in northern Tanzania and the Rwenzori Mountains situated on the border between Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Rainer Prinz, a climate scientist specializing in glacierclimate relationships, warns that the current rate of ice loss falls completely outside natural historical variations. "

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

During the past decade, we recorded a 40 to 60 per cent loss in East Africa's total glacier area meaning nearly half of the continent's equatorial ice melted in just ten years," Prinz explains, adding that while these glaciers may be as old as 10,000 years, the physical ice itself is considerably younger and rapidly disappearing.

Contrary to popular belief, these high-altitude glaciers do not act as regional water towers or major reservoirs for surrounding populations.

Prinz points out that the ice bodies are geographically too small to have a significant effect on downstream river systems.

Furthermore, a large portion of the ice loss occurs not through direct melting, but through sublimation a process where extreme dry air at high mountain altitudes converts solid ice directly into atmospheric vapor without producing liquid runoff.

On Mount Kenya, total glacier area measured approximately 69,000 square meters in 2022, holding roughly 500,000 cubic meters of ice.

If that entire volume were melted at once and distributed evenly across the mountain, the resulting water would equal no more than a single heavy rainfall event.

The true water towers of East Africa, scientists emphasize, are its montane forests rather than its summit ice caps.

Instead, the primary value of these tropical glaciers lies in their scientific importance as atmospheric indicators.

Functioning as natural instruments, glaciers translate complex, short-term weather patterns into long-term climate signals.

Located 5,000 to 6,000 meters above sea level in the mid-tropical troposphere, they provide vital data about atmospheric conditions in a highaltitude zone where traditional weather measurements are extremely scarce.

Research into these climate signals shows that the centurylong recession of East African glaciers is driven primarily by a steady decline in annual snowfall rather than direct temperature increases.

This drop in precipitation is triggered by shifting sea surface temperature patterns in the Indian Ocean caused by global warming. Warmer and colder ocean surface pockets alter atmospheric currents, reducing the transport of moist air masses toward East Africa.

Consequently, the lack of fresh white snow cover leaves bare, darker ice exposed to sunlight, lowering solar reflectivity and absorbing more solar energy, which further accelerates the retreat.

ASO READ: Six to represent Tanzania at Miss Tourism East Africa finals

The total disappearance of these glaciers will trigger significant ecological, economic, and cultural consequences across the region. Unique high-mountain ecosystems will be disrupted as specialized micro-organisms and algae lose their natural habitats.

At the same time, loweraltitude plant and animal species will migrate higher up the slopes, placing severe competitive pressure on the niche environments of summit areas. Economically and visually, East Africa will lose its signature white mountain tops.

While seasonal snow will still fall on the high peaks occasionally, permanent ice caps shining in the distance will be gone, impacting mountain tourism and eliminating rare tropical glacier research sites that exist in only a few other places globally, such as the South American Andes and Indonesia.

Close 

The loss also carries a profound, often overlooked spiritual impact for local communities. For generations, indigenous societies have viewed these icy summits as sacred dwellings for spirits or deities.

The permanent loss of the ice raises deep cultural and spiritual questions about the human disruption of these sacred landscapes. In theory, the retreat process is physically reversible; an estimated 40 per cent increase in annual snowfall could return Mount Kenya's glacier mass to equilibrium.

However, under current global climate trajectories, there is no realistic prospect of saving East Africa's glaciers. Even under wetter future scenarios, atmospheric temperatures will remain too warm for permanent snow to accumulate on the mountain tops, leaving the region set to shed its ancient ice caps for good.

World.title: How one Indiana city went from skeptical to serious contender for Bears' new stadium
World.content:
When the Chicago Bears kick off against the Minnesota Vikings for their 2026 home opener on Sunday, it will mark the start of their 55th season at Soldier Field. It also may be the last. Hammond, Indiana, certainly hopes it is.

The Bears announced in June that they were moving forward with stadium development plans across state lines in Hammond, Indiana. This isn’t the first time the Bears have talked about moving to Indiana, as there were discussions in the late 1990s, but none were serious.

Now? The discussions are as serious as Ben Johnson saying he wants the Bears to have the highest-scoring offense in NFL history. Hammond Mayor Thomas McDermott Jr. said that while the city has been preparing for this, even he didn’t think the work would eventually lead to Hammond potentially becoming the next home of the Bears.

"We did a lot of things in Hammond and in Indiana to prepare us for this day," McDermott told OutKick in a recent interview. "But you know, I'd be lying to you if I told you I thought that when we were doing this, I thought we'd be the future home of the Chicago Bears."

How Hammond Prepared for This

The Bears completed their review of the Lost Marsh site in Hammond while also doing their due diligence on the Lake Terminal site. McDermott said those potential sites for a stadium came to be through efforts to clean up the area.

"The site that we're talking about right now, if you were looking at it when I first took over, it was I don't think the Bears would have even thought it was possible to locate a stadium there because there was so many different landowners. it was underutilized and it was just old-fashioned, old thinking," McDermott said.

"For the first two or three terms, in cooperation with the state government, we started assembling dozens and dozens of acres and we got it to where we have about 300 acres available."

But even throughout the process of assembling the acreage, it was never done with the thought the it could one day be the home of the Bears.

"I'll be honest with you, never in a million years did I think that we'd one day be the home—the future home of the Chicago Bears. We were just doing it to clean up and hoping that good things would happen and improve the quality of life," McDermott said.

However, acquiring and developing land wasn’t the only thing Hammond did to prepare for the Bears. The state of Indiana has more favorable property tax caps than Illinois, which McDermott said was of interest to the Bears.

"Another thing that Indiana did to prepare for this day was there's a gap from one side of the state line to the other in what it costs to run a household, what it costs to run a business, and in Indiana, we enshrine tax caps, property tax caps, into our constitution. And one of the buzzwords of this whole ordeal with the Bears is property tax certainty, which is something the Bears are interested in, and they can't get property tax certainty in Illinois," McDermott said.

"And certainly in year zero and for the next 30 years, they certainly can't get property tax certainty. And in Indiana, ours are enshrined in our constitution. You can't pay over 1%, 2% or 3% depending on your classification."

Heather Ennis, president and CEO of the Northwest Indiana Forum, told OutKick in a recent interview that Northwest Indiana has seen billions of dollars invested in the region, not including any potential deal with the Bears.

"We're a $52 billion regional economy and we're seeing in the last 10 months over $30 billion of investment committed to the region, and that doesn't even include any of the Bears conversation. So we're really seeing people be bullish on Northwest Indiana and the opportunities that are coming to the region," Ennis told OutKick.

Another thing working in Hammond’s favor? Complete cooperation across the board.

WWE NXT STAR TALKS CHICAGO BEARS' POSSIBLE MOVE TO INDIANA: 'WHAT THE F?'

McDermott said he has never seen more bipartisan cooperation in his 23 years than he has during the Bears discussions.

"I'm in my sixth term and I've never seen the coordination across federal, state, bipartisan, Republican and Democratic lines, everybody working in lockstep. And I mean from the U.S. senators in Indiana, both of them are working on this project. The congressman in Indiana who's a Democrat, both U.S. senators are Republicans, the governor is a Republican and I'm a Democrat. And you wouldn't know it at all when you're looking at everybody working so hard on this project," McDermott said

"Governor Braun has been a great leader for Indiana. He is helping Hammond out tremendously. And this is a Democratic city that probably didn’t vote for Governor Braun for governor. So the bipartisanship, the federal partnerships that we have with the state partnerships, you need all that. And quite frankly, we started off on one location in Hammond and sort of changed course a couple months ago and nothing changed. We just shifted modes up here. And I think that impressed the - it was literally a gear shift and we just rolled right with it and they're the customer."

"If this is what the Bears want us to look at, no problem, sir. And we get to work. And it's been very business friendly. I think the Bears would tell you they're very impressed with the bipartisanship and the total cooperation they've received from Indiana."

Why a Move Feels Real

This is not the first time the Bears have considered moving to Indiana. In the late 1990s, they considered moving to Gary, Indiana.

But it didn’t work out, which is why McDermott, among many others, was skeptical that the Bears were serious about making a move this time around.

"I'll be honest with you, I started off skeptical. I really did because we've been through this drill before in Northwest Indiana in the '90s, a similar type of situation with the Bears. The location was supposed to be the city of Gary at the time and that never panned out. And there was a lot of skepticism in Northwest Indiana that the Bears were never serious in the '90s and they're probably not serious now," McDermott said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"So, I had that lingering doubt, but I'm a mayor. I'm a longtime mayor. I'm an economic development guy. I like to close deals. So, as a mayor, even if you think there's not much of a possibility, you're still going to work your tail off to try to make it happen. And that's the approach I took to it."

McDermott said he was brought in last year around the holidays but that Gov. Mike Braun and the speaker of the House were involved long before he was. McDermott said he had to sign nondisclosure agreements to keep things quiet.

For McDermott, things didn’t feel real until he got a call from a big company that he declined to identify about the potential acquisition of its property.

"When I started to finally feel like this was the real deal, I remember there was a big company in my city," McDermott said. "But a big company called my office and it panicked because they got calls from the state of Indiana about their property being acquired. And that's when I was like, 'Okay.’"

"It was a big company and they were like, 'Mayor, do you know what's going on? Why is the state of Indiana interested in buying our property?' And we couldn't tell them why, but there were a lot of high fives in City Hall that day because that's when it hit me. Wow, this isn't the 1990s. This is a totally different ordeal."

As for Soldier Field, the Bears’ lease runs through 2033, but they can pay a fee to break the lease early. Soldier Field is about 40 miles south of Halas Hall — the team’s headquarters in Lake Forest — and Hammond is about 20 miles south of the team’s lakefront stadium.

Indiana House Speaker Todd Huston was the lead House sponsor of Senate Bill 27, which passed with ease. The bill created a funding mechanism for the Northwest Indiana Stadium Authority to build a future stadium in the state.

Huston said the Bears moving to Indiana would create opportunities that would last for generations.

"This project would be a transformational opportunity for Northwest Indiana. It would deliver lasting benefits across the region and our entire state, building on a foundation that’s already been put in place for the last two decades. Northwest Indiana is experiencing tremendous growth and potential, and an investment of this scale would take that to another level — bringing new jobs and businesses, attracting visitors and residents, and creating opportunities that will benefit Hoosiers for generations," Huston told OutKick in a statement.

"Indiana has created an environment that keeps costs low for businesses and families, attracts investment, supports job growth and expands opportunity. When the potential of this project presented itself, state and local leaders recognized its potential and moved quickly. That combination of a low-cost, forward-looking environment and a willingness to get things done is what continues to attract businesses, investment and people to Indiana."

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Building the infrastructure

Becoming the new home of a professional football team means a lot more than just building a stadium and then calling it a day. The city also needs to have requisite infrastructure to harbor tens of thousands of fans, highways and roads for them to travel on.

With Hammond on the southern tip of Lake Michigan, McDermott said the utility infrastructure is already well developed.

"We have a lot of big businesses here. We have industrial businesses here. We have a data center here. We have big users of energy and our infrastructure. Hammond's located just to the south of the tip of Lake Michigan. So, all of the infrastructure, the utilities, the highways, the rail lines go through Hammond. And in a project like this, the fact that the utility infrastructure is already so built up because we're the southern tip of Lake Michigan is helping us tremendously when we're looking at bringing in a stadium because the stadium needs heavy infrastructure," McDermott said.

McDermott said Arlington Heights, Illinois, about 30 miles northwest of Chicago and another location the Bears are considering, faces a challenge in terms of infrastructure, while Hammond doesn’t have that same issue.

While Hammond doesn’t face that same issue, McDermott said the area does need significant highway, interstate and road infrastructure improvements, but it already has a good blueprint.

"Although we're going to need a massive infusion of highway and off-interstate and road infrastructure improvements, there's $600 million built into this deal for infrastructure improvements around the proposed footprint of the stadium. We already have a good blueprint and it's only going to get bigger and better," McDermott said.

Ennis said Indiana has all the infrastructure needed to bring a project like this to fruition, calling Indiana "the crossroads of America."

"We are the region that built America. Over 25% of the nation's steel is built here and in our region, and so we have all of the infrastructure to be able to bring a project like this to fruition. We've got great highway infrastructure connectivity to Chicago. We've double tracked the commuter rail line and have an extension of that commuter rail line to extend down further into Lake County," Ennis said.

"We are truly part of the Chicago metro area, and so that great base of infrastructure that is already here with the beautiful waterfront, the great highway infrastructure, the commuter rail system. There definitely will need to be improvements made to continue to connect these sites to the opportunities that already exist, but other regions around the country drool over the infrastructure that we have here in Northwest Indiana."

For fans who are concerned about the stadium moving from Soldier Field to Hammond, McDermott admitted it’s easier to get to Soldier Field but said there are many ways to commute to Indiana.

"If you're in downtown Chicago, I understand that it was a lot easier to go to Soldier Field, but we are connected by highway. We're connected by water during certain times of year and by rail. It's far easier to get to Hammond and quicker than it would be to get to Arlington Heights," McDermott said.

"And the Bears could build a heck of a lot more stadium in Indiana than they could in Illinois right now because of the financial situation in Indiana versus Illinois. So, if you're a true fan of the Chicago Bears, I think we're going to have a better fan experience in Indiana. I think the team's going to be better in Indiana."



New City, Same Name

McDermott made it clear: The Chicago Bears will remain the Chicago Bears. A name change was never discussed.

"Not even once. There is nothing. Listen, there's some Hammond Bears stuff going around Northwest Indiana, but I'm sure the Bears didn't authorize it. I just want you to know that was never—it's more of a local pride thing," McDermott said.

"Everybody knows the Chicago Bears are the Chicago Bears. That's never been broached by the state government or by the city government. The Chicago Bears are an icon, and there's no way we'd ever ask them to change their name."

The Bears themselves have echoed the same sentiment.

"We will be the Chicago Bears whether we’re in Arlington or whether we’re in Hammond," Bears chairman George McCaskey said in August.

McDermott also made it clear that while many people assume Indiana residents are automatically Indianapolis Colts fans, Northwest Indiana is Bears country.

"I know we're in Indiana. I know everybody thinks just because of our address in Indiana that we're Colts fans. That is not the case. In Northwest Indiana, it's the Bears, and probably the Packers are probably the second most liked team. The Colts are probably third in the region where we're talking about right now, but it's Bears country. So, like I said, I want the Bears to be good this year because everybody's happy when the Bears are good," McDermott said.

Where Do Negotiations Currently Stand?

The Bears scored 59 points in their Week 1 win against the Carolina Panthers, dominating in the red zone.

Using an analogy in which a touchdown means the Bears are officially moving to Hammond, McDermott said the ball is currently in the red zone.

"We're in the red zone for sure. So, where are we in the red zone? I think the only people that could answer that is Mr. McCaskey and Kevin Warren. But I definitely think we're in the red zone and there's a lot of work going on, and it's hard to punch the ball into the end zone, and that's where we are right now," McDermott said.

"When you're in the red zone, the defense is tightened up and everybody's shoved into a little box and it's even harder to score. I think that's where we are right now, but we're going to punch it in."

McDermott said the ball is in the hands of McCaskey and Bears President Kevin Warren and that things are out of his control.

"The ball is 100% in their court. So, I try not to make promises. I realize this is not in my control. I hope that it's done sooner. I hope that the Bears choose Hammond and we start moving forward, and that's all it is really. It's hoping," McDermott said.

"But, you know, the Bears are going to do it when they're comfortable, and if they're going to invest billions of dollars into a piece of property, they got to be very comfortable that what they're doing is the right thing, and that's what they're doing and I don't blame them, you know?"

Ennis said while landing the Bears would be great for Indiana, the Bears should feel just as excited about choosing such a booming area.

"The Bears would—we would be lucky to have the Bears come here, but they would be just as lucky to locate here because we really have our act together and our communities are really working in lockstep to make those investments happen. Working together with the state, you know, across the entire platform to really make things happen," Ennis said.

As a Bears fan, McDermott doesn’t want to disrupt the team and bug McCaskey or Warren too much.

If McCaskey and Warren are anything like the Bears’ offense, they might make it to the end zone sooner rather than later and make Indiana the team’s new home.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement partnered with more than five other federal, state and local agencies in a weeklong immigration-enforcement operation in Southwest Florida that yielded 500 arrests.

World.title: Alix Earle’s stepmom owns ‘reckless’ past, from Spitzer escort scandal to affair with influencer’s dad
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Ashley Dupré isn’t running from her "reckless" past anymore.

Alix Earle’s stepmother opened up about the choices that once made her tabloid fodder, including her connection to the Eliot Spitzer prostitution scandal and her affair with the influencer’s married father. Alix, 25, shot to fame on TikTok and has built a massive following by sharing her life online – including, at times, the complicated family history that played out in the tabloids when she was a child.

Ashley was thrust into the national spotlight in 2008 when she was identified as an escort connected to then-New York Gov. Eliot Spitzer in the prostitution scandal that preceded his resignation.

"At 19, while working as a cocktail waitress, a man approached me and told me I could make $1,000 an hour going on dates with high-profile men," she wrote in an essay for Elle. "My first answer was no, but I kept his card. Eventually, I made the call. I could spend paragraphs explaining why. I was young. I wanted money and independence. I’d spent years operating in survival mode and had become very good at compartmentalizing. But ultimately, I made the call. It was my decision."

ALIX EARLE SPOTTED DANCING WITH TOM BRADY IN ST. BARTS: WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE SOCIAL MEDIA SENSATION

According to Ashley, she managed the work for two years without anyone knowing.

"Then, when I was 22, the FBI knocked on my door and showed me a photograph of a man I had seen," she explained. "I didn’t know who he was. When they told me he was the governor of New York, I couldn’t begin to understand what was about to happen."

What followed was a level of attention Ashley said she never could have anticipated.

"Soon, my stage name and face were on the front page of The New York Post. There was an almost ridiculous irony to it," she recalled. "I had come to New York City wanting to be noticed, and suddenly everyone noticed me – for the one thing I never wanted anyone to know."

‘DUCK DYNASTY’ STAR SADIE ROBERTSON HUFF ADMITS ‘FEARS’ OVER PUTTING HER KIDS ON REALITY TV

Ashley said she can now look back at that period without minimizing the role she played.

"Context isn’t absolution. I made choices. Some were reckless," she wrote. "Some were selfish. They had consequences. I can own all of that without believing those choices have to be the most interesting thing about me forever."

Ashley's affair with TJ hit the tabloids in 2008, months after she made headline news with the Spitzer scandal. The two had met by chance at a restaurant in New Jersey and things escalated from there. "We talked for five or six hours, and our connection was immediate," Ashley recalled.

"TJ was married," she admitted. "We crossed a line we shouldn’t have crossed, and I take responsibility for my part in that. Our choices affected and hurt other people, including his wife, Alisa, and daughters, Alix and Ashtin, and I don’t take that lightly."

Alix was just a child when the affair turned her family life into tabloid news.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I remember the day very clearly," Alix said on a 2023 episode of "Call Her Daddy." "Paparazzi had shown up at my house and my mom quickly kind of got me and my sister out of the house over to our cousins. We stayed there for a few days and I had no idea what was going on. I didn't know they were paparazzi. I thought news broadcasters were interviewing the neighbors."

While Alix was too young to understand what was happening at the time, she later discovered who Ashley was.

"It was in like fourth grade," she told host Alex Cooper. "I started to kind of hear commentary from people and I had an iPad at the time. I'm Googling my family and, all of a sudden, I see that the past two years of my life had been a lie."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"My dad had an affair with someone who was well-known for her job having sexual relations with high-class people and one of them was even the governor of New York," Alix said. "She was very well-known from that and, in turn, my dad's affair became a very public situation."

Ashley and TJ later married in 2013. But the fallout followed Alix beyond her family’s front door and into her childhood. Friends often weren't allowed to come over to her home.

"The parents would kind of tell my mom, and she would tell me kind of the harsh truth of why this can't happen," she said. "She would have to sit me down and be like, 'They don't really respect us.'"

Behind closed doors, Alix was also grappling with her father's new relationship.

"When my stepmom started to hang around with my dad after he had moved out, she came into his life, and we were introduced to her, which was super weird," Alix explained. "And I was told that I had to be respectful to this woman, and we had to be nice to her. I wanted to rip her head off. It was very weird because I felt like I was a 10-year-old having to be more mature than someone 20, 30 years older than me."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Despite their difficult beginning, Ashley eventually became a permanent part of the Earle family. Their relationship evolved in the years that followed, as Ashley and TJ built a life together.

Nearly two decades later, Ashley said she no longer feels the need to convince the world that she is more than her past.

"Twenty years ago, I wanted everyone to understand me. Today, I don’t," Ashley wrote. "The people sitting around my dinner table know who I am. So do I."

"I’m not ashamed of the young woman I was," Ashley added. "I wouldn’t make all of her choices again, but I’m also done wishing her away. She was ambitious, reckless, complicated, and sometimes very wrong. But she kept going."

"We live in a culture that can preserve a person’s worst moment forever," she mused. "Accountability matters, but so does allowing people to grow. If we believe that no one can become more than the bad decision they made at 19 or 22, then we leave very little room for any of us to change."

World.title: Fantasy doesn’t need another 'Game of Thrones.' It needs what Tolkien understood
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Tales of dragons, noble kings, evil empires, heroic quests and the battle between light and darkness have captured imaginations across cultures for years. We’re drawn to the adventure of legends and lore because something deep inside us longs to be filled with wonder. Our hearts ache to know that courage still means something, that love is worth fighting for and that the world holds more mystery than the mundanity of our daily routines.

Tolkien and Lewis understood this and built Middle-earth and Narnia as entire worlds where wonder and danger were intertwined, and courage was meaningful because it came at a cost. Their books are still adored generations later because they never confused darkness with goodness.

Today, the epic fantasy genre is more popular than ever, with audiences spending billions annually consuming comics, toys, books, movies and video games. But much of it betrays what made it great.

RUSSELL CROWE SAYS 'GLADIATOR II' FAILED BECAUSE IT LACKED ORIGINAL FILM'S 'MORAL CORE'

Somewhere in recent years, creators began to confuse being mature with being explicit, turning the industry into a clickbait factory pumping out gratuitous sex and violence to lure eyeballs and dollars. Even worse, the industry seems to be trying to sneak it all in under parents’ noses.

Pick up one of the best-selling fantasy series of the last few years and you will likely find yourself in a world the cover never warned you about. "A Court of Thorns and Roses" and "Fourth Wing" are marketed as young adult fiction in stores and school libraries despite graphic content throughout — part of the trend toward darker and more explicit YA publishing. The "Game of Thrones" universe shows where that trajectory ends. The book series alone portrays 214 separate acts of rape across 117 named victims, and a survey of the show’s own viewers concluded its pervasive sexual violence served no purpose in the story at all.

WE SHOULD TELL REAL AMERICAN ADVENTURE STORIES TO TEACH OUR BOYS ABOUT HEROES

The smut is a distraction from the good of fantasy: the imagined worlds, heroes and adventures that call its fans to a higher ethos.

The question, then, is not whether evil exists, but whether fantasy creators ask their video game players to fight it or practice it, whether fantasy authors craft stories that expose darkness or train an audience to enjoy it.

This does not mean every creature, battle, or supernatural power is evil. The Bible is full of supernatural events. It contains war, betrayal, demons, giants, dragons, sorcery and miracles. "The Lord of the Rings" depicts monsters, magic, death, corruption and the temptation of power. But these stories make clear that evil has consequences, courage matters and darkness is never confused with goodness. Children who read the "Chronicles of Narnia" must confront serious themes of deception, sacrifice and death, yet come to understand that goodness is worth dying for.

DIRECTOR OF NEW ‘LORD OF THE RINGS’ REJECTS ‘POLITICALLY CORRECT’ CASTING AFTER SUGGESTIONS FILM IS TOO WHITE

And these are some of the best-selling titles of all time. Clearly, fantasy fans want danger, powerful enemies, imperfect characters, adventure, wonder, humor and hope. But do we really want our 15-year-olds engrossed in pornography, vulgarity, hopelessness or stories that present evil as good?

It would be easy to hear all of this and assume the answer is to steer strictly toward faith-based and conservative entertainment. Yet conservative or Christian creators must also do better. Audiences expect excellent writing, acting, music, visuals and production. Traditional or even Christian values cannot save a boring story, uninspiring characters, unconvincing worlds or bad gameplay.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Tolkien and Lewis did not build Middle Earth or Narnia as a sermon in disguise. The truth inside their worlds came alive because the craft came first. That is the standard worth chasing. Not just a cleaner version of what already exists, but a new golden age of fantasy, written by authors, filmmakers and studios — Christian and secular alike — willing to do the harder work of making something genuinely good.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

To every storyteller reading this: the desire for wonder without wreckage is enormous. We need to craft worlds worth losing ourselves in for an afternoon, with heroes worth following into the dark because we trust they’re going to lead us back into the light. We need to remember what made fantasy worth loving in the first place and go write it again.

World.title: Ed Sheeran calls situation in Gaza ‘unjustifiable’ in first concert since Macklemore controversy
World.content:
Demonstrators shouted “Free, free Palestine” in unison as motorists honked their horns in support.

Robert Boucher, 73, a retired surgeon, said he was there to take a stand for freedom of speech.

“The action that’s been taken by the stadium owners and folks who oppose Macklemore and what he represents and the comments that he’s made, that’s really an unjustifiable attempt to squelch free speech,” Boucher said.

The Philadelphia resident asserted that his criticism is of the Israeli government and its treatment of civilians in Gaza, not a stance against Jewish people.

“We’re here to specifically support our right to say the things that we’re saying and to not be labeled as antisemites or anti-Israel,” he said.

Gwen Myrick, 51, of West Philadelphia, said she supports Macklemore’s stand.

“I am here in support of Macklemore,” she said. “Because that is how a movement is born — standing up for the people who are brave enough to stand up.”

Robert Boucher, a retired surgeon, asserted that criticism of the state of Israel for its treatment of civilians in Gaza is not a stance against Jewish people. Nicole Acevedo / NBC News

The protest followed a weeklong controversy that began after Macklemore voiced support for Palestinians. He accused Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium, of organizing a boycott among stadium owners in response, an allegation Kraft did not deny.

In a statement, Kraft, a staunch supporter of Israel and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, said the decision was not intended to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminish Palestinian suffering but to ensure a “welcoming environment” at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Macklemore had been scheduled to open two “Loop” tour dates there later this month.

Sheeran said previously that the company promoting his tour made the final decision to drop Macklemore because it held the rapper’s contract.

Messina Touring Group did not respond to multiple requests for comment from NBC News. The promoter told Rolling Stone that it had been informed that multiple venues “will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup,” resulting in his removal.

Macklemore had been scheduled to open Saturday’s show in Philadelphia. Instead, the protesters outside Lincoln Financial Field repeated some of the same pro-Palestinian remarks that Macklemore said led to his removal.

Adi Chattopadhyay, who said he helped organize the demonstration, said Sheeran could halt criticism by donating money to Palestinian-related causes.

“Send that money to families in Gaza,” he said. “Will he support the innocent people of Gaza who have been bombarded? Will he actually do something?”

Macklemore has pledged to donate $1 million, which he said represented all of the net earnings from Sheeran’s tour, to six organizations supporting Palestinians. Kraft later pledged $2 million toward causes supporting people impacted by the war in Gaza to match a similar donation made by Sheeran.

On Saturday, Sheeran told fans at his show that he’s spoken to “people across the spectrum to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times.”

Sheeran, right, said previously that the company promoting his tour made the final decision to drop Macklemore, left, because it held the rapper’s contract. Getty Images

‘I just really came for Ed Sheeran’

Despite the controversy, fans inside the stadium said they were excited to watch Sheeran’s performance, and weren’t bothered by the lack of opening act.

Friends Karen Mossop, 59, and Karen Macort, 62, said they were there to experience only one artist — Sheeran.

Mossop defended Sheeran and said he just “got caught up in a really negative campaign.”

“Because he’s a really nice guy, he didn’t realize the ramifications of what would happen,” she said.

Mossop also questioned the professionalism of the artists who dropped out.

“It’s a shame that the opening acts quit,” she said. “They’re supposed to be professionals, and they should have acted professionally.”

Alexandria Rasa, 27, of neighboring New Jersey, said she was excited to experience her second Sheeran concert.

“I just really came for Ed Sheeran,” Rasa said. “I don’t really care about his opening acts, so that didn’t really affect me.”

Friend Hannah Luster, 26, also of New Jersey, was focused on the task at hand — basking in the music.

“[I’m] definitely going to enjoy it, probably going to take a video or two,” she said.

Fans inside the stadium said they were excited to watch Sheeran’s performance, and weren’t bothered by the lack of opening act. Heather Barry / Getty Images

Dale Dietrich, 46, and his friend, Jeanine Fusik, 47, were hoping that Taylor Swift, who has been known to join Sheeran on stage, and vice-versa, might appear with him Saturday night.

“Ed needs to be rescued,” Dietrich said, referring to fallout from Macklemore’s departure, “and there’s probably one person that can really do it.”

Sheeran did not appear to need saving once the show got underway, though. But he did address the absence of his normal “B stage,” saying it was missing “because I was afraid of what might happen if I stood in the middle, and I will admit that.”

Sheeran spent much of his time on stage as a one-man band — a style fans will recognize from past performances — letting his vocals, instruments and loop pedal command the stadium crowd. But he also got some backup after calling a friend for last-minute help.

The fill-in musicians — a drummer, keyboardist, bassist, guitarist and violinist — had three days to learn the songs, Sheeran said, and he thanked them for their support.

He seemed most grateful to the audience at Lincoln Financial Field.

“Today has honestly been the best show of my life” he said. “I’ve felt so much love from you guys, and I am so grateful.”

The concert ended with fireworks and a crowd on its feet.

Nicole Acevedo reported from Philadelphia, and Dennis Romero from San Diego.

World.title: King Charles accused of ‘gaslighting’ by Princess Diana’s brother in dispute over book claims
World.content:
Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of “gaslighting” him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct.

Buckingham Palace released an unusually forceful statement Wednesday ahead of the release of a memoir by Spencer, which charts the breakdown of then-Prince Charles’s marriage to Princess Diana, and the fallout from her death in a Paris car crash in 1997, one year after the royal couple finalized their divorce.

In an initial excerpt released ahead of publication, Spencer recalled a heated phone call with Charles amid a disagreement about funeral arrangements, claiming that a furious Charles had told him Diana would “soon be forgotten.”

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” the palace had responded.

In an interview with Britain’s Mail on Sunday newspaper, Spencer said: “It is not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king.”

“It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said,” Spencer added.

“Gaslighting” is a form of manipulation where the manipulator is trying to get someone to question their own reality, memory or perceptions.

Spencer also denied he was motivated by money in publishing the book, saying it “has never even been the remotest consideration” and stressing that “my primary responsibility as a historian is to tell the truth.”

The aristocrat, an earl whose family has generational ties with Britain’s royal family, has made a number of other allegations in excerpts since released from the book, published in advance by the Daily Mail newspaper.

In the excerpts, Spencer writes that Charles sounded “giddily elated” and “like a lottery winner” when they spoke by phone immediately after Diana’s death, adding: “I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.”

He also speaks about his sister’s mental health and recounts conversations with her, recalling that she had told him how “things became very difficult indeed in the marriage early on.”

Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be released publicly on Tuesday.

Since its initial statement, Buckingham Palace has remained silent on the further allegations from Spencer’s book. The palace again declined to comment Sunday.

There has been no public comment from Princes William and Harry, Charles and Diana’s two sons, on Spencer’s memoir.

Prince Harry, who quit as a working royal six years ago amid a reported rift with senior royals, has remained close to the Spencer family, with his own memoir “Spare” thanking “my mother’s siblings for their love, support, time, and perspective.”

In an interview with the BBC that is set to air Sunday, Spencer said that Harry and his wife Megan Markle’s treatment at the hands of Britain’s infamous tabloid press has “echoes” of what happened to Diana.

“If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant,” Spencer said when questioned whether he believed Diana would “identify” with the scrutiny faced by Harry and Megan.

He added: “I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana’s example. I’m not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who’s being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life.”

The royal family continued to undertake public duties this week even as Spencer’s book has dominated the headlines, with Charles also meeting with senior figures in AI at a summit in Scotland.

World.title: Is it too early to panic in the NFL? These teams don’t want to find out
World.content:
“My message is just echoing ‘don’t change, don’t flinch, don’t blink,’” Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott said. “This is a long year. We have to stick together.”

Two seasons ago, the Rams were one of three teams that started 0-2 and still made the playoffs. But as the Rams, the preseason Super Bowl favorite, prepare to face the Giants (1-0) on Monday, they have already lost more than their first game. Pass-rushing star Myles Garrett will miss at least four games after he underwent surgery last week to combat swelling in his left knee. The un-retirement of Aaron Donald will help absorb the loss of Garrett along the defensive line, but Donald won’t be an every-down player.

The Rams’ vaunted offense managed just 190 yards in its first performance against the San Francisco 49ers, as well.

“The big area of focus improvement will be in regard to the pass game and some of the different things that we can do collectively,” coach Sean McVay said. “It always starts with me.”

The Rams are one of five teams this season — joining the Broncos, the Packers, the Cowboys and the Washington Commanders — that already have one division loss. Of that group, NFC East rivals Washington and Dallas find themselves in the most precarious situations. When they play each other Sunday, one will leave 0-2 in its division.

“It’s another division game,” Cowboys pass rusher Rashan Gary said. “Understanding that, we know we just went 0-1, and we can’t do that going into this week. The urgency is up, for sure.”

The Patriots have been here before. Last season they responded to their 0-1 start by losing only two more times over the next four months en route to a Super Bowl appearance. The bounceback was helped, however, by playing the easiest schedule in 26 years.

It will be more difficult to keep this latest season-opening loss from snowballing into something bigger. The Patriots’ next three opponents all made the playoffs last season, starting with Sunday’s matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers — whose defense sacked New England quarterback Drake Maye five times and forced five turnovers when the teams met last season. An injured ankle will sideline the Steelers’ top offseason acquisition, receiver A.J. Brown, for at least the next four games.

World.title: American dream of owning a home out of reach for many as mortgage rates soar (again)
World.content:
The average interest rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage soared to 7.2% this week, its highest in a year and a half. Coupled with home prices near record highs, it’s putting the American dream of owning a home further out of reach for millions.

“We don’t want to buy this big, beautiful house only to just sit in it, staring at each other, stressing about a mortgage payment every month,” said Alexandra DeCandia, who teaches biology at Georgetown University.

DeCandia and her husband, Edward Schrom, both 33, are looking for their first home in the Washington area. They hope to start a family and want to buy a home before they do.

“It’s something that’s a huge decision and one that will impact us, as well as our future family,” DeCandia said. “It’s very stressful to try to figure that out in this shifting landscape.”

Mortgage rates were on a downswing earlier this year, hitting 5.99% in late February. But ever since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, they have skyrocketed.

Mortgage interest rates are heavily influenced by the yield on 10-year Treasury bonds, which has been rising as oil prices soar and drive up the cost of goods across the economy.

And mortgage rates could keep rising. The Federal Reserve this week hiked its key interest rate in an effort to get a handle on inflation — and it suggested it may raise rates again this year. Higher rates can drive up borrowing costs across the economy.

Meanwhile, the average home price nationwide is near a record high, at $429,100 as of August.

One bright spot for homebuyers, however, is inventory. There were 1.62 million unsold homes on the market in August, according to the National Association of Realtors.

That’s equal to 4.9 months’ supply, which is measured as the time it would take at the current pace of sales to sell all those homes. That is the highest level in more than a decade, and it gives prospective homebuyers more room to negotiate prices.
