World.title: World leaders return to UN amid wars in Middle East and Ukraine
World.content:
UN. File photo shows US President Donald Trump addressing the 80th United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US on September 23, 2025.

Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organization

UNITED NATIONS — World leaders gather in New York this week for the UN General Assembly, bracing for President Donald Trump‘s return to the rostrum for a second year running, with talks centering on the widening conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine and the risks of artificial intelligence.

Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War II order under strain and with the UN itself struggling to remain relevant and weathering attacks from Trump, who has slashed America’s contributions and withdrawn from dozens of UN bodies.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who last addressed the diplomatic jamboree via video in 2021, will skip New York in favor of one-on-one talks with Trump in Washington on Thursday, fueling debate about the UN’s relevance in addressing global crises.

Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organization: Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of 2026, with no clear frontrunner in the race to replace him.

The 15-member UN Security Council may hold high-level meetings on Ukraine, AI and the Middle East, including talks with Arab leaders, diplomats said.

More than a year into Trump’s second term, “we would no longer say that the UN is in freefall, but we would say that it’s stuck in an open-ended crisis,” said Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group.

“The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it seems to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future,” Gowan said.

The US avoided losing its vote at the assembly by paying $725 million in contributions to the regular budget this week, but it still owes the organization more than a billion dollars and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms.

Growing AI risks

The assembly meets shortly after several artificial intelligence industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and escape human control.

Guterres has said that AI will be a major topic, adding that countries pushing its frontiers should set up “common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level.”

The secretary-general has long proposed global governance of AI. In 2023, the UN created an advisory body on the technology, with members including tech executives, government officials and academics.

The warning has put Guterres at odds with Trump, who dismissed AI risks as a “hoax,” saying there is a “sick conspiracy” against it and that China would benefit from the doubt being cast on its development.

Middle East escalation

The Middle East will again be a focus of discussions, as the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to drive global inflation and destabilize the region. Recent gains by Houthi militants threaten shipping in ​the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and could further spike energy prices.

“It’s very difficult to have a military solution for that problem, and the experience of fighting in Yemen demonstrated how complicated it is to have successful interventions,” said Guterres, adding that the UN’s envoy on Yemen was making a “huge effort” to advance talks.

Peace talks remain stalled, however, as Iran and the US continue to exchange strikes and Trump threatens a major escalation of the war.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly on Wednesday.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza that Israel denies – is to speak on Thursday.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will for the second year running not be at the gathering in person. The US, a close Israeli ally, again denied him a visa. On Thursday, the General Assembly voted to allow Abbas to appear via video.

There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines, diplomats said, although a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely.

Ukraine, food security

Also on the agenda is Russia’s more than four-year-old war in Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will address the General Assembly. Zelenskiy will likely seek to shore up Ukraine’s position ahead of what is expected to be another tough winter, diplomats said.

The Security Council has been unable to take action to end the conflict because permanent member Russia holds a veto.

Trump has at times appeared frustrated that he has been unable to broker an end to the war, a goal he declared a priority when he began his second term in January last year. The US president spoke with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin earlier this month, but it was unclear whether he plans to meet Zelenskiy in New York.

Guterres highlighted the impact the war was having on civilians but also on food security and energy prices.

“The effective blockade existing in the Black Sea is creating enormous problems that add to the problems generated by the Middle East crisis, and I think it would be very important to find a way to allow Ukrainian exports and Russian exports of food, fertilizers and energy to take place in a safe way through the Black Sea,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Agatha Wong shifts focus to med school after Asian Games swan song
World.content:
FORM. The Philippines' Agatha Chrystenzen Wong in action in the women's wushu taijiquan and taijijian event in the 2026 Asian Games.

MANILA, Philippines – Filipina wushu star Agatha Wong turns her attention to her other calling after seeing action at the Asian Games for the last time.

Wong delivered her Asian Games swan song, finishing 10th overall in the women’s taijiquan and taijijian event at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall in Nagoya, Japan, on Sunday, September 20.

The 28-year-old stayed within reach of a podium finish after placing seventh in the taijiquan portion with 9.703 points before she bid her medal hopes goodbye as she landed 11th in the taijijian segment with 9.156 points for a total of 18.859.

China’s Tong Xin defended her throne with 19.553 points, Japan’s Shiho Saito (19.473) claimed silver, while Brunei’s Basma Lachkar and Singapore’s Zeanne Law tied for the bronze with identical 19.443 marks.

Although it was Wong’s lowest finish at the Asian Games after she won bronze in 2018 in Jakarta, Indonesia, and placed fifth in 2023 in Hangzhou, China, she remained proud of her effort.

“I think I could have done better but that’s how it is. I’m really happy that I did well in the first event. In the second event, I know that I did my best so that’s enough for me,” Wong told reporters in mix of Filipino and English.

Wong, a champion in the last five Southeast Asian Games as well as a silver and bronze medalist in the World Wushu Championships, earlier told Asian Games broadcaster Cignal that she will not be around for the next edition of the continental showpiece.

That may have something to do with her aspirations of becoming a doctor, as Wong has a lot of catching up to do with her studies at the University of the East Ramon Magsaysay Memorial Medical Center.

Wong, who started medical school in 2023, is now in her third year.

“I have to study already so I’m going to go back,” said Wong. “I’ll still continue training. I have competitions for next year so that’s going to be fun. But I’m already done for this year.” – Rappler.com

World.title: From Beda to UP: James Payosing brings premium spark to UAAP
World.content:
PUMPED. James Payosing in action for the UP Fighting Maroons in the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament.

James Payosing, an NCAA champion and a Finals MVP with the San Beda Red Lions, brings the same winning mentality to the UP Fighting Maroons

MANILA, Philippines – James Payosing needed just 15 minutes to show he truly belongs on the UAAP stage.

The former NCAA champion poured in 16 points on 4-of-5 shooting and added 3 rebounds and 2 assists as the UP Fighting Maroons dispatched the Ateneo Blue Eagles, 94-75, on Saturday, September 19.

Payosing did it at the Araneta Coliseum, the same venue where he led the San Beda Red Lions to the NCAA Season 99 championship in 2023 and earned Finals MVP honors.

Now, he is looking to bring that same winning mentality to UP.

“As a player, my mindset is that I’m in a team sport, so I’m just doing my role that complements the team. When one wins, everybody does,” Payosing said after just his second game with UP following his initial commitment in 2024.

“Since this is my first season here in the UAAP, I’m just embracing the games and the opportunity. Whenever I play, I aim to stand out in my role.”

That has always been Payosing’s approach, even during his time at San Beda.

The 6-foot-2 guard knows when to pick his spots, rarely forces the issue, and brings an unrelenting intensity on defense. He does not need the ball in his hands to make an impact, and against Ateneo, that versatility proved valuable.

Payosing helped contain Ateneo’s rookie sensation Kieffer Alas, who was held to just 3 points in the second half. Alas finished with 13 points on 5-of-11 shooting as Ateneo struggled to find answers against UP’s defense.

For Payosing, the performance was another glimpse of what he can bring to a team built around a collective identity rather than one dominant star.

The 23-year-old is also enjoying a rare opportunity to bring glory to two of the country’s proudest collegiate programs over the past five years, San Beda and UP.

“I expect a winning culture here at UP. Winning a championship isn’t easy, but I’ve been preparing for it since last year, my residency year,” Payosing said.

At UP, Payosing is expected to help fill the void left by Harold Alarcon, Reyland Torres, and Terrence Fortea, three key pieces of a Fighting Maroons team that reached the UAAP finals in each of the last five seasons.

Payosing appears to be comfortable with the challenge of filling those shoes.

UP now sits atop the standings at 2-0 after the first week of games, and Payosing hopes his role can help keep the Fighting Maroons on the same path that made them a fixture in the UAAP title picture.

“All I’m saying is that let’s be star players in each of our roles so that when the five of us are on the court, we’re all superstars,” Payosing said.

“The level of competition is almost the same [as the NCAA] and it really comes down the mindset that whoever wants to win the most will win,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] The tip that led us inside a non-consensual porn forum
World.content:
Since the investigation on NSFWPH came out, more people have started sending us their own cases

Earlier this year, student journalist Lance Bustos approached me at an event and told me about NSFWPH.

That was how this investigation began.

It sounds simple, but a lot of investigative work starts exactly that way: someone knows something, sees something, or has been watching something for a while, and decides to tell a journalist.

Lance, who would later become a Rappler fellow, had already been looking into NSFWPH for months. He wasn’t just browsing the site. He had been doing OSINT, or open-source intelligence — collecting publicly available information online, making sense of it, and connecting the dots.

You may have heard the term during the Sara Duterte impeachment trial when the National Bureau of Investigation began investigating the Vice President’s threats against President Bongbong Marcos.

In practice, it can be as basic as following usernames, social media posts, links, timestamps, website records, online videos, and other digital crumbs until a pattern begins to emerge. It has become an effective tool for journalists.

In my case, aside from NSFWPH, during the last presidential election campaign, we investigated DDoS attacks against us and other news sites. We followed the digital trail until it led us to one of the people behind the attacks.

With NSFWPH, Lance had already started doing the same thing. When I began working with him, we kept going.

For months, we tracked behavior inside the forum. We documented not just what people posted, but how the community worked, and how members communicated with one another. What earned attention? What behavior was rewarded? What did users brag about? What did they consider normal?

We felt that truly understanding this was important because online communities can shape behavior.

You may remember 8chan, the forum that became notorious after users linked to several mass shootings posted extremist material there before being shut down in 2019. Obviously, NSFWPH is a different case. But the broader point is the same: what gets normalized online can spill into the real world.

And as we’ve written, we found examples of real-world harm, including students who appeared to have been targeted.

After the Tacloban and Zamboanga shootings, whose shooters allegedly had been influenced by malign online forces operating within an amorphous NVE (nihilistic violent extremism) network, it’s only become more important to pierce through these online spaces.

We also looked at how NSFWPH was set up. Using publicly available tools, we found that it was routed through Cloudflare, which made it more difficult to identify the site’s operator.

That led us to another recurring problem in internet investigations: jurisdiction.

A site may target Filipinos and harm Filipinos, but the companies, servers, or operators behind it may be outside the Philippines. Local authorities can quickly hit a wall.

We see versions of this problem with other platforms too, whether the issue involves Roblox, Meta, or other global services. It is one reason authorities have pushed for foreign platforms to have a local legal entity that can be held accountable without having to rely immediately on international cooperation that may take time. New bills in recent months are legislating for exactly this: official local entities for international platforms that can be quickly held accountable.

And yet the most important part of this investigation was not technical. It goes back to the victims themselves, the people most affected. We wanted to find a person who had actually been victimized on the site and was willing to talk.

I eventually came across one who had already shared her experience online and had directly mentioned NSFWPH. I talked to her, and she articulated her experience bravely and well.

She said the shame belonged to the people who spread the material, not to the person who trusted a partner after being promised that those photos or videos would stay private.

Too often, when intimate material leaks, people ask the victim: Why did you send it? Why did you allow yourself to be recorded?

The better question is: Why did someone violate that trust?

Since the investigation came out, more people have started sending us their own cases. We are going through them now and looking at where our reporting can help.

One person came forward with a tip. That tip became months of monitoring and documenting, leading to our final report. The reporting reached victims. And now some of them are coming forward too. It’s a reminder that sometimes that is how an investigation grows, with one person deciding to speak.

Email us at desk@rappler.com. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Terribly sorry’: Wrong Korean anthem played in Asian Games hockey
World.content:
REPRESENT. Athletes of South Korea in the athletes' parade during the opening ceremony of the 2026 Asian Games at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium in Nagoya, Japan.

Lined up before their match in Asian Games men's hockey, South Korean players look around in confusion as the North Korean national anthem rings out at the stadium

NAGOYA, Japan – The South Korean men’s hockey team was left bemused before its Asian Games match against Bangladesh on Friday, September 18, when North Korea’s national anthem was played instead of its own.

Lined up before the match, the South Korean players looked around in confusion as the anthem rang out at Green Stadium in Gifu, Japan.

Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. The North Korean anthem is mistakenly played for the South Korean team. pic.twitter.com/SycDoRWlF1 — 由仁アリン Arin Yuni 🇸🇬 Singapore meetup (9/26) (@Arin_Yumi) September 18, 2026

The stadium announcer was quick to apologize for the mistake.

“We are really sorry, terribly sorry. National anthem for the Republic of Korea, we played a different song,” he said.

“I’m really sorry.”

South Korea won the match, 5-0.

The North Korean national anthem is banned in South Korea along with other symbols of its wartime foes.

The 1950-1953 Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, meaning the North and South are still technically at war.

The Asian Games organizing committee did not provide immediate comment on the anthem mix-up.

South Korea has complained of a number of organizational problems at the Games, with basketball players unhappy with the size of their rooms and transport issues disrupting preparations for the men’s football team, the defending champions. – Rappler.com

World.title: Eumir Marcial sits out 2026 Asian Games after latest pro win
World.content:
POWER. Eumir Marcial in action for the Philippines in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games.

Eumir Marcial is skipping this Asian Games edition owing to the 'tight timeline' that requires him to promptly fly to Nagoya, Japan, from San Diego, United States, where he scored a third-round knockout win over Omar Ulises Huerta

MANILA, Philippines – The power Eumir Marcial showcased in his latest professional fight will not be on display at the Asian Games.

The Olympic bronze medalist is sitting out this edition of the continental showpiece owing to the “tight timeline” that requires him to promptly fly to Nagoya, Japan, from San Diego, United States, where he scored a third-round knockout win over Omar Ulises Huerta on Saturday, September 19 (Sunday, September 20, Manila time), to keep his professional record unblemished at 8-0.

Association of Boxing Alliances in the Philippines president Marcus Jarwin Manalo said he spoke to Marcial after the bout, and they agreed that it would be best for the pride of Zamboanga to skip the Asian Games and allow himself to rest and recover.

The preliminary round of the men’s 80kg division, where Marcial was initially set to compete, begins on Wednesday, September 23.

“It would be very hard for him to immediately transition from a professional fight in the US, into long-distance travel to Nagoya with 16-hour time difference, and then into another high-level boxing competition with such a short recovery period,” Manalo said in a statement released on Sunday.

“Boxing is a physically demanding and inherently risky sport, and adequate time to rest and recover is extremely important, and we do not want to compromise Eumir’s health and safety because of the tight timeline.”

Losing Marcial is a major blow to the Philippines’ hopes of ending a 16-year gold-medal drought in Asian Games boxing, considering his performances in the last two editions.

Marcial fell short of gold in the 2023 staging in Hangzhou, China, where he suffered a contentious unanimous decision loss to home bet Tuohetaerbieke Tanglatihan in the men’s 80kg final.

He also bagged bronze in the men’s 75kg class at the 2018 edition in Jakarta, Indonesia.

But for Manalo, it was a necessary move, with Marcial’s long-term career in mind.

“Eumir himself was very much looking forward to the opportunity to represent the flag once again. This is therefore a difficult decision for everyone involved,” said Manalo.

“However, representing the Philippines is not only about stepping into the ring. It is also about making responsible decisions that protect our athletes and allow them to have long, healthy careers.”

Marcial is still slated to represent the country at the Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in December.

“We sincerely hope for understanding that this decision was made with Eumir’s best interests in mind. His commitment to Philippine boxing and to representing the country has never been in question,” said Manalo. – Rappler.com

World.title: Day jobs and dreams: Dubai OFWs chase indie film spotlight
World.content:
Despite the demands of their regular jobs, these passionate Dubai OFWs pursue unpaid acting projects, with some even earning recognition at international film festivals

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Some 70 overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), whose day jobs range from hairdressers and grocery store merchandisers to office clerks, teachers, DJs, and finance professionals, have pursued their dream of acting on camera with the help of an award-winning Filipino indie director who brought them together and produced films for competition.

No one gets paid, including the director, and the films explore alternative themes seldom found in the mainstream.

“Cinema has never been simply about entertainment,” said Francis L.J. Gacer, director and founder of Kikoman Films (KMF), an independent production outfit. “It is about bearing witness.”

Francis, fondly called “Direk Kiko,” said he has been engaged in filmmaking for the past 10 years because “every Filipino has a story worth telling, and every voice deserves to be heard.”

And so the KMF, a UAE-licensed “creative sanctuary” for migrant artists where every talent can “flourish,” hopes to discover more experiences that “could become stories…voices [that could be heard on] the screen.”

The production house has been the go-to place of OFWs wishing to hone their acting talents.

Actor Ron Jordan de Ocampo Actresses Pamela Villadiego and Trixie Mae Tautuan

“I wanted to continue growing as an actor and be part of a community of people who genuinely love filmmaking,” said Pamela Villadiego, who works in the marketing department of a company while freelancing as a DJ.

“Acting has been part of my life since I was young, and being in Dubai didn’t make me want to stop. Instead, I wanted to find a way to continue telling stories and challenging myself as an artist.”

Pamela has won Best Actor in the American Golden Picture International Film Festival (AGPIFF), Southeast Asia International Film Festival (SEAIFF), and the Sweden International Film Festival (SIFF) for her role as a human trafficking victim in the 45-minute, true-to-life short film Alimbukay (Nausea). The film also won Best Psychological Film in the recent Emirates Film Festival (EFF).

“I have upcoming films this year, Sa Manlulupig and When Life Gives You Lemons, which we will shoot this month. Aside from acting, I’ve also been involved behind the scenes, particularly in production as camera woman,” said Pamela.

Gudelia “Lia” Rodriguez said she was just a curious bystander when she found herself playing a role.

“Acting has always been one of the things on my bucket list and I really thought it was a long shot, but here I am. Never did I imagine that a dream, at my age, may come true,” she said.

“I joined because it gives ordinary people a chance to shine, explore their creativity and discover talents they may not even know they have,” added Lia, who has been working in finance for the past 24 years.

Lia Rodriguez

Lia played a role in the award-winning horror film Batingaw, where she played the lead character’s sidekick. She also appeared as an extra in Alimbukay and in 100 Uploads.

“There are two lined-up films where I am part of this 2026 for scheduled shooting as well,” Pamela shared

Another artist, Trixie Mae Tautuan, works as an administrative assistant at a trading company. She has starred in three short films — Alimbukay, Sa Paghupa ng Unos, and Salamism — and remains busy shooting other projects this year.

“At first, it was not in the plan. A friend just had me tag along to an acting workshop. I tried it out of curiosity, and, at the same time, for experience since I’m fond of movies. I thought there was nothing to lose anyway,” Trixie said.

Also looking for something new to do on her weekends, hairdresser and makeup artist Jessica Leano Miranda replied to a KMF social media casting call.

“As I am an artist doing hair and makeup, I worked in an Arabic TV Channel here in Dubai years ago and I love watching movies, I got so interested to try it,” she said.

Jessica so far has two films under her belt: Tahan Tahanan, her first supporting role where she played a grandmother left to take care of a physically-challenged grandchild; and Batingaw, where she won an EFF acting award.

Jessica Leano Miranda KMF director and founder Francis L. J. Gacer

Amor Nano Matildo, a finance and logistics assistant at a manufacturing company for 16 years, said acting is one of her “passions in life” and a dream she hopes to conquer.

“I joined Kikoman Films because the films I’ve seen have meaning and sense, and also lessons,” she said.

Amor has played roles in four films last year: Bidyo-Oke, Remember Mercy, Paghupa ng Unos, and Tilamsik sa Dakilang Apoy. She’s busy shooting two films this year: Ang Dalisay and Reasong Razon.

Amor Nano Matildo

Ron Jordan de Ocampo, a supermarket shelf stocker by day, has likewise become a regular actor for KMF, playing roles in 12 films.

“Each project has given me valuable experience and helped me grow as an actor,” he said.

Becoming an actor was “already a dream” for De Ocampo, who has always loved watching movies, especially indie films, even when he was still in the Philippines.

One of the most intense films De Ocampo has appeared in is Tilamsik sa Dakilang Apoy, where he starred as a former New People’s Army (NPA) combatant who, having been afflicted with a medical condition in the hills, returned home to his wife and daughter.

In playing the role, De Ocampo won Best Actor at the Global India International Film Festival (GIIFF) and Most Promising Actor at EFF.

He also won Best Actor in two other films, Apo and Malakaya, at the World Film Carnival Singapore (WFCS) and the Gully International Film Festival (GIFF).

Ron Jordan de Ocampo

What started as a dream became a passion for De Ocampo, who met his wife at KMF.

“And now we have our baby girl, Baby Melon, who has also become part of some of our film experiences,” De Ocampo shared.

The actors said time management plays an important part in their task, as they memorize and practice the scripts after work on weekdays and shoot the film on weekends.

Since KMF’s inception in 2016, more than 25 film productions have reaped awards and recognition in various festivals in France, USA, Russia, Singapore, India, Turkey, Czech Republic, Spain, Philippines, Sweden, Italy, Hungary, and UAE, among others.

Direk Kiko, who usually comes up with ideas for the scripts, said 12 films are being lined up for 2027. He also supervises the acting workshops.

The director noted that plans are also underway to open KMF to non-Filipino talent, building on the six foreign members already among its 76-strong roster.

“Whenever I drive, I record my voice and speak of an idea for a story. Also, most of the time, I keep a small notebook and a pen in my bag,” said Direk Kiko, who also works as a producer and designer at a big retail firm. His superiors at the company support him, he shared, even attending last month’s KMF Gala Night.

“I still remember writing a script on the plane on my way back to Dubai from Saudi Arabia and the film eventually won awards in Kalayaan Independence Day celebration.” He also listens to nationalistic and progressive songs, the director said, “and from there, ideas flood me.” – Rappler.com

Some quotes have been translated to English for brevity.

World.title: How to know if you can trust an AI’s answer to your question
World.content:
It might be useful to sort AI answers into an ‘answer typography’ of four broad types: factual, interpretive, constructive, and strategic

I recently typed a simple question into Google search: How much screen time is too much for teenagers? Instead of presenting links, as Google had been doing for many years, it gave me an AI-generated answer.

The artificial intelligence agent cited a number, then complicated that reply, noting that quality and balance of time could matter more than the number of hours, and that “too much” time could depend on a teenager’s sleep, exercise, school demands and mood.

I tried another search: Should I take a daily aspirin? This time the AI answer presented me with medical information, warned about risks and offered more tailored guidance if I provided my age and medical history.

These were good replies. What interested me was that they were different kinds of replies.

Debate about AI answers has focused on accuracy: Did the system get the answer right? That matters, but accuracy is only one test. Each kind of answer requires a user to judge something different.

I find it useful to sort AI answers into an “answer typography” of four broad types: factual, interpretive, constructive, and strategic.

A factual claim can often be checked against a source. An interpretation can be accurate and still reflect choices about which evidence matters. A construction can be well reasoned and still be wrong for the person receiving it. A beautifully written strategic document may not be true. Yet AI presents all four types of answers in much the same fluent, authoritative form; the differences are easy to miss.

I’m university librarian and dean of libraries at the University of Virginia who leads national efforts to develop AI competencies for library professionals, and I consult widely on AI literacy. I first proposed the typography in the Journal of Academic Librarianship.

The four categories are not airtight boxes. A response from an AI agent can reflect several types. That said, I describe each type of answer below, and offer guidance for deciding whether a reply is ready to use or needs more investigation.

Which answer is Google giving you?

A factual answer makes a claim that can, in principle, be checked against evidence. When was the University of Virginia founded? What is the chemical symbol for gold?

To determine whether a factual answer is robust enough for you to use, verify the claim against an appropriate source. If the answer cites a source, follow that link instead of simply treating the answer itself as proof.

An interpretive reply is built on evidence, but there is not a single takeaway. How much screen time is too much for a teenager? Does remote work raise productivity? The answer depends on what evidence is included, what is left out and how disagreement is understood.

Google’s initial answer to my screen-time question indicated that two hours was a limit for teenagers. Then it noted that pediatric guidance puts more weight on the quality and context of screen use than on simple hours. The American Academy of Pediatrics says there is no exact recommended amount for teens and emphasizes the kind of screen use and what activities it might be displacing. A question that looked numerical turned out to require interpretation.

To assess interpretive answers, do more than check facts. Ask yourself what evidence the system emphasized, what it left out and whether another defensible interpretation exists. A useful follow-up question to present to the search engine is: “What is the strongest evidence for a different conclusion?”

Constructive answers are made rather than discovered. Ask AI to draft a cover letter, write a eulogy, suggest a lesson plan or reorganize a paragraph — there is no single correct result.

You can judge the response by considering purpose, audience and voice. A eulogy can be grammatically perfect and still sound nothing like the person delivering it, or it may land flat on family members hearing it. It may not capture the deceased person well, either. Consider these kinds of effects as you read.

Strategic questions ask what to do. Should I take a daily aspirin? Should I buy the house? The answers combine information with judgment about goals, risks, trade-offs and personal circumstances.

My aspirin search shows why context matters. Google warned about risks, told me to consult a medical professional and offered more tailored information if I provided my age, cardiovascular history and risk of bleeding. That caution matches the US Preventive Services Task Force guidance. It says the decision to start low-dose aspirin for prevention of heart attacks and strokes should be individualized and weigh cardiovascular benefit against bleeding risk.

For strategic answers, ask what the system would need to know before its advice could reasonably apply to you individually. Consider the stakes, the alternatives and whether a qualified person should be involved. For the aspirin question, a useful follow-up would be: “What details about my age, medical history or bleeding risk could change this advice? What should I discuss with my doctor before deciding?” The final judgment remains yours because you are the person who has to live with the outcome.

The first question after an answer

My questions began as ordinary Google searches. I did not open a chatbot. The AI-generated responses simply arrived, and links were appended.

The responses were useful. Google added context, acknowledged complications and offered tailored guidance if I supplied additional information. Within each response, though, the type of answer could change. Reporting what a medical guideline says is different from deciding how it applies to a particular person. A fluent response can move between those types of answers without a noticeable change in voice.

As a user, try to recognize what kind of intellectual work the AI agent did for a response you receive. Consider whether the interpretation is persuasive or the advice fits your circumstances.

Before asking whether an AI answer is right, ask a more basic question: What kind of answer is this? The type will tell you what to do next. – Rappler.com

Leo S. Lo is a dean at the University of Virginia.
