World.title: Australia begins campaign for seat at world's most powerful table
World.content:
Anthony Albanese plans to trade on Australia's good name and international reputation when he officially launches the campaign for a two-year term on the powerful United Nations Security Council.

Declaring Australia is "in a pretty strong position" to nab one of the two spots available, the prime minister will release the campaign video, brochure and logo — featuring the kangaroo — in New York on Monday, where dozens of world leaders are gathering for this year's UN General Assembly.

"Australia played a pivotal role in the founding of the United Nations — because we have always understood how important it is for small and mid-sized nations to have their voices heard on the challenges facing our world," he said in a statement.

"Our vision is simple: We listen with respect, we partner as equals, and we protect what matters most."

Campaigning under the banner, "We listen. We partner. We protect", Australia plans to leverage its position as a first mover when it comes to online safety and tech regulation, as well as its leadership on climate change, as this year's COP31 president of negotiations.

Anthony Albanese plans to highlight Australia's leadership on climate change in the bid for the Security Council seat. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

So far, only Australia and Finland have nominated for the two non-permanent positions on the 15-member council from 2029.

A secret ballot will take place in mid-2028 and, to succeed, a country must secure a two-thirds majority of UN General Assembly members, or at least 128 votes if all 193 members vote.

"We're in a pretty strong position. We're well regarded around the world," Mr Albanese told Insiders on Sunday.

Australia last held a non-permanent spot in 2014 and used the position to push for an international inquiry into the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 over Ukraine, in which 298 passengers and crew were killed, including 38 Australians.

The UNSC is responsible for maintaining international peace and security and seeks to mediate disputes using peaceful methods.

But it persistently faces criticism of its ability to handle global crises, particularly because Russia and China both have veto rights along with the other permanent members.

Mr Albanese acknowledged it was an institution in need of reform and needs to be made more effective.

But with ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, and rising strategic competition, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said having a seat at the table would give Australia the chance to advocate for a world governed by rules, not by force.

Penny Wong has criticised Vladimir Putin at the UN over the war in Ukraine. (Supplied: DFAT)

"A safer world is one governed by rules, not power and force alone. Australia's vision is a world where all countries have the freedom to decide their own future," Senator Wong said in a statement.

" As an active and ambitious middle power, we have a practical contribution to make to international peace and security. "

"There's a need for middle powers such as Australia to exercise the influence that we have."

World.title: Australian music stars pay tribute to John Farnham in special concert
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australian and international entertainers, from the past and present, have paid tribute to John Farnham in a concert raising funds for head and neck cancer.

Thousands filled Melbourne's Rod Laver Arena for the sold-out show, with many more watching around the country as the concert was beamed to select cinemas live.

The concert marks the beginning of the Lend Your Voice campaign to raise $1 million for Head and Neck Cancer Australia over the next year, with Farnham partnering with the organisation that helped support him through his own journey with cancer.

Farnham underwent a marathon surgery to remove a cancerous tumour in his mouth in 2022, and was given the all clear by doctors the following year.

John Farnham was unable to attend the concert personally, with his family reporting his health has declined in recent months. (ABC News)

Richard Wilkins served as MC for the evening, introducing what he described as a "cavalcade of supreme talent".

Wilkins said Farnham had sold out 94 shows at Rod Laver Arena over the years, the most of any performer ever.

"So I guess tonight makes it 95, an unbelievable 95," he said.

Farnham himself was not able to attend the concert, with his family confirming that the 77-year-old's health had declined recently, leaving him unable to take the stage at Rod Laver.

"John's health has deteriorated in recent months. He now requires continuous oxygen support and uses a wheelchair for mobility," the Farnham family said in a statement.

"It has also become necessary for John to receive 24-hour nursing care at home, ensuring trained support is always available when he needs it."

But Farnham was still a presence in the arena, with footage of his former sell-out performances beamed on screens as the musical numbers began.

Australian and international stars pay tribute

The concert began firing on all cylinders, introducing an all-star opening line-up of Jessica Mauboy, John Stevens, Jack Jones, Mahalia Barnes and Human Nature to sing a medley of Farnham songs, including the title track to 1988's Age of Reason, 1986's Reasons and 1996's Have a Little Faith (In Us).

A star-studded opening act including Jessica Mauboy and Human Nature got the night started off. (Supplied: Martin Philbey)

The Farnham clan was still represented onstage, with John's son Rob Farnham singing Love To Shine from the album Whispering Jack.

He thanked those in attendance, following his performance, and said his dad would be touched to see the turnout.

"We all know he's a little bit too humble for his own good sometimes," he said.

" To see all these people here would just absolutely warm his heart. "

Rob Farnham thanked the crowd in attendance for its support on behalf of his father. (Supplied: Martin Philbey)

The concert also paid tribute to Farnham's theatre career, including his 1992 turn in the title role of Jesus Christ Superstar.

His then co-stars Kate Ceberano and Jon Stevens performed Everything's Alright from the hit musical before sharing a hug onstage.

The night took a theatrical turn with Jon Stevens and Kate Ceberano performing a song from Andrew Lloyd Webber's Jesus Christ Superstar. (ABC News)

The crowd couldn't contain itself as Wilkins announced the next guest, saying he had flown in from Nashville, Tennessee to be at the show.

"Tonight, he is back home and he's all ours," Wilkins said as the crowd roared and Keith Urban made his way onstage, stunning the audience with his rendition of 1990's Burn For You.

Keith Urban gave a soulful rendition of Burn For You, which won the 1991 ARIA for Song of the Year. (ABC News)

The international guests kept coming, with Celine Dion beaming in from a stage in Paris to perform, apologising to fans in attendance for a scheduling conflict.

"John, you've always been such a deep inspiration to me; I always loved to hear you sing," Dion said.

"The way you sang one song in particular is one of my very, very favourite performances ever."

Celine Dion performed You're The Voice via simulcast from a stage in Paris (ABC News)

Dion said she sang this song as a duet with Farnham during her last visit to Melbourne and launched into You're The Voice, bringing the crowd at Rod Laver Arena to its feet.

The duets continued as Jimmy Barnes came onstage to perform When Something Is Wrong with My Baby, a 1991 track Farnham and he collaborated on, with Barnes's daughter Mahalia Barnes filling in onstage for John.

Father-daughter team Jimmy and Mahalia Barnes left it all onstage with their bluesy duet. (Supplied: Martin Philby)

Actor Hugh Jackman also performed via simulcast, sharing stories of sneaking in to see John Farnham do his sound check at the Perth entertainment centre as a youth, before singing the country-flavoured track Talk of The Town.

"I've been a fan of yours as long as I can remember. I have seen you at least 30 times live, and I would say you are one of the greatest I have ever seen onstage," Jackman said.

"The person I am onstage, the entertainer I am, is largely because of you."

Hugh Jackman credited John Farnham with helping him become the performer he is today. (ABC News)

The concert ended with all the stars from the evening returning for another rendition of You're The Voice, this time backed by 24 bagpipers.

Fans flock from around the nation for Farnsy

Leanne, who travelled to Melbourne from Tasmania for the concert, said she had plenty of tissues ready for an emotional evening.

Proudly wearing an autographed T-shirt, she said her whole house was filled with Farnham memorabilia, in tribute to a man who helped her during a health scare of her own.

"Years back I was in a coma, and my family said that the only thing I actually responded to the whole time was John Farnham music, so I'd kick my leg and tip my hand," Leanne said.

Leanne and her friend Yvonne were ready for the big concert. (ABC News)

Leanne said she had heard the news that Farnham would not be able to attend, and was hoping for the best.

"I think I knew deep down it was coming, but it's just been devastating and all we can do is pray that he's going to be OK," she said.

" He is our voice, he's always been my voice and he'll never walk alone. "

For some, just attending the concert wasn't enough to show their affection for Farnham.

Geelong residents Rob, Angie and Jo went the extra mile to unleash their best mullets and whip out the double denim.

For Angie, the trip to Rod Laver Arena was particularly special, as it was where she saw Farnham perform for the very first time.

"First ever concert when I was 13 years old was right here, 36 years ago, and I saw John Farnham," she said.

"I'm going to get teary already, it's already started … I plan to cry a lot."

Rob, Angie and Jo went the extra mile to show their love for John Farnham. (ABC News)

Angie owns a karaoke bar in Geelong, where the final song of the night is always You're The Voice, and she said the place was full of mullets and denim last night in preparation.

"All his songs, I get goosebumps now just thinking about it, his music has changed the hearts and minds and lives of people all over the world, why wouldn't we come and celebrate him?" Jo said.

Fans Kate and Jason travelled from Brisbane for the show, with Kate saying she has loved Farnham "so badly" ever since seeing him perform in Jesus Christ Superstar.

Jason and Kate made the trip from Queensland to be at the concert on Sunday night. (ABC News)

She said the fundraising effort behind the concert carried an even more personal meaning.

"My sister's had treatment for 17 years for head and neck cancer, and the work that field does is tremendous," she said.

"When I found out that the proceeds were going towards that, it just made it even sweeter."

Focus on raising awareness

Head and Neck Cancer chief executive Nadia Rosin said the organisation was incredibly grateful to Farnham and his family for shining a spotlight on the disease.

"They're cancers that affect the very essence of a person, it's obviously affected John's voice," she said.

Nadia Rosin says the concert is just the first step in a campaign to build awareness about head and neck cancer. (ABC News)

Spot check-up sites were set up at Rod Laver Arena, with concertgoers able to have their mouths swabbed and checked for signs of cancer.

Ms Rosin said a similar initiative at a John Farnham concert earlier this year in Melbourne to raise awareness about cancer was highly successful.

"We had dentists checking people for oral cancer," she said.

"We had about 300 people through in the space of an hour, and six of those people were referred for further investigation because of something suspicious in their mouth."

Ms Rosin said about 14 Australians were diagnosed with head and neck cancer every day, making the concert a crucial opportunity to raise awareness.

"If everyone can walk away thinking about oral cancer and head and neck cancer and having that on their radar, then our job will be done," she said.

World.title: Moscow faces 'largest ever' attack as Ukraine fires over 1,000 drones
World.content:
Ukrainian forces have fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, officials say, including what Moscow's mayor has described as the "largest ever" attack on the Russian capital.

Russia's Ministry of Defence said that its forces shot down 1,100 Ukrainian drones across the country on Sunday, as well as over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 450 drones had been destroyed en route to the Russian capital, and a residential building was hit.

The drone strikes killed two people in the Moscow region and two more in the Russian-held part of Ukraine's Kherson region, including an election official, according to Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin and election authorities.

A residential building hit by a drone strike in Sofyino, close to Moscow. (Reuters: Stringer)

Central Election Commission (CEC) chairwoman Ella Pamfilova said a drone attack on a civilian bus killed two people, including an election official.

The attack happened in a Russian-controlled part of the Kherson region in Ukraine, RIA news agency reported on Sunday.

In the village of Sofyino, south of Moscow, a body covered in a stained blanket lay in front of a damaged apartment block, the upper windows of which were blown out.

"Glass went flying; people started screaming and shouting. I turned around, and the entrance doors had already been blown out, debris everywhere," said resident Vitaliy, who gave only his first name.

Moscow oil refinery struck

A facility at the Moscow refinery was damaged in the attack, Mayor Sobyanin said, without giving further details, news agency Interfax reported.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the strike on the refinery in a post on X on Sunday.

Plumes of smoke rise from fires at an oil refinery following what authorities say was a Ukrainian drone strike. (Reuters: Stringer)

"One of Russia's key oil industry facilities and the aggressor's logistics facility were hit. These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine," Mr Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia's oil refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country's 11 time zones.

The Moscow plant, which has been targeted multiple times, processed 11.6 million metric tons of oil in 2024, producing 2.9 million tons of gasoline and 3.2 million tons of diesel, the latest available data shows.

In the wider Moscow region, in addition to the two deaths, 400 people, including 70 children, were evacuated from a 21-storey apartment block in the Ramenskoye district and a number of homes were damaged, said Governor Andrei ​Vorobyov.

A voter casts his ballot at a polling station in Donetsk, a Russian-controlled city of Ukraine. (Reuters: Alexander Ermochenko)

Russia enters final day of voting

The major attack came on the third and final day of voting in Russia's first wartime parliamentary election, with balloting virtually devoid of opposition to President Vladimir Putin's policies and all but certain to cement the Kremlin's dominance.

Behind his strongman image, Putin's world is shrinking To his supporters Vladimir Putin restored Russia's pride. His opponents describe a strategist, strongman, gangster and mafia godfather who is living in an increasingly shrinking world.

Mr Sobyanin said on Sunday that the "unprecedented attack" on the capital was an attempt to disrupt the elections.

"The enemy failed in this regard," he said.

Russia held voting in four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began but still does not fully control, and in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula illegally annexed by Russia in 2014.

Kyiv has denounced the action as illegal.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Watch and Act issued as bushfire burns in Victoria's Central Gippsland
World.content:
Central Gippsland communities have been told to monitor conditions as firefighters battle an out-of-control bushfire at Seacombe, about 42 kilometres east of Sale.

The CFA issued a Watch and Act warning on Sunday afternoon, "strongly" recommending residents in Golden Beach, Paradise Beach and Seacombe prepare to leave after a fire broke out on the Longford-Loch Sport Road.

It later added Dutson Downs to the Watch and Act warning.

In its 8:30pm update, the CFA said the threat had reduced, but residents should "monitor conditions and be ready to act" because "the situation can change at any time".

People were also advised not to travel to the area, and that it was "not safe to return".

Residents of Loch Sport were warned not to travel south along Longford-Loch Sport Road, while those west of the fire were told not to travel on that road toward Loch Sport, and instead to travel toward Yarram or Sale.

A CFA firefighter near an out-of-control bushfire at Seacombe. (Supplied: Candice Dockett)

Fire cause unknown

A CFA spokesperson said crews responded to reports of smoke about 1:20pm on the Longford-Loch Sport Road in Seacombe.

The fire, located south-west of the coastal town of Loch Sport, is burning in a south-easterly direction towards Paradise Beach.

By 8:30pm Sunday, 28 CFA vehicles were on scene fighting the blaze, while air attack support had also been requested.

The cause of the fire is yet to be determined.

Firefighters were called out to a blaze on the Longford-Loch Sport Road on Sunday afternoon. (Supplied: CFA)

Longford-Loch Sport Road closed

On Sunday afternoon, authorities said they had closed the Longford-Loch Sport Road at the Seacombe turn-off so that people could not enter the area, but said they were still free to leave.

They encouraged people to monitor the situation, including increases to wind speed or a change in wind direction, and to note that smoke or poor visibility can mean the situation is worsening.

A column of smoke rises on the horizon after the fire broke out. (Supplied: Gerard Walsh)

Earlier, a CFA spokesperson advised people in the affected communities to leave as soon as they were ready, "as roads will become busy".

"Those affected can travel to Yarram or Sale, or friends or family away from the fire," they said.

People are still being encouraged to leave the area if the situation changes or they feel unsafe.

As of 9:30pm, CFA crews were continuing to fight the blaze, and residents were advised to monitor warnings via the Vic Emergency site.

World.title: Alex de Minaur fires as Aussie pair clicks in Davis Cup triumph
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Alex de Minaur has returned to form to seal Australia's Davis Cup progression, with the hosts beating Poland 3-1 in Brisbane also thanks to some earlier doubles brilliance.

The world No.9 found top gear on Sunday at Pat Rafter Arena, beating Kamil Majchrzak 6-3 6-3 to clinch a 3-1 result that sends Australia into the Cup's penultimate round next year.

With his backhand and serve firing, de Minaur followed up his 57-minute annihilation of Maks Kasnikowski on Saturday with another therapeutic response to a disappointing second-round US Open exit earlier this month.

Earlier, Max Purcell's scintillating tiebreak tennis alongside rock-solid Rinky Hijikata swung their doubles match, and the tie, in Australia's favour.

The pair's 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 defeat of Jan Zielinski and Karol Drzewiecki followed the win and the loss posted in singles by de Minaur and James Duckworth respectively on Saturday.

Purcell, on the comeback from a controversial 18-month anti-doping ban, turned the match on its head after a tight first set progressed to an inevitable tie break.

He drilled a backhand return to win the opening point on the Polish serve, then produced a pair of aces to shoot the hosts clear 3-0.

De Minaur wins Davis Cup opener After a long and winding road to Brisbane in 2026, Alex de Minaur rides a partisan home crowd to an impressive victory in the first rubber of Australia's Davis Cup tie against Poland.

An unforced error from Poland was followed by two more Purcell winners, and he then held his nerve on a series of low volleys to eventually clinch the set.

Hijikata then held impressively and, after missing two break-point chances, nailed a forehand return to nab the match's only service break.

That was all Australia needed, with the composed pair energising the sold-out Pat Rafter Arena to secure a pressure-relieving victory in 77 minutes.

Australia's win followed a shock loss on the road to Ecuador earlier this year that plunged it into the must-win encounter against Poland.

The Aussies still need to win next year's qualifying round, against an opponent still to be decided, to progress to the finals in Italy in November, 2027.

AAP

World.title: 'Needle in haystack': Expert says little chance of finding shark that killed Greg O'Neill
World.content:
A behavioural biologist and shark drone expert has criticised the WA government's response to the state's most recent fatal shark attack, saying the chances of finding the shark responsible for a 63-year-old swimmer's death are slim to none.

WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis on Saturday took an "extraordinary" step of issuing a catch-and-kill order for the shark that killed Greg James O'Neill at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north.

Ms Jarvis said the decision was made under "the exceptional circumstances of the attack" where "the hazard posed by the shark" and "the potential recovery of coronial evidence" were taken into consideration.

Culum Brown is not convinced that the WA government will catch the shark responsible for Mr O'Neill's death. (Supplied: Culum Brown)

Culum Brown, from Macquarie University's Ecology and Evolution of Fishes Laboratory, said the chances of finding the shark responsible for Mr O'Neill's death were like finding "a needle in a haystack".

" The reality is that white sharks move a long, long way, they are literally on the move all the time … by now, that shark could be hundreds of kilometres away. "

The only way to determine whether a shark is responsible, according to Mr Brown, is to kill and gut it to see if it has human remains in it.

"So what are they going to do? Catch every white shark on the west coast until they find the one? I mean, it's a bit ridiculous."

The NSW government announced a further $34 million in shark-spotting drones this June. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

Mr Brown said he believed a better response would be to invest more funds in shark-spotting drones, an approach the New South Wales government took after a shark attack at Sydney's Coogee Beach in June.

"They [drones] are just a very highly effective technology," Mr Brown said.

Third person killed by sharks in WA this year The often-heated debate over how to protect beachgoers from sharks is likely to get hotter after the death of a third person this year.

"They are a lot cheaper than fixed-wing or helicopters … and one of the many benefits is that you can intervene before the shark attacks anybody and … there's no bycatch as there is with shark nets and things like that."

He said that it was a "win-win" situation for swimmers and sharks.

Ms Jarvis added that deploying more drones to spot sharks along WA's vast coastline was "absolutely under consideration".

She said the government would first review its current mitigation strategies — which focus on tagging and tracking, an app for notifications, warning sirens, shark enclosures and personal deterrents — to see what more could be done to protect beachgoers.

Body yet to be recovered

Mr O'Neill was swimming close to the Sorrento Beach shoreline when a suspected three-metre great white took him on Friday morning.

Authorities soon began a wide-scale search for his body and the white shark responsible, which they believed they had located before losing track of it.

The body of the 63-year-old is yet to be recovered.

Flowers are being laid to pay tribute to Greg O'Neill after he was taken by a shark. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) has set shark capture gear, a type of drum line normally used to tag sharks, about 1.5 kilometres off Sorrento Beach.

On Sunday, WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti said she "100 per cent" supported Ms Jarvis's response to the attack, including the catch-and-kill order.

"The minister made a decision based on advice. That advice was given by, as I understand, both police and fisheries," Ms Saffiotti said.

WA Greens healthy oceans spokeswoman Sophie McNeill earlier criticised the order, describing it as cruel and ineffective.

Ms McNeill instead called for more funding for shark-spotting drones and helicopters, and an expansion of the shark tagging program.

World.title: Hot, dry day ahead for Qld with unusually high temps in some areas
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Hot and dry weather is forecast for the start of the week across much of Queensland, with unusually high temperatures predicted in some parts of the state.

On Monday, some areas of the Darling Downs could see their hottest September day since 2017, according to the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM).

Maximum temperatures for Brisbane could reach 32 to 34 degrees Celsius on Monday, about 5 degrees above average.

Warm temperatures coupled with school holidays are delivering crowds to beaches across the Gold Coast. (ABC News: Emily Dobson)

The Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast will be spared that kind of heat, with both regions expecting a top of 28C. Bundaberg is headed for 29C.

While Toowoomba's forecast top is 31C, some areas of the Lockyer Valley could be among the hottest parts of the state, with highs of up to 36C forecast.

"We're expecting around 28 in Cairns, 28 in Townsville, 26 for Mackay [and] 32 for Rockhampton," BOM senior meteorologist Steve Hadley said.

Hot and dry weather is set to continue in north Queensland. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

In the very north, there could be cloud and shower activity, mainly north of Ingham.

Early-morning fog patches are forecast for eastern areas south of Cairns, clearing to a fine day.

To the north of Townsville, temperatures are expected to be average for this time of year.

South of Longreach may see temperatures about 5 to 10 degrees above the September average.

"Longreach is expected to be on a high of 36 degrees, Mount Isa on 34, and we could see some areas getting up to around 36 or 37 in the Channel Country," Mr Hadley said.

Fire warnings

Mr Hadley said there was a broadscale fire risk across most of the state, with dry conditions and elevated temperatures, especially in the south.

A high fire danger means fires can be difficult to control under some circumstances. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

"Places like Townsville, where they get regular sea breezes in that part of the world, you can see quite drastic changes through the day as temperatures warm up," he said.

"The winds then can change, and come in from a different direction in the afternoon as the sea breeze comes in and that presents challenges for people fighting fires."

On Saturday, firefighter crews worked through "extreme winds" to contain a grass fire beside Townsville Airport.

Windy conditions posed a challenge for firefighters in Townsville. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Station Officer Chris Maguire said crews had to work through volatile conditions to contain the flames and heavy plumes of smoke.

He said the grass fire was fast-moving, with challenging, windy conditions fuelling the flames.

Wind changes across other parts of the state are expected for the next few days, including sea breezes along the east coast.

World.title: Jim Chalmers flags fresh tax cuts, warns of ‘confronting’ news in economic outlook
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAustralian economy Jim Chalmers flags fresh tax cuts, warns of ‘confronting’ news in economic outlook Matthew Knott September 20, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has flagged a desire to deliver Australians a fresh round of tax cuts as he prepares to release a 40-year economic forecast that he warns will contain confronting findings about the nation’s future. Chalmers will release the seventh intergenerational report on Monday as the Coalition promises to cut fuel costs when global prices spike in a bid to appeal to voters concerned about the cost of living, a move slammed by the government as economically irresponsible. The intergenerational report, which forecasts how the nation’s economy and population will develop over the next four decades, will say this year’s budget lowered the tax burden on working-age Australians and it will float opportunities for further tax cuts. Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government’s decisions had created scope for future tax cuts. Alex Ellinghausen “Combined, the government’s tax reforms will rebalance the tax system and reduce the tax burden on workers,” the report will say, according to excerpts distributed by Chalmers’ office.



“By the end of the medium term, the share of personal income tax burden on workers is expected to be 2 percentage points lower than it would have been without reform. “Over time, this share is expected to fall further as an increasing share of property investment and capital gains will become subject to the new tax settings. “In addition, the government’s efforts to improve the budget position have created more room to provide further tax relief in future budgets.” Chalmers said: “People are under pressure, which is why we’ve delivered multiple rounds of income tax cuts, including tax cuts targeted specifically to workers. “At the same time, we’ve improved the budget position, which has created more room for tax cuts into the future. ”



This year’s budget contained a new tax offset of $250, to begin next July, and reduced the tax rate for those in the lowest tax bracket. Related Article Federal budget What six failed predictions taught Australia about its future Independent economist Saul Eslake said the prospect of more tax cuts was “plausible” but he said he was concerned that estimates of improved debt and deficit figures were based on “fanciful” assumptions of productivity improvements that were unlikely to be delivered. Chalmers told reporters on Sunday the report would contain some “confronting” findings and that it would show “that we are dealing with serious risks to our economy and serious pressures on the budget, but that we’ve got substantial advantages as well”. The report will reveal that the nation’s fertility rate will drop dramatically over the next 40 years. The government forecasts the number of children born to the average woman will decline to just 1.34 by 2066, down from 1.48 currently.



Fertility has remained below the replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman for about 50 years, leaving governments few options other than increasing overseas migration to fuel economic growth. Chalmers will say in his speech launching the report: “The world is becoming more dangerous, more unpredictable, more unequal and more divided. “These are not just individual threads but part of a bigger fraying of that intergenerational promise, of better times.” Excerpts released over the weekend show life expectancy at birth is forecast to reach almost 90 for women by 2066, up from about 86 years now, while life expectancy for men is expected to rise from 82 to 86 over the next four decades. The report will say that artificial intelligence will be the “defining influence” on the economy over the next four decades. Chalmers says the new tech will come with “very substantial risks”.



Related Article Population Australia’s population hits 27.9 million as newborn numbers dip Opposition treasury spokesman Tim Wilson said the government had attacked aspiration by scrapping negative gearing and cutting the capital gains tax discount for future investors. “Jim Chalmers is kneecapping young Australians before they get their first foot on the ladder of opportunity with higher rents and inflation outstripping wealth and wages,” he said. “Young Australians are already struggling to save for a home, invest and build something of their own. Now Labor is hitting them with higher taxes on housing, investments and small and family businesses. “No one believes the treasurer’s spin even if he repeats it 50 times over because Australians are living the biggest drop in living standards in the advanced world.“



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor on Sunday released a plan, called the fuel price shield, that would halve the fuel excise when the global price of Brent crude oil averages $US100 a barrel over two weeks, slashing around $15 off the average tank of petrol. “The fuel price shield would provide certainty. When a serious oil shock hits, the tax comes down automatically. When oil prices return to more normal levels, the ordinary rate is restored,” Taylor said. Chalmers rubbished the fuel policy as “uncapped and unfunded”, telling News24’s Sunday Agenda that the policy was aimed at winning back voters from One Nation. “I think what we’ve seen overnight from Angus Taylor is more about polling numbers than petrol prices,” Chalmers said.

World.title: Albanese takes AI fight to UN as Australia launches Security Council bid
World.content:
PoliticsFederalUnited Nations Albanese takes AI fight to UN as Australia launches Security Council bid Rob Harris September 20, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Australia will state its case for a seat at the world’s most powerful diplomatic table, with Anthony Albanese pitching the country as a middle power capable of helping write the rules for artificial intelligence as the US and China race for technological dominance. The prime minister will formally launch Australia’s campaign for a two-year term on the United Nations Security Council in New York on Sunday (local time), using the bid to argue that smaller and middle-sized nations must have a greater say over the global response to AI, wars and rising geopolitical tensions. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks at the Two-State Solution Conference at the UN in New York last year. Dominic Lorrimer Albanese also urged Washington and Beijing to help strike a global agreement on artificial intelligence akin to a nuclear non-proliferation treaty at the weekend, saying nations need international rules to ensure humans “remain in control” amid doomsday predictions. His call came as US President Donald Trump doubled down on the race for AI supremacy, declaring the United States must maintain its lead over China and announcing an “AI force” to guard against the technology’s “decimation or destruction”.



Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it “We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump wrote on social media, adding he would not “hinder or stifle” growth in the industry. Albanese told ABC’s Insiders he hoped there would be progress when Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House this week amid potential doomsday offerings in recent weeks from industry insiders. He said that middle powers could help bridge the gap between the major powers competing for technological and strategic advantage. “The truth is, they’re the big two giants here,” he said. “We want to see co-operation. We’ve seen that in the past with new technologies, even on nuclear weapons, for example. I think middle powers, such as Australia, have a role to play here as well.”



Albanese will argue that a seat on the UN Security Council would give Australia greater influence over conflicts including Ukraine and the Middle East, while allowing it to push issues including AI, climate security, ocean protection and international law up the global agenda. “The hopes of Australians are the hopes of people everywhere – to live in peace and to build a better future,” Albanese said. “Australia played a pivotal role in the founding of the United Nations – because we have always understood how important it is for small and mid-sized nations to have their voices heard on the challenges facing our world.” Australia will point to its previous Security Council term in 2013 and 2014, when it worked on issues including accountability for the downing of MH17, humanitarian access, women, peace and security, and international peacebuilding. It has had a seat on the council five times, including holding the first Security Council presidency in 1946, and two-year terms in the 1950s, 1970s and the 1980s. The Security Council has 15 members, including five permanent members – the US, Britain, China, Russia and France – and 10 non-permanent members elected for overlapping two-year terms.



Australia and Finland are so far uncontested for the two positions but still must secure two-thirds of members present and voting in the secret ballot. If all 193 countries vote, it would require at least 128 votes. Related Article Opinion

AI Albanese isn’t just betraying authors like me. He’s selling out Australia to AI colonists Richard Flanagan Writer The campaign will be built around the slogan “We listen. We partner. We protect.” A kangaroo features in the campaign logo and promotional material. Australia is seeking a seat for 2029 and 2030, with members to vote in June 2028. A campaign brochure also highlights Australia’s record in UN peacekeeping, saying more than 65,000 Australian personnel have served in more than 60 UN and multilateral peace and security operations since 1947. Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong said Australia had a practical role to play as an “active and ambitious middle power”.



“A safer world is one governed by rules, not power and force alone,” Wong said. “Australia’s focus on the UN Security Council will be conflict prevention, the protection of civilians and defending the rules that protect us all.” The government will also use Australia’s relationships in the Pacific and its role in climate negotiations to argue it can amplify the concerns of smaller nations, alongside its campaign on climate and ocean security. The campaign will also call for reform of the UN and uphold the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Albanese raised the need for international AI rules during his visit to California, where he met Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and the global technology giant’s executive team. “Australia’s national interests are served by us engaging, by us recognising that there are risks which need to be mitigated,” he said. “That is something that we will continue to pursue, and something that is common.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Don’t mention the football
World.content:
Lisa Clarke of Watsons Bay is “still waiting to use my high school German (C8) phrase of ‘Football? No. Lemonade? Yes,’ Although I’d much prefer the football.”

“I can sympathise,” says Ned Snow of Lilyfield. “About all that remains of my time in German class at school is ‘Ich kann meine Gummishuhe nicht finden’ – ‘I can’t find my overshoes’. I have to admit it hasn’t been very useful over the many years since.” You’ll get over it.

Marita Lennon of Enfield recalls a hot Christmas Eve in the 1960s, when, “as an 8-year-old, I was sitting in the back of our Holden, parked in a quiet Strathfield street. My mum and Aunt were yacking in the front when I saw the Bee Gees (C8) appear with another Bandstand performer (can’t remember his name). Suddenly, they stopped, sang a long note in harmony, then went up the steps of a terrace and rang the doorbell. Their mum (I assumed) answered the door in her apron and they entered. The screen door was still shut when they broke into Silent Night. My heart soared. Best concert of my life. Superb. It had to be because it stopped my mother chatting mid-sentence.”

For Genevieve Frederiksen of Roseville the encounter was with the other Gibb brother, Andy, performing at lunchtime at Santa Sabina College, Strathfield: “I remember the principal standing at the back with her fingers in her ears. When the bell went, she started filing everyone out, row by row, even though he was still singing. However, I decided to run backstage to procure his autograph because I thought that he was going to be famous like his brothers.”

There’s black humour, and then there’s Vicky Marquis of North Sydney’s mate: “I’ve just spoken to an equally old friend who has been to a tattooist and had DNR tattooed on each arm.”

World.title: Sydney Kings thump Cairns to launch NBL title defence in style
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Keanu Pinder was comfortably the Taipans’ standout, scoring 27 points at 65 per cent in his return to the league.

Kendric Davis was again the star for the Kings.

Superstar guard Kendric Davis, last season’s grand final MVP, starred with 26 points and six assists at Sydney’s Afterpay Arena on Sunday.

The Sydney Kings have made a great start to their NBL title defence, thumping the Cairns Taipans 111-90.

Cairns scoring machine Jack McVeigh was held to a paltry seven points, which was pivotal in the final result.

Pinder was everywhere early as Cairns, one of last season’s stragglers, ambushed the reigning champions with a 14-8 start. But once the Kings awoke from their early slumber, they were always going to be difficult to contain.

Sydney pulled ahead 32-26 at quarter time and maintained that margin when they led 59-53 at the long break, with Davis influential and new import centre Andrew Carr efficient.

The Snakes, living and dying from the perimeter, closed the gap to 69-65, before being dominated late.

Davis, Matthew Dellavedova, Makuach Maluach and first-gamer Will Johnston caught fire from outside as Sydney went on a 13-2 run and led 90-73 at three-quarter time, with Shaun Bruce waging a lone vigil for the visitors by that stage.

World.title: AFLW round six: Bombers beaten up at Windy Hill; Demons claim top spot
World.content:
Gold Coast’s band of youngsters have strengthened their grip on a third AFLW finals berth, beating Essendon by 41 points at Windy Hill.

The Suns have surprised many this season after starting the campaign as one of the more youthful and inexperienced sides in the league.

Their 7.9 (51) to 1.4 (10) win over Essendon on Sunday was their third consecutive victory and moved them into fifth spot, just four points behind second-placed defending champions North Melbourne.

Niamh McLaughlin racked up 33 possessions for the Suns in Sunday’s win. AFL Photos

Gold Coast’s defence was resolute in the blustery conditions, and the Bombers didn’t score a point until late in the second quarter.

In the same time, the visitors were dominating territory and snagged three goals courtesy of a trio of players all aged under 21.

After leading by 20 points at half-time, Suns forward Anne Hatchard and midfielder Charlie Rowbottom added their names to the scoresheet, before Emily Gough found the Bombers’ only major late in the third period.

The visitors grabbed another two goals in the final term to complete the win.

Defender Niamh McLaughlin (33 disposals, 506 metres gained) and Rowbottom (36 disposals, one goal) were busy for Gold Coast (4-2), while Hatchard and Havana Harris scored two majors each.

The loss kept the Bombers (0-6) winless, although midfielder Madison Prespakis was outstanding with a game-high 38 disposals.

World.title: ‘I am a proud man’: Hedge fund billionaire Crispin Odey’s fall from grace
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeHedge funds ‘I am a proud man’: Hedge fund billionaire Crispin Odey’s fall from grace James Warrington , Tom Saunders and Louis Goss September 20, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stooped about the witness box, Crispin Odey was barely audible as he was cross-examined by a lawyer for the City of London watchdog. The normally ebullient hedge fund boss, 67, was giving evidence as part of his attempt to overturn a lifetime ban from the Financial Conduct Authority. The hearing earlier this year focused on an arcane section of the watchdog’s rule book: whether Odey – who twice fired his executive committee before it could discipline him about allegations he “lacked integrity” – had acted “recklessly” and breached its rules. Hedge fund billionaire Crispin Odey failed in his attempt to overturn his lifetime ban from financial services. Michael Howard But everyone in the room knew the subtext to the proceedings: the hedge fund tycoon’s history of alleged sexual misconduct stretching back decades.



Perhaps it was the toxicity of these allegations that made Odey vacillate between proud and evasive when answering questions from FCA chief counsel Clare Sibson, KC. Asked later by the judge why he chose to close Odey Asset Management, his eponymous hedge fund, instead of trying to sell his stake, he responded: “I am a proud man.” ‘Mr Odey’s only purpose was self-preservation and to avoid being held to account for his behaviour.’ Financial Conduct Authority This defiance pushed Odey into an expensive legal battle with the London City watchdog – one that cast fresh light on repeated allegations of sexual misconduct stretching back decades. That battle ended in defeat for Odey on Monday. A court upheld a £1.53 million ($2.89 million) fine for the financier – reduced from an initial claim of £1.8 million – and a lifetime ban from financial services, ruling in favour of the watchdog of the City financial district.



The Upper Tribunal, which decides on appeals against the FCA, ruled in its favour, finding Odey had deliberately worked to frustrate an internal investigation into misconduct allegations, while showing “reckless disregard” for City rules. Related Article MeToo movement Famed hedge fund manager ousted in wake of sexual misconduct allegations It said Odey had “repeatedly prioritised his own interests at the expense of risk of detriment to OAM, its staff members and investors” while seeing “nothing wrong with his approach”. “Mr Odey’s only purpose was self-preservation and to avoid being held to account for his behaviour,” the FCA said. For many observers, the spectacle of Odey in court laid bare the other side of a man once lauded as one of the “sharpest and most contrarian brains” in the City.



Who is Crispin Odey? Odey was a rarity among his secretive hedge fund peers, enjoying an outsized and flamboyant public persona. Born to Yorkshire industrialists, Odey was educated at Harrow and Christ Church, Oxford, where he read history and economics. After graduating, Odey was handed control of the 1619-hectare Hotham Hall estate that had been in his family for centuries, but he soon sold everything off to settle his father’s substantial debts. After entering the City, he was briefly married to Rupert Murdoch’s eldest daughter, Prudence, but the relationship lasted just 15 months before they divorced.



Then, in 1991, he married Nichola Pease, a fund manager whose family helped found Barclays, creating a power couple often called the “Posh and Becks” of the City. The same year, Odey set up his eponymous firm, with backing from early investors, including billionaire George Soros. Crispin Odey at his wedding to Rupert Murdoch’s eldest daughter Prudence in May 1985. The marriage didn’t last long. AP During the ensuing decades, Odey became one of London’s best-known hedge fund tycoons, in part because of his astute ability to cash in on chaos. The hedge fund boss correctly predicted that the value of insurance companies would rise after 9/11, before pocketing £28 million in 2008 after successfully predicting the global financial crisis. The Brexit-backing financier gained further notoriety among political opponents in 2016 when he made £220 million by betting that markets would drop after the referendum result.



Odey has not been immune to failure. OAM, whose assets under management stood at $US13.3 billion at its peak in 2015, went through volatile shifts in fortune. One of his funds lost 44 per cent of its value in 1994. Undoubtedly, though, Odey has done well out of his bets. His pay peaked at £36 million in 2010 and he and his wife were estimated to be worth £775 million in 2019. In addition to his own fund, Odey held a significant stake in Sky, which he cashed in after its $US39 billion takeover by Comcast. Odey, who in 2010 threatened to leave Britain in protest against high tax rates, has complemented his financial gains with forays into politics. He made political donations valued at £1.7 million between 2007 and 2019. Some went to Boris Johnson and the Conservative Party. More recently, he donated to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. The majority of his donations were channelled into groups campaigning for Brexit.



Related Article Billionaires The $1.1b fortune of Rupert Murdoch’s former son-in-law is trapped Odey also captured the imagination with his wholehearted embrace of the rarefied world of Mayfair high finance. More than 1.80 metres tall and of ample build, Odey strikes an imposing figure. Known for his trademark City uniform of red braces, the financier has also been described as a “country gent”, whose passion for enriching himself was rivalled only by his enthusiasm for country pursuits, such as hunting and fishing. Nor has he shied away from displays of extravagance. He spent more than £130,000 building a Palladian-style chicken coop in 2012, nicknamed “Cluckingham Palace” by the tabloids, at his Gloucestershire estate, Eastbach Court.



The financier, who has a sausage named after him, was also notorious for his prodigious appetite. At one midweek meal with a journalist, he paired steak and kidney pudding and mash with a “side order” of a loin of beef and two bottles of wine. The “Posh and Becks” of the City: Crispin Odey and his then wife Nichola Pease outside Westminster Magistrates’ Court in London in 2021. Bloomberg Odey’s larger-than-life personality contrasted with allegations of a more menacing side. Media reporting and the lengthy dispute with the City watchdog have detailed incidents in which women were allegedly sexually assaulted. In one case, a woman accused him of rape, which he strenuously denied. His reputation earned him the nickname “the octopus”. The allegations first emerged publicly in 2020, when Odey was charged with indecent assault on a woman in 1998 after she accused him of groping her in his Chelsea home.



The trial, which came after the “Me Too” movement, gained significant publicity. The hedge fund chief was pictured leaving court clad in a mask and flanked by his wife. ‘Maybe I am a dinosaur; I cannot see how any of that can be sexual harassment.’ Crispin Odey Odey admitted propositioning the woman, then 26, but he denied assault. He was acquitted in 2021. The judge ruled there were “inconsistencies” in the woman’s account. Two years later, Tortoise Media and the Financial Times published investigations outlining allegations that Odey had sexually harassed or assaulted 13 women over 25 years. Odey settled civil claims from five women in May, weeks before they were to be heard in court.



The lawsuits include allegations that Odey raped a woman in the mid-1990s, an accusation he called “wholly false”. Odey also mounted a £79 million defamation claim against the Financial Times, but dropped it in April. The consequences have already rippled through Odey’s private life. He and Pease, who have three children together, divorced soon after his court case in 2021. Odey has since remarried Diana Vitkova, a Bulgarian-born finance executive 26 years his junior. Meanwhile, OAM collapsed in 2023 as major banks cut ties and investors pulled their money, forcing the company to start winding down its funds.



‘Playing the victim’ Odey mounted his challenge against the FCA ruling earlier this year, seemingly in an attempt to cling on to what might have remained of his status within the industry. Yet the hearings in the Upper Tribunal did little to repair his reputation, particularly after he failed to have the sexual harassment claims excluded from the case. By the end of the hearings, the FCA’s lawyers had accused Odey of submitting “false evidence” to the court and a “brazen” attempt to create a “false history” of events. “Mr Odey displayed a remarkable absence of self-awareness, was evasive, inconsistent, and had a tendency to attack others whilst playing the victim,” the regulator argued in submissions to the court.



Witness statements paint a picture of a working environment controlled by a domineering and at times abusive boss. Related Article Sexism ‘Indefensible’: The star-studded London club that won’t let women join Odey Asset Management, which was based in a five-storey Georgian townhouse in Mayfair, operated much like a feudal state, with Odey controlling 75 per cent of the fund. He had a reputation for reportedly hiring “earls and girls”, with women hired usually only as receptionists. The court heard claims that OAM was an “old boys’ club”, with documents suggesting that executives at the firm had “very similar backgrounds” to Odey. For a string of women at the firm, however, it went far further than a gender imbalance.



OAM commissioned law firm Simmons & Simmons to carry out an investigation in 2020 into its founder’s conduct. The resulting report detailed at least 46 misconduct claims against Odey dating back to 2003. The court heard one incident in which it was claimed Odey gave a female employee a massage before “groping her breasts”. He was then accused of trying to manipulate the woman “into silence”. The hedge fund boss has blamed his actions on a dental sedative he had taken earlier that day. A brass nameplate, with the Odey Asset Management name removed, outside the company’s office in central London in 2023, when Odey Asset Management was closing down. Bloomberg Yet this incident was described as part of a culture of “prolific sexual harassment” at OAM. As one of his former employees testified, Odey was a “sex pest” who found it “hard to control himself” around women. On the stand, Odey acknowledged staff thought he was a “creepy old man” but he defended his behaviour with female subordinates. “Maybe I am a dinosaur; I cannot see how any of that can be sexual harassment,” he said.



‘Evidence of gross misconduct’ After the damning internal report was published in 2021, OAM’s executive committee issued a final written warning to Odey regarding his behaviour. The court heard that it cut Odey’s pay by 40 per cent, after pressure from the FCA. It also banned him from physical contact with other staff members, excluding handshaking, and inviting or accompanying any female members of staff to events or shopping trips or contacting them by text or email. That summer a new allegation surfaced after Odey told a receptionist she should “take a lover”, the court heard, and then accidentally showed her an indecent photo of his girlfriend while sharing pictures from a fishing trip. The executive committee scheduled a disciplinary hearing in November to consider whether Odey had breached its final warning. But Odey acted first. On Christmas Eve, the tycoon sacked the entire committee – a move described by one witness as the “nuclear option”.



Odey subsequently decided that the disciplinary hearing into his conduct would be indefinitely postponed. He appointed new committee members, but after disagreement about how to proceed with the hearing, he sacked this board as well. Some of Odey’s former employees tell a story of bullying. Thomas Richards, a former OAM chief operating officer and a member of the committee, said the hedge fund boss had called him “f---ing spineless” and threatened to shut down the fund. Another executive said he felt “physically threatened” by Odey after recommending he work from home or take a sabbatical. Jack Satt, the firm’s compliance chief who resigned in the wake of the scandal, said Odey offered him £1 million and a future role as chief executive if he stayed on. There was no doubting Odey was a force to be reckoned with. The hedge fund tycoon even took an aggressive approach towards the FCA itself, at one point threatening to “go straight to the f—ing press”. For now, the City watchdog triumphed. The tribunal ruled against Odey, upholding all five of the FCA’s allegations against the hedge fund manager, including that he threatened the watchdog’s staff.



He has two weeks to file a further appeal. Instead of restoring his reputation, Odey’s appeals have only caused a deluge of allegations to resurface. FCA executive director of enforcement Therese Chambers said: “During the hearing, he reinvented history, painted himself as a victim and displayed no contrition. “That arrogant entitlement and the resulting complete disregard for proper governance means Mr Odey is unfit to work in financial services.” And, despite Odey’s claims to the contrary, it is a crisis entirely of his own making.

World.title: The AI app that Silicon Valley thinks is actually useful
World.content:
Analysis TechnologyAI The AI app that Silicon Valley thinks is actually useful Nick Bonyhady September 20, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last year, Open AI chief executive Sam Altman declared he used the technology pioneered by his company in “boring ways”. The uses he named, though, weren’t just boring but narrow: organising emails and summarising documents. For many customers, ChatGPT turned out to be better at writing bad fiction than life administration. One can only imagine Altman’s anger then, that a different AI company, Instinct, has stolen a march and introduced a bot that can complete basic life tasks. Sam Altman’s ChatGPT pioneered the AI bot category, but has proved better at creative, rather than menial, tasks for many users. Bloomberg One Australian technology investor showed this masthead screenshots showing how the bot repeatedly followed up a manchester company for a missing refund from a linen set he had returned. “We chase,” the bot told the investor, and it did. In another example circulating online, Instinct emailed a hotel in Canada on behalf of a user, had the concierge locate a missing Apple device, organised shipping and paid for the transaction with the user’s card.



On Sunday, this masthead used Instinct to find and buy a t-shirt from Everwear Denim, a small store in Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula, when a different store was out of stock of a similar model tee. Aside from the generally questionable decision to spend $88, plus shipping, on a t-shirt, the transaction shows the pleasures and perils of Instinct. Instinct AI founder Noah Shinn, as pictured on his plain text website. It was a seamless process. Instinct does not require an app to work; users simply text or WhatsApp a phone number. The bot replies with emojis to let a user known it is working on a task, and then follows up with brief messages, rather than the walls of meaningless text generated by Gemini or ChatGPT. It gave an indicative price when it first found the shirt, but only proceeded with the purchase when it had double-checked shipping and received a firm instruction to go ahead. Other AI tools can do this, but Instinct, as Apple co-founder Steve Jobs once said, “just works”. Yet to get the full benefit out of Instinct, the user has to be willing to let the tool act as their doppelgänger. That means granting full access to all emails, contacts, calendar appointments and a credit card. It’s even more powerful if you hand over logins for other online services, like an airline loyalty account or restaurant booking site.



In other words, all it needs is your entire digital life. What could go wrong? For the most part, nothing. But the Atlantic magazine has reported several cases of users reporting charges for restaurants they never agreed to book. In a demonstration of its capacity for strange behaviour, after Instinct bought the t-shirt for this masthead, it followed up with the non-sequitur “Anything you’ve been meaning to be more consistent about?” “That was a hard left turn after buying a t-shirt,” it admitted when questioned. “Ignore me.” The company users are trusting with such extensive personal information has a short history. It was founded in San Francisco by 23-year-old Noah Shinn last year, started testing its bot privately in February, raised $US250 million from investors at a $US2.5 billion valuation in August and, according to technology news site The Information, is now in talks to raise a further $US1 billion. That would make the less-than-two-year-old company worth $US10 billion. For now, the company is using some of those funds to subsidise its users because Instinct is available for free. Its website, which was so spartan until last week that it could’ve been built in 1996 and is still bare bones, advises curious visitors that signing up only requires a referral from an existing user. In time, Instinct will have to start charging. Whatever happens to its commercial fortunes, Instinct has made two major contributions to the conversation about AI.



Editor's pick Opinion

AI Why AI hasn’t taken your job yet Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer First, there has been discussion for the last few years about when the first one-man, billion-dollar company would emerge. Shinn has staff, so Instinct is not quite in that category, but it is such a young company that it must be close. It’s already too close to comfort for tech giants such as Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta and Elon Musk’s SpaceX that have launched the personal assistant tools Muse and Grok Bot respectively, and had their fanfare snatched away. Second, after a year of panic that big software companies were vulnerable to artificial intelligence creating knock-off versions for cheap, the markets calmed down in the last couple of months. In part, they concluded that the big software companies could incorporate AI into their products faster than their clients could put general purpose AI bots to work replicating their pricey IT tools. That calm now looks like it could be the eye of the storm. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.
